articles.title: Man who killed three during psychotic episode ‘had been released after catalogue of failures’
articles.summary:
Alexander Lewis-Ranwell was arrested and let go twice by police in the 48 hours before he killed three men in their 80s in Exeter

A man with paranoid schizophrenia who killed three people…

blocks.text: A man with paranoid schizophrenia who killed three people while experiencing a psychotic episode had been released from custody after a “catalogue of failures” by police and medical professionals, an investigation has found.

Alexander Lewis-Ranwell was arrested and released twice by police in the 48 hours before he killed Anthony Payne, 80, and the twin brothers Roger and Dick Carter, 84, in their homes in Exeter in 2019.

Officers were found to have ignored warnings from a national database as well as a mental health assessor, according to a joint investigation by the Sunday Times and BBC Radio 4’s File On 4 Investigates.

Numerous failings were found in hours of police video, detention logs and witness testimony. The medical professional who was sent to examine Lewis-Ranwell, 27, did not have expertise in mental health and dismissed his unpredictable behaviour.

There were also failures to record and share key details that would have built up a picture of the severity of Lewis-Ranwell’s mental illness. Officers did not know that by law they had the power to detain him under the Mental Health Act without a medical assessment. Warnings from Lewis-Ranwell’s mother, that he was having a psychotic episode and should be kept in custody, were also ignored.

blocks.caption: Alexander Lewis-Ranwell. Photograph: Devon and Cornwall police/PA

blocks.text: The families of the three men have called on the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) to open an investigation into Devon and Cornwall police, but they are still waiting for answers and an apology. The watchdog has said that the force should investigate itself, but they have heard nothing for two years.

Two days before the murders took place, Lewis-Ranwell was arrested after breaking into a farm. After his release he was arrested a second time for attacking a farmer with a 1.2-metre (4ft) logging saw. Despite exhibiting disturbing behaviour in custody – police bodycam footage shows him semi-naked, hissing, spitting and punching at the hatch window to his cell, while ranting about paedophiles and seeing animals – he was released again.
Following a rampage that lasted hours and in which he threatened multiple people, he killed the three men, bludgeoning Payne with a hammer and killing the twins with a spade.

A trial at Exeter crown court in December 2019 found Lewis-Ranwell not guilty by reason of insanity. He was given a hospital restriction order, where he will stay until agencies are confident he could be released back into the community.
One psychiatrist who studied the case told the court he believed Lewis-Ranwell, a former public schoolboy from Croyde, north Devon, was “one of the illest people” he had come across.
Last month an inquest found failings by police led to his release after a doctor missed “clear signs of delusion and disordered thinking”.
Amanda Taylor told the Sunday Times that her family was still seeking justice for her uncles the Carter brothers and that they want the IOPC to revisit the case.

“All I want is for just one of the agencies involved to stand up and say: ‘We are so sorry. Serious mistakes were made. We recognise the devastating consequences of those failures and we will do everything in our power to make sure this never happens again,’” she said.
Lewis-Ranwell’s case is one of several where failures from the police and mental health services to manage risk have resulted in tragedy.

A review by the Care Quality Commission of the treatment of Valdo Calocane, who has paranoid schizophrenia and killed three people in Nottingham in 2023, concluded that a “series of errors and misjudgments” led to him being discharged, despite repeatedly not taking medication and showing signs of aggression.
The report concluded that there are “systemic issues with community mental health care which, without immediate action, will continue to pose an inherent risk to patient and public safety”.
NHS England has since strengthened guidance around community mental health support for people with severe mental illnesses who face high risk or struggle to engage with services.

Noting that there are an estimated 100 to 120 mental health-related killings in the UK every year, Julian Hendy, of the victims’ charity Hundred Families, said: “In my view, had the lessons in the Lewis-Ranwell case been learnt earlier, and effective action taken, there is a real chance that the Nottingham attacks could well have been prevented. Services aren’t learning and totally innocent people are losing their lives as a result.”

A police spokesperson said the force was addressing “areas of learning” and would reflect on the recommendations of the inquest jury, adding: “Our thoughts, as always, remain with the loved ones of Anthony Payne and Dick and Roger Carter.”
The IOPC said the family had a right to ask for a review of the internal investigation and that it had not yet received a request.

articles.title: COP31 climate talks end without consensus on how to fund vulnerable countries or move the world away from coal, oil and gas use
articles.summary: After two weeks of tough talks, the COP31 climate summit has closed without a consensus on how to quit fossil fuels or fund countries struggling to adapt to a hotter world.

image.caption: Delegates gather around the COP31 president Turkey Murat Kurum. Turkey and Australia hosted what some say was the worst UN climate summit everImage: Khalil Hamra/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Almost two days into overtime, climate talks in the Turkish city of Antalya have collapsed as countries led by the European Union rejected a deal that critics say undermines the shift away from planet-heating fossil fuels.

After two weeks of tough negotiations, the EU said it could not support the proposed agreement, known as the Antalya Pact, put forward by the COP presidency, saying it does not respond to the science.

"We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time," said Irish climate minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU on Sunday.
He said adopting a decision that omitted fossil fuels would be "unconscionable" and risked "deepening the chasm between global commitment and the action required."

Panama also rejected the deal, describing it as a step backwards in addressing the climate crisis, and adding that any decision must acknowledge "the truth about the collective failure on 1.5 degrees Celsius [2.7 degrees Fahrenheit]." That is the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avert runaway climate change.
"Those who contributed to this crisis ... must shoulder the responsibility to deal with it," the Panamanian delegation said.
The Marshall Islands, which faces an existential threat from sea level rise, formally objected to the cover decision, saying "we will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests."

Russia, however, supported the decision to leave out wording on accelerating a phaseout of fossil fuels, arguing that they are still a necessary power source and that each country should be able to determine its own pathway on how to cut emissions.
Pakistan and Ghana, defended the agreement as a necessary compromise in the spirit of multilateralism. "We need to build bridges not barriers," said the Pakistan negotiator.
Deep divisions over climate finance

The marathon talks, held at a time when the window is rapidly closing to avoid the escalating impacts of climate change, including drought, deadly heat and flooding, also saw major disputes over financing.

Developing states blamed the collapse in talks on the EU and other wealthier nations for failing to scale up financing to help them adapt to climate-linked weather extremes and the damage they cause. The EU is the largest provider of climate finance and has resisted new adaptation finance targets.
COP31 talks run overtime as fossil fuel divisions deepen
Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign accused wealthy countries of demanding greater climate ambition while refusing to stump up the cash to pay for it.
"You can't ask developing countries to transform their economies while they're drowning in disasters and debt," he added.

The final cover decision had proposed further discussions on "an implementation pathway for tripling adaptation finance by 2035" but without mentioning a figure. It noted that developing countries need some $300 billion annually for adaptation until 2035, and expressed concern about "the gap between climate finance flows and needs."
Fossil fuel exit on the sidelines
Outside formal negotiations, a separate initiative to Transition Away from Fossil Fuels (TAFF) has been gaining momentum.

Maina Talia, Tuvalu's minister for climate change and the environment, said TAFF was "moving beyond debating whether fossil fuels are simply mentioned in a text, to creating detailed plans for a global transformation."

At the same time, a growing number of states, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany and Finland, have either completed or are working on so-called national roadmaps to wean themselves off fossil fuels.

But Brandon Wu, director of Policy and Campaigns ActionAid USA, dismissed such plans as "meaningless" and "nothing more than restatements of inadequate existing policy" on the part of rich countries not stepping up on climate finance.

"COP31 was one of the worst COPs ever, and it's because the EU and other developed countries came with zero spirit of solidarity, cooperation or compromise. They may as well have come to the COP shouting at vulnerable communities: 'we don't care if you die.'"
COP31: Can electrification replace fossil fuels?
The push for global electrification
The rejected cover decision had recognized that electrification can deliver emissions reductions, improve energy security and expand access to energy.
It included a call to increase the share of electricity in final energy demand from around 20% now to 35% by 2035 — a proposal heavily touted by co-host Turkey.

Still, about 75 countries, including solar powerhouse China, adopted the pledge outside of the formal negotiations. It is non-binding and does not specify whether that additional electricity must come from clean sources. Critics say this leaves open the possibility that expanded electricity demand could be met by fossil fuels.
Hottest ever climate conference

The talks in Turkey marked the first time a COP was taking place under the explicit knowledge that global temperatures will exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Countries were split on how to deal with that so-called "overshoot."

The cover decision had called on states to commit to limiting overshoot , acknowledging that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems.”
It also recognized the need for "deep, rapid ​and ‌sustained" emissions cuts and for action on ramping down potent greenhouse gas methane.
Maldives environment minister: 'We are not going to live in the dark'

Another contenious issue at the talks and in the final draft decision was a call for "increasing" carbon capture and storage technologies that entails capturing CO2 and burying it. The text said the world should aim to reach "gigaton scale" by 2035.

Scientists say some carbon removal technologies will be necessary to curb emissions and bring temperatures back down. But critics argue they are unproven at scale, expensive and risk giving polluters an excuse to keep burning fossil fuels.
Vanuatu's climate minister Ralph Regenvanu said carbon capture and storage "had been singled out for special attention that it doesn't deserve."
A year of extremes
The stakes were high at COP31. The summit followed a string of recent climate-related disasters, from deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people.
At the same time, geopolitical shocks that sent oil prices rising globally shifted the focus onto energy security and the future of fossil fuels.

Speaking near the end of the conference in Antalya, Ethiopian foreign minister Gedion Timothewos, who will preside over COP32, said his country aimed to "restore hope, rebuild trust and mobilize collective action" at the next summit to be held in 2027 in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa.

"We will work with you all to rebuild confidence in multilateral climate cooperation. This confidence must be earned through delivery. The decisions we take at COPs must advance climate action and implementation."
With reporting from Tim Schauenberg and Katharina Schantz in Antalya.

articles.title: The life, death and improbable rebirth of LA’s most beloved diner
articles.summary:
For decades, it served pancakes, hash browns and steaks to hungry Angelenos. Then came closure, and a city mourned – but now the Original Pantry is back

Sometimes, an old-school American…

blocks.text: Sometimes, an old-school American diner is just a diner. And sometimes, like the Original Pantry in downtown Los Angeles, it feels like the heart and soul of a city, a bellwether of good times and bad.

For decades it was famous for never closing. Located in a low-slung shotgun building on a busy corner, it fed politicians, movie stars, students, criminals and street bums around the clock, seven days a week. The doors had no locks, because the place had no need for them. The portions were huge, the prices dirt cheap, and many of the servers, in bow ties and white shirts, looked like extras from a Harold Lloyd two-reeler.

The diner survived speculative booms, depressions, an emergency relocation due to freeway construction, periods when downtown seemed to roll up its sidewalks at the end of the business day, and epidemics of homelessness, drug abuse and crime.

Long after the Pantry started to feel like a time capsule from another era – its Depression-era menu of pancakes, omelettes and steaks making no attempt to keep up with the evolving tastes of a global culinary capital – it clung on thanks to the determination of its businessman owner, Richard Riordan, who bought it during the Reagan era and went on to serve two terms as LA’s mayor.

Riordan wasn’t daunted when a 37-storey financial services tower sprang up on the next-door lot, or when a large corporate event space, LA Live, ate up much of the vacant land to the south and east. When the county health department forced the Pantry’s first closure in 1997 after finding dozens of minor food safety infractions, Riordan rushed over from city hall and worked the phones himself until his beloved restaurant, now dwarfed by skyscrapers, was back open.

blocks.caption: Richard Riordan at the Pantry in 1993. Photograph: Gary  Leonard/Getty Images

blocks.text: Still, the restaurant could not stave off decline forever. When Riordan died in 2023, the business was in a post-Covid funk it couldn’t shake, the staff was in an uproar over unpaid back wages and – the ultimate indignity – the kitchen had started making its once-fabled pancakes from a packaged mix.

It wasn’t long before Riordan’s heirs put padlocks on the door and had the police escort out the last of the workers, many of whom had worked there for decades. The local papers wrote obituaries, and Los Angeles plunged into mourning for another historical landmark run over by the relentless march of history.
And yet, this week, the Pantry has made the most improbable of comebacks.

blocks.caption: Diners enjoy coffee and danishes as the Pantry reopens this week. Photograph: MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News/Getty Images

blocks.text: It is no longer open around the clock. The hash browns no longer look like bricks that could feed a family for a week. But it is open once more, under new ownership and with a new mission as a nonprofit devoted to helping LA’s large homeless population. A dozen of its former workers have put their uniforms back on, giving the place much of its old flavor even as it seeks to define itself as something new.

“What I see,” LA’s mayor-elect, Nithya Raman, said at a raucous, packed opening ceremony on a rain-swept Thursday morning, “is a room full of people who never gave up hope.” Since the Pantry has no liquor license, everyone raised coffee mugs instead.

To the many fans who either attended with an invitation or stood in line in the pouring rain for a chance to be among the first ordinary diners to place their orders, the Pantry’s reopening carries symbolic weight for the city as a whole. Restaurant union leader Kurt Peterson called it “one of the great Los Angeles love stories” – the romantic notion that in one spot, at least, all distinctions between the city’s haves and have-nots melt away like butter in a pan.

blocks.caption: The Pantry’s neon sign in this 2015 picture. Photograph: Bob Berg/Getty Images

blocks.text: The turnaround at the Pantry comes after a painful couple of years in which two foothill neighborhoods were wrecked by wildfires, the cost of living has soared, thousands remain homeless, immigration raids have torn apart families and communities, and retail businesses – including restaurants – have shuttered faster than new ones have been able to take their place.
“Hopefully, this is a sign that the doom loop is finally reversing,” said the Pantry’s new owner, Ukrainian American businessman Leo Pustilnikov.

Such optimism might have been less warranted if Pustilnikov had wanted to run the Pantry as a conventional business. Instead, he decided the only money-making part of the venture would be a digital billboard on the roof. For the restaurant itself, he turned to a local homelessness services provider called Hope the Mission and offered a roughly 50% break on the rent if in exchange they would bring the Pantry back and commit to ploughing any profits into helping homeless people get back on their feet.

blocks.caption: Nithya Raman, the newly elected mayor of Los Angeles, at the reopening on Thursday. Photograph: MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News/Getty Images

blocks.text: It was not a difficult sell. “Pancakes with a purpose,” was how Hope The Mission’s founder, Ken Craft, saw the concept, and he set about raising more than $1m to replace the Pantry’s ageing kitchen equipment, update the tables and chairs so they would no longer be sticky with chewing gum and bacon grease, replace the black-and-white checkered floor, and rethink the menu for a city more cosmopolitan and eclectic than it was on opening day in 1924.

The Pantry still looks like its old self, with pictures of Marilyn Monroe and Humphrey Bogart on the wall, an old taxi phone, and a cashier’s cage taking up pride of place near the front door, even though the restaurant mostly uses hand-held credit card machines. The new operators have also left an area in front of the cage, an archeological showcase of sorts, where customers over the decades wore through 12 layers of flooring.

The eggs and hash browns no longer land like bowling balls in the diners’ stomachs but come gently crisped on the edges. In a nod to LA’s multiculturalism, there are poblano chilis in the Denver omelette and Korean pickles in the coleslaw. For the first time, the Pantry now has an in-house baker producing a vanilla-bean cheesecake and a chocolate crunch cake that taste refreshingly light.

Unlike many American cities, which have slowly lost their fabled delis and diners, LA has a track record of putting up a fight whenever its culinary history is on the line. A similarly storied establishment, Cole’s, which once played host to Hollywood’s most notorious gangster, Mickey Cohen, and claims to be the home of an LA special, the French dip sandwich, had its own reopening after a threatened closure earlier in the week.

blocks.caption: People outside the Original Pantry Cafe for its grand reopening. Photograph: MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News/Getty Images

blocks.text: Langer’s Deli, the only fully unionized restaurant in town aside from the Pantry, has been making noises about giving up because of drug and crime problems around its MacArthur Park home, but its customers have so far successfully pleaded to keep the doors open.

For Raman, who is eager to turn the page on Karen Bass’s unpopular single term as mayor and prove, once she takes office next month, that she can enact tangible change, the Pantry is a feelgood story too good not to latch on to. During her election campaign she visited twice and promised, if elected, to issue an executive order declaring that the Pantry serves “the best damned pancakes” in town.

Hope the Mission’s staff tried to hold her to that on Thursday – she smiled and shrugged when it came up – but her presence alone was a gift to a restaurant seeking to put itself back on the map. Along with Raman, the festivities attracted the city council member for downtown, a county supervisor and a former mayor.

“Our city is crying out for a comeback story,” said Rowan Vansleve, Craft’s deputy at Hope The Mission. And he made a vow of his own: that the Pantry, if successful, would go back to opening around the clock.
“If people can come back in the wee hours and have a slice,” he said, pointing to the chocolate cake, “LA will be back.”

articles.byline: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez, Emmy Sasipornkarn, Nik Martin, Dmytro Hubenko, Patrick Große, Mark Hallam, Karl Sexton

image.caption: Despite weeks of talks and an extension, a deal has remain elusiveImage: Khalil Hamra/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: November 22, 2026
COP31 fails to agree climate deal amid fossil fuel rift

blocks.caption: Weeks of tense negotiations have failed to yield a dealImage: Murad Sezer/REUTERS

blocks.text: The COP31 climate summit has failed to agree on a final joint declaration.
During a plenary session, the summit's Turkish president acknowledged there would be no climate deal.

"I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted," Murat Kurum, who is also Turkey's environment minister, told a closing plenary in the Mediterranean city of Antalya.

The rift centered on whether to include the phaseout of fossil fuels in the final declaration. Scientists say the burning of fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas is the main cause of global warming.
European nations, smaller island states and climate activists have criticized oil-producing countries for the omission.

articles.title: ‘Just wrong’: British right distances itself from Trump after Putin ‘friend’ post
articles.summary: Reform deputy leader calls Russian leader ‘a murderous dictator’ after US president appears to endorse him

blocks.text: Reform UK and the Conservatives have distanced themselves from Donald Trump after the US president posted a photo of himself shaking hands with Vladimir Putin with the caption: “My friend.”

The US president had already used the term to describe the Russian president while at last week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, southern China, where he also met the Chinese president, Xi Jinping.

But the photo with Putin, showing Trump leaning towards the Russian leader to talk to him as they met at the summit, posted by Trump on his Truth Social platform overnight, prompted condemnation in the UK.
Asked for his reaction, Richard Tice, the deputy leader of Reform UK, the British party most closely associated with Trump, replied: “Horror.”
He told Sky News: “It’s just wrong at every level … And it’s a grave mistake. He is not our friend, Putin. He is, as others have said, a murderous dictator. And no one is in any doubt about that.”

Asked whether Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, who is a friend of Trump, would speak to the US president about this, Tice replied: “Oh, there have been a number of occasions where one could agree with Trump, and then disagree with him.

“There have been more occasions recently when clearly we have disagreed with him and said so very explicitly. And in a sense, that’s the nature of long friendships. Sometimes you’ll agree and sometimes you’ll disagree. And, I think the disagreements are growing.”

blocks.caption: Nigel Farage speaks during a Trump rally at Goodyear airport in Phoenix, Arizona in October 2020. Photograph: Rick D’Elia/EPA

blocks.text: Reform and the Conservatives under Kemi Badenoch, both of whom welcomed Trump’s re-election in 2024, have increasingly tried to dissociate themselves from the US president amid questions over his temperament and judgment, while his attacks on Iran have driven up global energy prices.

Polling last month for YouGov found that just 10% of British people have a favourable opinion of Trump, with 86% holding an unfavourable view. Asked about the “My friend” post, Alex Burghart, Badenoch’s deputy, said he was “very sad” about it.

He told Sky News: “I’m sad and I’m depressed, because the world that I grew up in was one in which the United States was a defender of freedom. I worry that we might be moving into a world where that isn’t the case any more.”
after newsletter promotion

Asked about his party’s previous support for Trump, Burghart replied: “If you look at what the Conservative party is proposing in terms of defence and foreign policy, it’s very clear that we are still on the side of freedom, and we’re the party that has said that we will put up defence spending to what Nato wants it to be.

“So I think you can trust Kemi Badenoch and the Conservatives on this. But, I very much hope that we don’t enter a world in which large, aggressive powers feel that they can occupy their neighbours and get the approval of the United States.”
When asked about the Trump post, Hamish Falconer, a Foreign Office minister, called Putin “a butcher” and said Andy Burnham would make the UK’s views known.

Falconer told Sky News: “The prime minister speaks to the president regularly and is in absolutely no way pulling his punches about the strength of feeling that the UK has as a whole about Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.”

articles.title: CEO of funding agency for UK science and research criticised by union over cuts
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Prospect’s Mike Clancy tells Ian Chapman at UKRI that union has ‘lost confidence’ in his leadership

A trade union that counts scientists and engineers among its members says it…

blocks.text: A trade union that counts scientists and engineers among its members says it has lost confidence in the leader of the UK’s national funding agency for science and research, citing concerns about plans for major cuts.

The letter from Mike Clancy, the general secretary of Prospect, to Ian Chapman, the chief executive of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), is the latest development in a row over changes in funding for projects and research facilities.
“Writing to a CEO in this tone and to this intent is an extraordinary step for this union to have to take,” Clancy wrote.
He warned: “Whilst there are legitimate cost pressures facing UKRI, ultimately any cuts will reduce the UK’s national science capability at a time when it is most needed.”
This year the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC), the government’s infrastructure funding agency, which is part of UKRI, revealed it needed to make £162m in savings by 2030.

While the core budget of the STFC remains broadly flat at about £835m a year, it is under financial pressure as a result of several factors. These include soaring energy costs at its national facilities, increasing staffing costs, an expanded portfolio of activities and “unfavourable movements” in foreign exchange rates. The last has resulted in an increase in costs relating to international facilities such as Cern.

blocks.caption: The future of Jodrell Bank Observatory is at risk.  Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

blocks.text: As a result, in July UKRI released a plan to balance the STFC’s budget by 2030, revealing research projects and national facilities are to face significant changes.

“As responsible custodians of public funds, which I very much view our job is to be, we have to make sure that our costs are in line with our budget and that we don’t overspend the budget available to us,” Chapman said at the time, adding that it was important to prioritise spending in areas that made the biggest scientific impact.

The future of the UK’s largest telescope at the Jodrell Bank Observatory in Cheshire has been put at risk, while the Diamond Light Source, the Central Laser Facility and the Isis Neutron and Muon Source, all in Oxfordshire, will remain operational but have been told to make efficiency savings.
The Clara facility in Cheshire – one of the world’s most advanced medium-energy electron beam facilities, which develops and tests next-generation accelerator technologies – is to be mothballed.

Clancy wrote in his letter to Chapman: “Our members working at UKRI do vital work which puts our country at the cutting edge of scientific developments and industrial applications and has considerable benefits across high-growth sectors, as well as in medical research and treatment. To pause or ‘mothball’ funding for many of the facilities where they work is to risk permanently losing the expertise that underpins the sector.”

The opening of a voluntary exit scheme to UKRI employees was also flagged by Clancy, who said the scheme was launched in parallel with the STFC cuts and without the requisite consultation on the organisational change plan with the recognised trade unions. His letter urges a pause to enable proper consultation and evidence-gathering on the cuts’ potential impact.
“In the absence of our requests leading to any productive engagement, we have lost confidence in your position as CEO,” Clancy wrote to Chapman.

blocks.caption: The Diamond Light Source, at the Harwell science and innovation campus in Oxfordshire, produces intense beams of light for scientific research. It has been told to make efficiency savings.  Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian

blocks.text: Prof Leszek Borysiewicz, the chair of UKRI, said the board had full confidence in Chapman and his leadership team.

“We support the direction of the ambitious reform programme UKRI is undertaking to become more effective, agile and better able to respond to the country’s priorities and needs,” Borysiewicz said. “Delivering transformation on this scale is a substantial undertaking involving difficult decisions about how UKRI operates, where resources are focused and how we deliver the greatest impact.

“UKRI has been clear with staff and unions about the direction of change, including its new mission and funding model, greater join-up across programmes and the unification of professional services. The decisions announced this year followed extensive engagement with staff, research and user communities, alongside detailed consideration of the impacts of different funding choices.”

The science minister, Chris McDonald, said: “I have full confidence in Ian Chapman’s leadership of UKRI. The organisation’s ongoing and essential transformation programme will ensure projects supported through our record £86bn commitment to R&D will deliver maximum impact and value for money – as the British public rightly expect.

“I know from personal experience that this transformation will have a significant and personal impact on workers and others affected, and we will continue to engage the UKRI workforce. I am committed to working closely with UKRI, the workers, and their trade unions as we continue to progress the transformation plan.”

articles.title: They went out to celebrate at a Memphis bar. Then, ICE descended
articles.summary:
More than 120 people in the Tennessee city were detained in one of the largest single-day ICE raids in the US in 2026

The date 1 September, or 9/01 Day, is a festive day for Memphians. The…

blocks.text: The date 1 September, or 9/01 Day, is a festive day for Memphians. The date mirrors the city’s 901 area code, and gives residents a reason to come together to celebrate the city and the people who love it. When 9/01 Day falls on a weekday, as it did this year, the celebration starts the weekend prior, extending the festivities. Groups across the city hosted celebrations featuring food vendors, DJs, musicians and members of the Memphis Grizzlies, the local NBA team, while dozens of local businesses offered $9.01-themed specials.

But for the families of 121 people, this past 1 September will be remembered for a different reason – just days prior, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers detained their friends and relatives, conducting one of the largest single-day raids in the country this year, and the largest known one in Memphis.

On Beale Street during the 9/01 Day celebration, a 9 year old child, Valentina*, stood solemnly, holding a sign that read: “ICE took my mom!” (*The Guardian is using a pseudonym to protect the child and her family’s identity.)

On 30 August, Valentina’s mother and sister had both been at work at El Corralón, a bar on the edge of Memphis’ Berclair neighborhood, which is primarily Hispanic. Valentina went to sleep anticipating celebrating her birthday with family and friends the next morning. Instead, she awoke to the news that her family members were among the 121 people who were detained by ICE.

blocks.caption: A girl holds a sign during a protest in Memphis on 30 August 2026. Photograph: Erika Konig/Institute for Public Service Reporting

blocks.text: According to reports, more than one dozen agents entered the building that night, and quickly spread across the bar. They turned off the music and ordered those inside to gather on the dancefloor. Some people screamed; others attempted to hide. Some prayed.

El Corralón had been under investigation by the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation (TBI), which had a warrant signed on Wednesday of the week leading up to the raid, to search the premises for illegal gambling machines and potential drug activity. Saturday, when the nightclub was full of patrons, TBI executed the warrant. One by one, agents asked people if they were in the country legally. People were zip-tied, taken outside and led onto buses that waited to take them to detention centers.

A statement released by the Department of Homeland Security shortly after the raid highlighted five of those arrested, whose crimes, the department alleges, range from cocaine possession to assault, prostitution and child endangerment. Maria Oceja, a co-founder of Vecindarios 901, a volunteer group that monitors the actions of the Memphis Safe taskforce, said the raid predominantly targeted innocent people. “This is just another example of that rising level of authoritarianism and white supremacist tactics that we’re seeing,” Oceja said.

El Corralón, which has been closed since the raid, had a “juke joint environment”, she said. Spanish language music blared and working class people could have a drink on a Saturday night. Many of the workers and patrons were parents. The morning after the raid, Hunter Demster, a co-founder of Vecindarios 901, said Valentina’s family tried to figure out next steps. “Her mom was a breadwinner and worked three different jobs trying to keep food on the table and the utilities paid,” Demster said. He’s friends with Valentina’s older sister, Camila, who is now responsible for her younger siblings. “Now her entire family is devastated. When I went over there the next day, I asked her, ‘What do you need?’ The sorrow and almost the vacancy in her eyes was jawdropping. The pain was palpable.

blocks.caption: People are arrested in a raid on El Corralon in Memphis on 30 August 2026. Photograph: Vecindarios 901

blocks.text: “These are our friends and our neighbors and for every one of those 121 people, there’s another family going through that exact same thing. They’re figuring out how they’re going to navigate life without a loved one. It is a gutwrenching, horrible, traumatic experience for a family member.”

For days after the raid, no one knew where the girls’ mother was. Eventually, volunteers learned she was being held in a detention center in Louisiana, Gisela Guerrero, lead organizer for Memphis Interfaith Coalition for Action and Hope (Micah), said. “A lot of immigrant children right now, regardless of their age, are very clear about the possibility of their parent being taken away any day. It’s scary. It’s overwhelming,” she told the Guardian.

An ICE spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian that the agency does “not pick and choose which laws to enforce or where to enforce them”. The spokesperson said that the detainments make “the Memphis community safer”. According to the agency, 69 of the 121 have been removed from the country. “The rest will remain in ICE custody pending their immigration proceedings, and they will receive due process,” the statement read.

On the night of the raid, portions of the street were blocked off by federal agents according to Dexter Britt, a volunteer and co-chair for the immigration and inclusivity team with the Micah who made it to El Corralón, shortly after 1am. He saw the Memphis police department (MPD), sheriffs, state troopers and other personnel, he said. Buses and vans idled, waiting to be filled with people who were detained.

blocks.caption: Protesters march outside of the CoreCivic operated West Tennessee detention facility on 2 September 2026. They stood in solidarity with what they say were over 400 detainees taking part in a hunger strike. Photograph: Brad Vest
The Memphis bar El Corralón has been closed since the September ICE raid. Many of the workers and patrons were parents. Photograph: Brad Vest

blocks.text: Britt said that there were also community members observing and documenting what was happening. He saw family members, including children, who were there to catch a glimpse of their relatives, perhaps for the last time. “You start seeing people getting ushered out of the building,” Britt told the Guardian. “I remember hearing the chains shackling as they were loading people into the vans, into the buses. It was very harrowing to hear.”

The Memphis mayor, Paul Young, issued a statement saying that MPD was not involved in the planning or execution of the raid. Instead, he said, they assisted with crowd and traffic control after people began gathering in the area. According to witnesses, multiple agencies – TBI, Tennessee Highway Patrol, and ICE – seemingly worked in conjunction with each other.
‘Here to intimidate’

On 15 September 2025, Donald Trump signed a presidential memorandum creating the multi-agency Memphis Safe taskforce. The initiative, which includes the national guard, highway patrol officers, and agents from more than federal agencies, began operating in the city on 29 September. Though the memorandum establishing the taskforce alleged that Memphis was “suffering from tremendous levels of violent crime that have overwhelmed its local government’s ability to respond effectively”, crime in the city was at a 25 year low prior to the taskforce’s arrival.

In the year since it began operating, members of the taskforce have killed four people, all Black men, including 20-year-old Tyrin Johnson who was fatally shot in the back. A woman was killed after being ejected from a vehicle when it crashed while being pursued by members of the Memphis Safe taskforce. Five young people were killed in a crash involving the MPD and a man died during a traffic stop by members of the taskforce. An analysis by the Institute for Public Service Reporting Memphis identified 75 vehicle pursuits over the taskforce’s first five weeks of operation.

According to the Tennessee Lookout, immigration arrests and detentions multiplied nearly four-fold in Tennessee during Trump’s first year back in office. Weeks after the Memphis Safe taskforce was created, more than 400 people were arrested. The taskforce has made nearly 23,000 arrests, 64% of which were for non-violent crimes. A growing number of businesses are calling for an end to the taskforce’s operations in the city, while others are mobilizing to document its actions. “It’s not just impacting immigrant communities who are Latino or Hispanic, but it’s also impacting Black Memphians because the city is majority Black,” Britt said. “There’s a lot of harm being done to the Memphis community because of the presence of these agents who are really just here to intimidate.”

blocks.caption: Local police at the scene of a raid on a nightclub in Memphis on 30 August 2026. Photograph: Vecindarios 901

blocks.text: The El Corralón raid happened the same weekend that people detained at a detention center in Macon, Tennessee, protested “deplorable conditions” and abusive tactics inside” the facility. Some of those detained at El Corralón were initially sent to the center in Macon.

In mid-October, the US attorney general, Todd Blanche, and federal and state leaders visited Memphis to discuss the taskforce. Unlike similar operations in Minneapolis or Chicago, which had intense surges that lasted a few months, there is no end date to the Memphis Safe taskforce’s occupation of the city. Though Blanche celebrated the taskforce’s record and presence, he said that it would be in the city “as long as it takes. We haven’t won yet. It’s not over”.

On 20 October, the Memphis City Council passed a resolution calling for the removal of the taskforce. The non-binding resolution said that the El Corralón raid raised “concerns about due process and the impact of federal immigration enforcement on local communities, including the disruption and separation of Memphis families”.

“Memphis is literally an occupied city with law enforcement agencies all doing immigration work, causing real harm to the city of Memphis,” Demster said of the taskforce. He said that people are afraid to leave their homes. “This is un-American. They’re violating people’s rights by not giving them due process. They’re criminalizing people when they have done nothing wrong. This is the beginning of fascism. This is the beginning of a dictatorship.”
Filling the gap

On 31 August, photos of Valentina holding her sign and mentioning her birthday were posted across social media. Demster and other volunteers purchased a birthday cake and presents and dropped them off for the child. “In the midst of such horror, at least it put a smile on that baby’s face,” he said. “She literally hugged the cake. ‘Devastating’ doesn’t measure up to what people are experiencing at this point … . It’s just another example of how they’re not out for the worst of the worst. They are out for people with brown skin.”

Vecindarios 901, Micah, Indivisible Memphis, Latino Memphis, TIIRC, World Relief and organizations collaborated to see how they could support the families. In the week following the raid, many of the organizations met with families of detainees to help connect them with legal aid and other resources.

blocks.caption: People packed into Tuesday’s regularly scheduled Memphis city council meeting on 15 September 2026 to protest the recent ICE raid in the city. Photograph: Brad Vest

blocks.text: “We had a seven-year-old who was saying, ‘I don’t think I’m going to see my mom anymore,’” Guerrero said. “We had a 14-year-old who was trying to figure out what he needed to do to be responsible for his younger siblings. We had a senior in college who’s trying to figure out how he is going to pay tuition. Because his parents, hardworking people, are now detained.”

Guerrero said that about 100 people from various families stopped by the meeting. They were grandparents, aunts, neighbors, coworkers and children themselves who are now responsible for younger children who were left behind.

“There are children who lost both of their parents in that raid,” Amber Hampton, of Indivisible Memphis, a chapter of the nationwide civil rights organization, said. “You’re talking about children who are now displaced, who have to possibly move, change schools because their parents are no longer there and they have to go with a different caregiver.”

At a city council meeting shortly after the raids, family members told city council people about the impact of the taskforce. More than 40 children, some of whom testified, were left without parents. Children also testified when the city council decided to vote to call for the taskforce’s removal.

“There’s a lot of confusion, especially with the younger kids,” Demster said. “Families are scattering to try to keep their heads above water, to pay these utility bills, to find food, to fill that void of the parent being targeted and detained and deported. One of the hardest things about this work is talking to these children and seeing the pain and seeing the devastation of these families. For every one person that were taken in that raid, there’s usually two to four family members here in Memphis that were devastated.”

articles.title: Cloned number plate victims in England and Wales to get new reporting tool
articles.summary:
Police launch initiative after steep rise in criminals using method to evade detection and avoid paying penalties

Sandra Yarwood has a file “about 2in thick” of paperwork relating to the 32…

blocks.text: Sandra Yarwood has a file “about 2in thick” of paperwork relating to the 32 driving fines she received this summer after her car’s number plate was cloned.

Yarwood’s black Volkswagen Golf did not move from outside her London home while she was on holiday in Canada, but a similar vehicle with a fraudulent copy of her registration racked up penalty notices totalling £2,560 across five London boroughs.
Criminals are using cloned plates to evade detection and avoid paying penalties for dangerous or illegal driving.

A record 11,400 drivers contacted the DVLA last year after being issued with fines for offences they said they did not recognise or accept responsibility for: most of which are believed to be a result of cloning. The number of complaints was 9% higher than in 2024 and almost double the number recorded in 2018.

To help victims, a new reporting tool has been launched in England and Wales. The tool is designed to make it easier to alert the authorities by allowing victims to report a cloned plate directly to the police online who will also inform the DVLA. There is a new section on the government’s website that explains how to appeal incorrect fines or charges.

The government has also issued consumer guidance on how to avoid falling foul of driving with an illegal number plate after it emerged that a third of motorists stopped in number plate operations this year had no idea they had one.

Early findings from the police suggest that, in addition to deliberate criminal use, the public are unwittingly being sold incorrect plates. Stolen secondhand cars can be fitted with cloned plates and the government advises that you check the car’s registration number is consistent with information held by the DVLA.

The roads minister, Justin Madders, said: “Illegal plates are being used by criminals, but it is also the case that innocent motorists can have illegal plates on their vehicles without their knowledge.
after newsletter promotion

“We are going to make it easier for victims of cloned plates to report them as well as [launching] webpages to help drivers when they buy number plates and used cars from reputable sellers. These are small everyday fixes from the government which could help you avoid unwelcome attention from police.”
It took Yarwood months to sort out the mess left by the criminals who racked up the fines in six days.
“I never paid any of them … but the difficulty contesting them is gobsmacking,” she said. “You have to prove your innocence and the fact that I was not in the country was not enough.”
She said after she had reported the cloned plates her husband was stopped while driving the car. “But not in an unpleasant way,” she added. “It was fine.”
If it happens again, Yarwood has been advised to change her registration which she says is a “whole thing I didn’t want to have to do. So I’m waiting. I hope they don’t.”

articles.title: COP31 climate talks break down as EU, others reject deal
articles.summary: 'It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognize that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted,' says COP31…

blocks.text: People walk past an installation set up by protesters as they leave the venue of the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, November 20, 2026. REUTERS/Murad Sezer
Murad Sezer/Reuters

'It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognize that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted,' says COP31 President Murat Kurum, referring to the proposed Antalya Pact

ANTALYA, Turkey – UN climate talks fell into disarray on Sunday, November 22, as COP31 presidents Turkey and Australia failed to secure a consensus agreement on how to advance the fight against climate change, with the European Union and others rejecting a final draft deal.

After more than two weeks of negotiations, which had been due to end on Friday, November 20, but stretched deep into the weekend, Turkey’s COP31 President Murat Kurum said at the closing plenary that a deal was not approved.
“It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognize that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted,” he said.

The collapse of the talks comes in a year that has seen the most destructive impacts of global warming, such as extreme heat in Europe and glacial floods in Nepal, overshadowed by the demands of wars and public outcry over soaring living costs.
The last major breakdown in UN climate talks came in Copenhagen in 2009, when countries failed to adopt the Copenhagen Accord by consensus in a setback for multilateral climate diplomacy.

Australia, which was leading the negotiations, and host nation Turkey had issued multiple drafts of a text that sought to find compromise between the needs of nations most vulnerable to climate change and those whose economies depend on either the production or consumption of fossil fuels.

The text acknowledged for the first time that global warming is on course to exceed the 1.5 degree Celsius threshold countries had sought to preserve, while calling for faster development of carbon-removal technologies to eventually reverse the overshoot.
But the bid to win consensus backing proved unsuccessful, with critics of the text calling it unambitious.

The COP process is the main vehicle through which countries coordinate their efforts to curb global warming. Its annual summit is seen as an important opportunity to signal that nations are willing to work together to find solutions and help finance the myriad problems caused by rising temperatures.

While a major blow to efforts to ratchet up international action, the failure to agree on a political declaration in Antalya does not wipe out the obligations agreed by previous summits or erase the technical and legal frameworks governing multilateral action against climate change. – Rappler.com

articles.title: A local company won a global award for noise-cancelling innovation
articles.summary: Mobile services provider Smart Communications, Inc. (Smart), the wireless subsidiary of PLDT Inc. has bagged the Best 5G-A Service Innovation at the Global Core Summit Awards in Bangkok, Thailand,…

blocks.text: Mobile services provider Smart Communications, Inc. (Smart), the wireless subsidiary of PLDT Inc. has bagged the Best 5G-A Service Innovation at the Global Core Summit Awards in Bangkok, Thailand, for PureVoice, Asia-Pacific’s first commercially launched native artificial intelligence (AI) voice enhancement service built on the core network.

Smart was the only Philippine telecommunications company shortlisted in the awards, which brought together innovative solutions and technologies from operators around the world. The recognition highlights Smart’s role in advancing network-based AI and redefining the mobile voice calling experience for Filipino subscribers.
Device- agnostic AI

Officially launched for Smart Infinity members on Nov. 6, PureVoice delivers clearer mobile calls by filtering out background noise directly through the telecommunications network, allowing users to hear and be heard more clearly in noisy environments. Smart will also roll out PureVoice to more subscribers soon.

Unlike noise cancellation features that rely on a smartphone’s built-in hardware and software, PureVoice processes background noise at the network level. This allows the service to reduce distractions from traffic, crowds, music, and other environmental sounds without requiring users to upgrade their devices or download a separate application.

“Winning at the Global Core Summit is a strong affirmation of Smart’s commitment to making connectivity more meaningful for our customers. We are constantly looking for ways to go beyond keeping people connected and make every interaction better. With PureVoice, we are bringing an advanced network capability into everyday conversations, helping our subscribers communicate with greater clarity,” said Lloyd R. Manaloto, First Vice President and officer-in-charge of Smart.
Bringing AI innovation to everyday conversations

Designed for real-world calling conditions, PureVoice helps subscribers stay focused on conversations in busy environments, whether they are coordinating work on the road, speaking with clients, or catching up with family and friends.
The service requires no additional application or new device. Eligible Smart Infinity subscribers can simply dial 8# during an active call to enable or disable PureVoice.

PureVoice builds on Smart’s continuing investments in network expansion and modernization, including its rollout of Voice over LTE (VoLTE) in 2020. VoLTE enables high-quality voice calls while allowing subscribers to continue using mobile data during conversations. Smart also supports Video over LTE (ViLTE), enabling video calls directly through compatible phones’ dialers without requiring third-party applications.

“Delivering AI-powered voice enhancement through the core network takes the right capabilities and careful engineering to make the technology work seamlessly in real-world conditions. PureVoice demonstrates how we can translate these capabilities into tangible improvements in call quality, while creating a foundation for further innovation in network services,” said Debbie M. Hu, First Vice President and Wireless Network Business Partner of Smart.

articles.title: Bayern Munich bosses under fire over Jamal Musiala comments
articles.summary: Officials have publicly questioned whether Musiala will ever fully recover from a debilitating neurological condition and queried the validity of his contract, prompting criticism from fans, media…

image.caption: Former Bayern CEO and current supervisory board member Karl-Heinz Rummenigge (background) has led public criticism of Jamal Musiala (foreground)Image: Frank Hoermann/SvenSimon/picture alliance

blocks.text: In the space of just two days this weekend, Bayern Munich were held to a 1-1 draw by FC Cologne, saw Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane ruled out until the new year with a serious ankle injury and lost first place in the Bundesliga to rivals Borussia Dortmund.

But even those setbacks – as well as the return of head coach Vincent Kompany to the sideline following health issues – have been overshadowed by explosive public comments made by Bayern club bosses regarding young attacker and Germany international Jamal Musiala.
What is wrong with Jamal Musiala?
Back in July 2025, Musiala suffered a fractured fibula and a broken ankle at the Club World Cup.

Since then, the 23-year-old has been battling to recover not only from that injury but also with a debilitating neurological condition diagnosed as "absence seizures" which led him to collapse on the pitch in two consecutive pre-season games in August this year.
Musiala has struggled to replicate the sort of form which led to a well-remunerated contract extension in January 2025, prior to the ankle injury and the seizures.
The situation has now prompted a series of controversial public remarks from the Bayern hierarchy seemingly questioning the validity of that contract.
What have Bayern Munich officials said?

"It is well known that he has a contract which contains some considerable sums," former chief executive and current supervisory board member Karl-Heinz Rummenigge told broadcaster Sky on Friday evening following the 1-1 draw with Cologne, in which Musiala had made a 20-minute substitute appearance.

blocks.caption: Bayern head coach Vincent Kompany (who himself has just recovered from a serious infection) brought Musiala on as a substitute against CologneImage: Tom Weller/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "It's in all of our interest that he comes back, ideally in top form, but what happens if that's not the case?" asked Rummenigge, adding that Musiala's condition "leads us to suspect, unfortunately, that it will be difficult [for him] to return to the level that he has often shown in this stadium" and that "then we of course have to think about the finances."
Rummenigge suggested a need for Bayern to hold talks with Musiala, his family and his representatives because "such sums are, with respect, no longer justifiable."

Asked whether Bayern would consider selling Musiala, Rummenigge said he considered it unlikely that any club would be prepared to buy the player out of his new contract, which is set to run until 2030 and which reportedly sees Musiala earn up to €30 million per year.
"I cannot imagine that Jamal would leave the club or that any other club would buy him under these conditions," said Rummenigge. "And that is a problem."

Rummenigge was not the first senior Bayern official to express such doubts. Earlier this month, former club president Uli Hoeness had told local broadcaster Bayrischer Rundfunk that Musiala's situation presented the club with a "dilemma."

"He has an illness which cannot be cured but which can be somewhat controlled through medication," said Hoeness, who also sits on Bayern's supervisory board, questioning "whether he will ever regain the ability he once had" and stating that "he continues to receive money."

Bayern chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen has also weighed in, telling Munich's Abendzeitung newspaper last week: "We all have a responsibility towards the club and we all hope that Jamal will come back. Of course this will take time. We will assess the situation and speak to his family and management. Either we'll all be happy that the old Jamal [will return] or, if he becomes a different [player], we'll have to hold talks."
FIFPRO: 'Bayern should know better'
The comments by Hoeness, Dreesen and Rummenigge landed like a bombshell in Germany and beyond.

The global players' union FIFPRO issued a statement on Saturday slamming what they called "a coordinated strategy to put pressure on Musiala and his representatives ahead of any negotiations," highlighting Bayern's "duty of care" towards their player, and stating: "A club of Bayern's standing should know better."

"Across professional football, uncertainty about a player's future can take a toll on their mental health, particularly when they are recovering from injury," the statement continued. "Making Musiala's health and future a matter of public debate adds to that pressure. Contracts are there to be respected. An injury or a dip in form gives a club no grounds to reopen terms it agreed to, just as a run of outstanding performances gives a player no automatic right to a pay rise."

Former Bayern Munich and Germany defender Lothar Matthäus also criticized the club, saying in his role as a pundit for Sky: "I've been a bit shocked throughout the entire week. It started with Uli Hoeness, continued with Jan-Christian Dreesen, and yesterday Karl-Heinz Rummenigge chose the strongest words of all. I have enormous respect for Karl-Heinz. I've known him for over 30 years. But he chose those statements very deliberately. The person who suffers most from all this is Jamal Musiala."

The comments by the Bayern bosses also came just hours ahead of the club's annual general meeting on Saturday, where club members – who hold a majority 70% stake in the club in accordance with German football's "50+1" ownership rule – took to the stand to criticize the club's hierarchy.
One member, professional neurologist Jonatan Hoffmann, expressed his "absolute respect" for Musiala and said that patients suffering from such conditions require "support."

He said Musiala had received such support from head coach Vincent Kompany and director of sport Max Eberl, but said Hoeness', Dreesen's and Rummenigge's comments were "not helpful" and had "little to do with the much talked about Bayern Munich family" – earning considerable applause from fellow members.

blocks.caption: Bayern Munich member Jonatan Hoffmann, a neurologist by trade, criticized his club's executivesImage: Harry Langer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Bayern president: 'Musiala will get time and support'

Bayern president Herbert Hainer, the club's most senior elected official, attempted to deescalate the situation, responding to Hoffmann by saying: "Health and difficult situations are fundamentally always taken into account at FC Bayern."

Indeed, Bayern have recently been praised for their considerate handling of captain Joshua Kimmich following the unexpected death of his father, and of head coach Kompany, who returned to the touchline against Cologne on Friday following a month-long absence after collapsing due to a particularly serious viral infection.
"When it comes to Jamal, we all want the old Jamal back as he was before his injury," said Hainer. "And he will receive all the support and time he needs from the club."

Speaking on the sidelines of the meeting, chief executive Dreesen also attempted to row back on his comments, insisting to reporters that he and his colleagues had not been trying to put Musiala under pressure.

"We all want Jamal to return to the old Jamal. He needs time. We've said that several times. And he must get that. And then we'll see how things look in the new year," he said, adding that there was no need "to talk about the contract."

President Hainer also dismissed questions from journalists as to whether Bayern felt they had been misled by Musiala's agents before offering him a new contract, inferring that the player's representatives may have known about his neurological condition.
"I absolutely do not think that anyone knew beforehand," Hainer insisted.

blocks.caption: Bayern club president Herbert Hainer attempted to diffuse the situation at Saturday's annual general meetingImage: Harry Langer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German media criticize Bayern

But the public criticism has continued. Leading German sports publication Kicker said it was understandable for the Bayern bosses to be frustrated but called their approach "irresponsible" and said their anger "harms the wrong person" in Musiala.

"He can't help his injuries or neurological condition," wrote editor-in-chief Matthias Dersch. "Musiala is only 23 … and is in the most difficult phase of his career. We cannot imagine how he must be feeling, his insecurities and perhaps also fears about his health and his future. And no: the amount of money he earns is no cure."

German football magazine 11Freunde said the Musiala case offered "a glimpse into the abyss of professional football … an unembellished look behind the scenes of a business which is generally portrayed only as glamorous and exciting … into a shadow world where human beings are damned to function … where the value of a person is measured only by their ability to perform over and over again … That's football: capitalism in its purest form."

Meanwhile, the business of football continues. Borussia Dortmund capitalized on Bayern's draw to go top of the Bundesliga with a 1-0 win away at Borussia Mönchengladbach, Harry Kane underwent an operation on a torn ankle ligament but will be out until the new year, meaning he will miss Bayern's trip to Lille in the Champions League on Wednesday.
And the young Jamal Musiala will continue to battle the effects of serious physical and neurological conditions.
