articles.title: Conservative media weighs its future as cracks emerge in Trump’s movement
articles.summary:
Two weeks after Democrats flipped Congress, conservative outlets are having conversations on whether to distance themselves from Trump or double down on Maga

As a so-called “blue wave”…

blocks.text: As a so-called “blue wave” crashed across the country on the night of 3 November, conservative hosts and commentators on Fox News displayed an almost virtuosic ability to avoid directly blaming Donald Trump for the Republican party’s defeat, instead pinning the blame on impertinent voters who didn’t grasp the strength of the economy.

“In some sense, Mr Trump was too successful in the first year and didn’t sell it enough in the second year,” said Larry Kudlow, a Fox Business Network host who served as the president’s director of the National Economic Council during his first administration.

But two weeks on, Trump’s electoral wipeout is facilitating difficult conversations about the future of the conservative media ecosystem – and whether outlets that target a Republican-voting audience need to create some distance from an unpopular president. Some other outlets, like the Maga-aligned Real America’s Voice News network, are planning to go the other direction and double down on Trump.

blocks.caption: FOX Business anchor Larry Kudlow at Fox Business Network studios on 16 January in New York City.  Photograph: John Lamparski/Getty Images

blocks.text: “The whole landscape can now be reordered, and I think it will be,” said Steve Bannon, a former chief strategist to Trump during his first administration who now hosts a show for Real America’s Voice.

Several conservative media personalities pinned the blame on Fox News for leading the party – and Trump – astray, with former host Tucker Carlson saying that the results signaled the end of “the Fox News era”. (Carlson didn’t respond to a message seeking comment.)

Bannon, who contends that Rupert Murdoch has long “hated Trump”, predicted that the network will utilize the party’s recent “rejection” at the polls to move away from Trump and embrace more traditional, George W Bush-era Republican priorities.

“They’re going to try to kick Trump into the dustbin,” he said. “They clearly have moved beyond Trump and they want to move beyond Trumpism … What they’re going to do is, with a thousand cuts, convince their ageing audience that Maga and what Maga stands for is too extreme.”
In contrast, Bannon said he expects Real America’s Voice and other outlets to “triple down” on the Maga movement and “populist nationalism.”

Bannon is not alone in his criticism of Murdoch’s media empire. Conservative commentator Ann Coulter said that she views the channel and its sister outlet, the New York Post, as “90% responsible for the GOP wipeout in the midterm elections”, blaming voices in the Murdoch media empire for encouraging Trump to launch – and sustain – an unpopular war against Iran.

blocks.caption: Steve Bannon speaks at the Conservative Political Action Conference at the Gaylord Texan Resort and Convention Center, in Grapevine, Texas, on 27 March.  Photograph: Callaghan O’Hare/Reuters

blocks.text: Atlanta-based conservative radio host Erick Erickson said a realignment away from Trump will probably start in his medium before it carries over to conservative television – though he said it will take time, and will depend on how important access is for certain personalities.

“The more often you spend time at Mar-a-Lago, the less likely you are to distance yourself from Trump, because you still want in,” said Erickson, who vocally opposed Trump in 2016 before coming around ahead of his 2020 re-election bid.

Charlie Sykes, a former conservative radio host who also opposed Trump from the beginning, said the election has shown “cracks in that alternative reality silo” on Trump-aligned channels and platforms.

“In general, I think the scope of the blowout was just so great that even deep in the rightwing media ecosystem, they had to feel the tremors of it,” said Sykes, a former MS Now commentator who now writes on Substack. “And so that has been kind of interesting, this sense of like, ‘OK, we need to really come to grips with this and maybe figure out a way to move on.’”

Trump’s decision to attack Iran in February fomented division within the conservative media ecosystem, with many commentators viewing it as an abdication of his promise to abstain from foreign wars and focus on the US.
“I think those divisions are just going to widen,” Sykes said.

The Daily Caller, which was co-founded by Carlson in 2010 as something of a conservative alternative to the New York Times, made waves ahead of the midterms for calling out Trump’s war against Iran – and the high prices that have come out of it. “The Daily Caller is clearly positioning itself for a landscape not just post-midterms but post-Trump, and for a bitter and intensifying intraparty media battle,” the digital publication Semafor wrote on 1 November.

blocks.caption: Tucker Carlson speaks at his Live Tour at the Desert Diamond Arena on 31 October 2024 in Phoenix, Arizona.  Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

blocks.text: In an interview, Daily Caller editor-in-chief Amber Duke said the publication is more focused on reflecting the mood of the American people – particularly younger people affected by a challenging economy – than boosting Trump and the Maga movement.

“I think what we are doing is so unique that we are really setting ourselves apart,” she said. “We view ourselves as a principled, America-first outlet. I think there’s a difference between Maga and America-first.”

Duke also acknowledged the economic opportunities that drive support for the president. “Trump is a content goldmine. He drives a lot of traffic, a lot of clicks,” she said. “That content mine is eventually going to dry up. I would definitely be concerned if I had my entire business model tied around this uniquely celebrity-oriented newsmaker. How am I going to continue to stay in business after that? For us, it’s: Let’s just tell the truth to the American people, and that truth is not going to be dependent on any one person or political party.”
Some conservative outlets that are closely tied to Trump, however, don’t see any reason to do anything differently.

“Nothing changes with us,” Newsmax chief executive Christopher Ruddy said. “We’re going to continue reporting on the administration and we will continue to cover the Congress. We make a very concerted effort to always get both sides on our reports and in our TV opinion segments.”

blocks.caption: Christopher Ruddy, chief executive officer of Newsmax, speaks during the Conservative Political Action Conference in National Harbor, Maryland, on 2 March 2023.  Photograph: Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images

blocks.text: Charles Herring, president of the far-right One America News Network, echoed that sentiment: “Our reporting doesn’t change based on the political pendulum or who resides in the White House. We are working hard every day to further enhance our coverage for our viewers.”

Still, there are limits to how far some conservative media organizations can stray from the president, considering the economic imperative to retain a pro-Trump audience. “The thing to understand about conservative media is that it’s not necessarily always top down,” Sykes said. “It’s often: What will the audience tolerate? … Nobody wants to get too crosswise with their audience.”

But the vast majority of conservative news sites have already seen declines in online traffic in recent months, according to industry tracker Howard Polskin, an early warning sign for the party’s midterm chances. “Audiences are not buying what Maga media is selling anymore,” he said.

“My prediction would be that in the next two years, rightwing media will become fractured with more infighting, breaking into two camps: pro-Maga/Trump and anti-Maga/Trump,” Polskin added. “Traffic to rightwing websites will continue to nose dive, much more so than mainstream media.”

Several conservative media veterans who spoke with the Guardian said the selection of a 2028 Republican presidential nominee will probably be a defining moment for the sector, and one that could split conservative media into different camps.

On the notion that vice-president JD Vance will be Trump’s heir apparent, Erickson said: “I actually am kind of encouraged by the level of pushback after the election that maybe this isn’t a good idea.” Brian Kilmeade, the co-host of the influential Fox News morning show Fox & Friends, has been particularly critical of Vance for seeming to distance himself from Trump’s decision-making on Iran. On his radio show this past week, Kilmeade said that Vance “never should have been vice-president” and that he’s “amazed that President Trump puts up with it”.

blocks.caption: Brian Kilmeade is seen on Fox & Friends at Fox News Channel Studios in New York City on 21 July 2025.  Photograph: Noam Galai/Getty Images

blocks.text: Over the next two years, conservative media personalities will have to put their chips down on a candidate. The challenge, Sykes said, is “figuring out where the audience is going, and getting there first”. He also expects conservative media outlets to prioritize attacking Democrats and undermining their control of Congress.
“It’s no longer about defense of Trump,” he added. “It’s like: What’s next? And everybody’s got to make that pivot.”

articles.title: Arizona grandfather hailed as a hero after finding missing toddler in desert
articles.summary:
Jay Stewart joined search party after two-year-old Vella Campillo wandered off into desert from front yard of home

An Arizona…

blocks.text: An Arizona granddad has been formally recognized as a hero after recently volunteering to help search for a toddler who wandered off alone into the desert while wearing only a diaper – and finding her safely within several hours curled up under a bush, leading to her rescue.

“I’ll never forget it as long as I live,” Jay Stewart said of recovering Vella Campillo, two, while recalling the moment at a news conference held later. “I’ve never wanted to find something so bad in my life – or somebody to find her, anybody to find her.”

Stewart’s emotional comments came at the end of an ordeal for Vella that began with her toddling off by herself from the front yard of her family home in the desert community of Eloy, Arizona, wearing only a diaper, at about 5pm on 17 November, authorities reported to local media. Vella’s parents, Joseph Campillo and Deanna Fritz, later told news station KSAZ that Vella was playing with her siblings and being cared for by another family member when she ran off.
An intense search effort ensued, drawing in dozens of law enforcement officers and community members volunteering to help comb the remote surrounding desert.

Stewart, described as both a father and grandfather, was among the volunteers. And at about 12.15am on 18 November, with temperatures cold at about 50F (10C), Stewart was shining a flashlight through the darkness along a particular ditch lined with bushes.

Vella suddenly “popped out” of one of the bushes, Stewart would later tell reporters. The girl was shivering, about two miles (3.2km) away from her home. Stewart said Vella came up to him and jumped into his arms, and he called first responders to alert them of his discovery.

A deputy with the local Pinal county sheriff’s office soon came up on Stewart and Vella, with his body-worn camera recording video of the scene. “That’s where she was at, right in that spot – I was just walking the ditch,” a visibly relieved Stewart told the deputy, pointing to a nearby bush with a shirtless Vella in his arms.

blocks.caption: Vella Campillo. Photograph: Pinal County Sheriff’s Office

blocks.text: “Are you OK? Are you so cold?” the deputy could be heard saying on the video as he covered her in a blanket and Vella babbled excitedly.

Stewart tried to hand Vella over to the deputy, saying, “She’s got a hold of me.” He managed to do so after the deputy gently asked Vella, “Can you let go? We’re going to move you over here and sit you in [a] chair.”
“I’ll go with you,” Stewart reassured her.
Paramedics subsequently brought Vella to the hospital for a medical evaluation, and soon she was back with her family.

At a news conference later that day, the Pinal county sheriff, Ross Teeple, explained that the timeliness of Stewart’s intervention was vital for Vella. Prolonged exposure to the temperatures Vella experienced wearing only a diaper during her night alone in the desert could lead to hypothermia, which is life-threatening.
“Very remote areas like this can get extremely cold very fast,” Teeple remarked. “And she’s a small body producing very little heat.”

Teeple’s office later published a video on social media showing the sheriff presenting Stewart with a plaque recognizing him as an outstanding citizen. He also gave Stewart a badge distinguishing him as an honorary member of the office’s search and rescue posse.

As the sheriff put it in the video, Teeple had heard Stewart express discomfort with being labeled a hero. Yet “I’m here to tell you that when you watch the body camera footage, it’s obvious you’re that little girl’s hero”, Teeple said. “And today you’re Pinal county’s hero.”
Fritz, Vella’s mother, told KSAZ that Vella’s disappearance marked “the worst day of our entire lives”.
“We’re beyond blessed for the man [who] found her,” Fritz said to the outlet, while also thanking everyone else involved in the search for Vella.

In the video with Teeple, Stewart said he would treasure the tokens of appreciation that the sheriff presented him. He also said at the news conference that it was not necessary for Vella’s parents to thank him, declaring: “It’s what we do.”
“The scariest thing for parents is to lose a child,” Stewart said. “I can’t imagine what they were going through.”
He added that everyone searching for Vella was “doing it for the same reason”.
“We loved her and wanted her back – she may not be our child, but she could be,” Stewart said.

articles.title: UK-EU food deal hailed by British firms: ‘We’re pretty aligned anyway’
articles.summary:
Exporters welcome end in sight for Brexit checks – but are frustrated that implementation will take so long

British producers have broadly welcomed the UK’s deal with the EU, designed to…

blocks.text: British producers have broadly welcomed the UK’s deal with the EU, designed to remove the vast majority of physical checks on food, plants and animal products.

The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal is expected to benefit Britain’s food exporters and will enable UK delicatessens and other small retailers to import European cheese and wine again, something that became economically unviable because of costly Brexit checks.
The agreement is due to take effect on 1 March 2028 and is also intended to reopen the EU market for UK products including fresh sausages, burgers, seed potatoes and molluscs.
However, several years after the UK left the bloc, upending many decades-old trading arrangements, some food exporters said they would remain cautious until the deal came into force.
“Nobody’s going to believe this until it has actually physically happened,” said Iain Barbour, the operations director of the Scottish seed potato producer Jamieson Brothers.

Seed potatoes were not included in the post-Brexit trade deal after the two sides disagreed over certification, halting exports from the UK to the EU despite Scottish seed potatoes’ high health status classification.

The exclusion particularly hit the Scottish industry, whose farmers were among the biggest exporters for the production of chips and crisps in the world, as well as growers in northern England. Scottish seed potato farmers previously accounted for three-quarters of UK production and the sector was worth about £112m a year.

Ireland and the EU represented a fifth of Jamieson Brothers’ trade before Brexit. The company particularly suffered from the loss of the Irish business, given it grew many varieties that were popular on plates in the north and south of Ireland.

blocks.caption: Scottish potato farmers were among the biggest exporters for the production of chips and crisps in the world before Brexit. Photograph: Skully/Alamy

blocks.text: While the company adapted its business to start packing work that would have previously been carried out in the EU, Barbour estimates this change cost about £500,000.
“We evolved, we worked with more partners and that’s what kept the business going,” Barbour said.

Barbour is looking forward to supplying his Irish customers once againHowever, he said it would take at least three years until he could revive varieties that were no longer being grown and were instead stored in a seed bank.

“A lot of Scottish farmers stopped producing varieties that were popular in Ireland as they weren’t desired in England. Varieties that had been going about 100 years were killed off in a couple of years,” he said. “So we’ll have to look at bringing them back.”

The planned implementation of the food deal in March 2028 would also be “a couple of months late for the trade”, given most sales happen at the start of the year and the crops needs to be grown in advance.
Barbour anticipates most growers will be wary and will only fully resume trading in 2029. “People are obviously going to be a little bit hesitant to grow anything until it’s 100% official,” he said.

blocks.caption: Devon’s Offshore Shellfish has managed to continue exporting to its European customers despite post-Brexit red tape. Photograph: Offshore Shellfish

blocks.text: British exporters of live bivalve molluscs – the collective term for shellfish including mussels, oysters, clams, cockles and scallops – hope the deal will give the sector a shot in the arm.
The industry is small and specialised. It was valued at less than £12m a year before Brexit, but it is crucial for some coastal communities.

Offshore Shellfish, a family-run business produces rope-grown mussels in the waters of Lyme Bay, Devon, has managed to continue exporting to its European customers despite the administrative burden and occasional blocks by French customs.
after newsletter promotion

The company exports the vast majority of the blue mussels it produces. It sends to the Netherlands for processing, before most end up in restaurants or on supermarket shelves in Belgium, where they are prized as a key ingredient in moules-frites, one of the country’s national dishes.

blocks.caption: Offshore Shellfish’s Sarah Holmyard says the deal’s provisions are ‘a huge win for us’. Photograph: Offshore Shellfish

blocks.text: Sarah Holmyard, the commercial director of Offshore Shellfish, said the most important detail was an assurance that the deal would allow live bivalve molluscs to be exported even if they did not come from waters with the highest quality rating.

Offshore Shellfish’s farms are in waters which are considered “class A” for most of the year, but before the new SPS deal, any change in water quality to “class B” could have temporarily halted exports.
“That’s a huge win for us because we’ve been pushing and pushing and pushing for that,” Holmyard said.

However, the deal will come too late for those UK shellfish producers that have closed down since Brexit. Three out of four mussel fishing companies in the Menai strait, the channel that separates the north Wales mainland from the island of Anglesey, stopped trading after exports became too difficult.

The promised end of physical border checks on dairy, fish and meat products was welcomed by Rich Clothier, the managing director of Wyke Farms. The Somerset-based cheese and butter maker exports about a quarter of its cheddar to the EU, particularly France, Germany and Spain.

blocks.caption: Rich Clothier, the managing director of cheesemaker Wyke Farms, says the deal ‘will save a huge amount of cost and product waste’. Photograph: Josh Campbell

blocks.text: Dairy exports to the EU have been less contentious since Brexit than seed potatoes or mussels, but not without challenges. The removal of veterinary checks is viewed as a significant benefit by Clothier.

“It’s a very bureaucratic process to get everything signed off, in what is not a very modern sort of system,” he said. “The agreement will save a huge amount of cost and product waste as well, because these are perishable.

“Any reduction in friction saves cost, it makes business more efficient. But it is really frustrating that it’s going to take so long [to be implemented] because, to be honest, we’re all pretty aligned anyway.”

articles.title: ‘Proud Bisdak’ KZ Tandingan wants Filipino music to transcend borders
articles.summary: KZ Tandingan takes pride in seeing that many newcomers from all across the archipelago aren't afraid to sing in their mother tongue

items: The Filipino music scene is primarily centered in Metro Manila, where many successful artists begin their careers in local venues, often requiring aspiring musicians from provinces to travel long distances for auditions.

KZ Tandingan, a prominent singer-songwriter, rose to fame after winning X Factor Philippines in 2012, using her platform to advocate for music in various Philippine languages and to challenge traditional beauty standards in the industry.

Despite the challenges of accessibility in the music industry, Tandingan remains optimistic about the growing acceptance of diverse musical expressions in different languages, encouraging new artists to embrace their cultural roots.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

The Filipino music scene has long largely operated in the metro, with many of today’s most successful local acts starting out as performers in dive bars around different cities close to the capital before their meteoric rise.
Major concerts are usually held in venues across Pasay and Quezon City, and the TV shows that are known to produce successful stars operate from Metro Manila, too.
And to get a shot at making it big, aspiring artists from provinces often have to travel long hours and spend thousands on plane rides just to audition for these music shows.

It’s a reality KZ Tandingan is all too familiar with. In 2012, the acclaimed singer-songwriter, who hails from Digos, Davao del Sur, packed her bags to audition for the first season of X Factor Philippines.

Just 20 years old then, Tandingan had joined the reality singing competition with a brave mission to help her family, and to prove that you didn’t need to conform to traditional beauty standards to become successful.

“Gusto ko pong sumali ng ‘X Factor’ hindi lang para tulungan ang pamilya ko, kung ‘di patunayan na ang industriya ng musika sa Philippines ay hindi lang para sa mga magaganda, sa mga makikinis ang balat, sa mga matatangkad, at sa mga biritero’t biritera,” she said during her audition.

(I want to join X Factor not just to help my family, but to prove that the music industry in the Philippines isn’t just for the beautiful, for those with clear skin, those who are tall, and those who can belt easily.)

blocks.caption: ‘Proud Bisdak’ KZ Tandingan wants Filipino music to transcend borders

blocks.text: Tandingan had confidently told the judges that she would sing her own version of “Somewhere Over The Rainbow,” and she had, right off the bat, proven that her soulful, raspy vocal tone would take her places far and wide. It was a goal she would see through at each round of the competition, until she would eventually emerge as X Factor Philippines’ first-ever winner.
And over a decade, countless chart-topping hits, and plenty of large-scale shows later, Tandingan has not once forgotten where she came from.

Tandingan had developed most of her career in Manila — having been signed to major record labels before going independent earlier this year. Despite being so far away from home all the time, she and her husband, fellow famed musician TJ Monterde, have made it a point to stand as staunch advocates of music sung in different languages across the Philippines.

blocks.caption: ‘Proud Bisdak’ KZ Tandingan wants Filipino music to transcend borders

blocks.text: “For a really, really long time, when music is recognized, artists who sing in their native tongue would always be boxed into that small category of regional music. I think a big factor is that we don’t expose the whole Philippines to all the songs sung in different languages,” Tandingan told Rappler in a mix of English and Filipino.
With the platform she’s built with her own craft, Tandingan then makes it a point to sing in Bisaya as much as she can.
Just take her latest Coke Studio track “Bugsay” for example. It’s sung entirely in Bisaya, and it was a creative choice Tandingan knew she had to make.

“‘Di ba, sabi nga nila, kunwari, nag-Bibisaya ako, tapos lumipat ako ng Manila, [nag-Fifilipino] na ako ngayon. If hindi ko ipapractice ‘yung Bisaya ko, if I don’t get to connect with my roots, makakalimutan mo ‘yun. And part ‘yun ng kultura ko as a Mindanaoan,” she told Rappler.

(They say that, for example, I speak Bisaya, then I moved to Manila and started speaking Filipino. If I don’t practice my Bisaya, if I don’t get to connect with my roots, you’ll forget it. And it’s part of my culture as a Mindanaoan.)
“Bugsay” is a Bisaya word for “oar.” It carries a strong message: to keep paddling, no matter how strong the current gets.

While the song strives to inspire those who listen to it, it bears a bigger aspiration for Tandingan: to make it known that there are songs by musicians from across the archipelago that aren’t just sung in Filipino or English. After all, some stories are better told in their original languages.

“If ‘Bugsay’ is able to [encourage more Filipinos to listen to non-English and Filipino songs], nagawa ko na ‘yung purpose ko as an artist. That’s why it’s important for me to always champion my roots — kasi Bisaya ako. Proud Bisdak talaga ako.”

(If “Bugsay” is able to encourage more Filipinos to listen to non-English and Filipino songs, I’ve fulfilled my purpose as an artist. That’s why it’s important for me to always champion my roots — because I’m Bisaya. I’m a proud Bisdak.)
The “Two Less Lonely People in the World” singer is still waiting for the day music auditions become more accessible to people from all over Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao.

“I know so many talented artists that weren’t given a chance to audition because of the fact that you have to pay for a plane ride to Manila. That’s already a luxury for so many talented musicians back home,” Tandingan said in a mix of Filipino and English.
There’s still a long way to go, but Tandingan remains hopeful.

blocks.caption: ‘Proud Bisdak’ KZ Tandingan wants Filipino music to transcend borders

blocks.text: “Masaya pa rin ako sa nangyayari sa atin ngayon kasi ang daming mga bagong salta na mga musician and they’re not afraid to sing in their own language. May mga kumakanta ng Ilocano, ng Bisaya, at Chavacano,” she mused.
(I’m still happy because there are so many newly minted musicians who aren’t afraid to sing in their own language. There are people who sing in Ilocano, in Bisaya, or in Chavacano.)

It’s always heartwarming for Tandingan to see Filipino musicians shine as they are. More and more Filipino artists are now unafraid to break out of the mold of what supposedly means to be successful, and are more than willing to gamble on the big possibility of virality that singing in more widely recognizable languages can give them.
Through it all, they do it all in the name of honoring the roots and the land they came from. – Rappler.com

articles.title: The US midterm elections and this Norman Rockwell painting
articles.summary: Following the historic victory of Democratic Senator-elect Scott Colom in the US midterms, it would have been nice to visit the Freedom Summer marker to remember three voting rights activists—to say,…

blocks.text: The US midterm elections, especially in Mississippi where Democratic challenger Scott Colom became the state’s first Black senator since 1874, reminded me of this painting by Norman Rockwell.

It depicts the final moments of three young men: voting rights activists James Chaney, a 20-year-old Black Mississippi native, and two Jewish New Yorkers, Michael Schwerner, 24, and Andrew Goodman, 20. They were kidnapped, beaten and killed by Klu Klax Klan members in June 1964 for taking part in the campaign to register Black voters in Mississippi.

blocks.caption: DEFIANCE. Norman Rockwell’s painting “Murder in Mississippi,” depicts a defiant civil rights advocate Michael Schwerner (in white shirt), with his colleague, a wounded Black Mississippi local James Chaney clutching his arms, facing a US deputy sheriff and Klan conspirators holding guns (only thei…

blocks.text: Michael Schwerner, in white shirt, is shown holding his colleague in the voting rights campaign, a wounded Mississippi local James Chaney. Another colleague in the campaign, Anthony Goodman, is lying face down on the ground.
There’s a look of defiance on Schwerner’s face. What was he thinking shortly before he too was gunned down?
They were killed the day after I was born in Manila. That’s one reason what happened to them resonated with me — even though I didn’t know about them until I moved to California in my ’20s.

blocks.caption: The US midterm elections and this Norman Rockwell painting

blocks.text: I first heard their names in Mississippi Burning, which drew heavy criticism for downplaying the stories of Chaney, Goodman and Schwerner and the activists of the Freedom Summer campaign. FBI agents, played by Gene Hackman and Willem Dafoe, were the heroes in the movie. (READ: Actor Gene Hackman and wife found dead alongside dog at home)

I learned more as a student at the UC Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism where we watched Jon Else’s documentary Eyes on the Prize. The series led me to read Taylor Branch’s books bout the Civil Rights movement, Parting the Waters, Pillar of Fire, and At Canaan’s Edge.

blocks.caption: The US midterm elections and this Norman Rockwell painting

blocks.text: Years later, I came across Race Beat: The Press, The Civil Rights Struggle and the Awakening of A Nation, by the legendary journalist Gene Roberts and Emory University professor Hank Klibanoff. The winners of the Pulitzer Prize in 2007, this powerful book is an account of the US Civil Rights movement through the eyes of the journalists who covered it.
I spent a bit of time in the South last summer.

My family and I spent a week in Alabama to celebrate my son’s graduation from Army flight school at Fort Rucker. We visited our other son in New Orleans where he lived while interning at the NASA Space Center in nearby Mississippi. We celebrated the Fourth of July in the New Orleans Riverfront and watched fireworks on the Mississippi River. (READ: Letting go on the road to Idaho: Notes on fatherhood)
I had one regret about my summer in the South, which became more pronounced after the midterms.

Just a two-hour drive from New Orleans, at the intersection of County Road 515 and State Highway 19 near Philadelphia, Mississippi, there’s a plaque marking the area where James Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner were killed.

blocks.caption: KILLED. Newspaper clipping shows voting rights advocates Michael Schwerner, James Chaney, and Andres Goodman. Courtesy of Normal Rockwell Museum YT

blocks.text: I had thought of driving there to see it. But that didn’t happen.
It would have been nice to visit the marker, to remember James Chaney, Michael Schwerner and Andrew Goodman. To say, “Thank you.” – Rappler.com
(This article was first published in the author’s LinkedIn.)

Benjamin Pimentel is a journalist and technology editor based in the San Francisco Bay Area. His novel, ‘Mga Gerilya Sa Powell Street,’ won the 2007 National Book Award for Fiction and was staged by the Cultural Center of the Philippines’ (CCP) Tanghalang Pilipino in 2008.

articles.title: [Inside the Newsroom] Why road safety is a budget issue
articles.summary: An ambitious goal to achieve zero road deaths requires adequate funding, and right now Congress has just given it zero allocation

blocks.text: An ambitious goal to achieve zero road deaths requires adequate funding, and right now Congress has just given it zero allocation

I’m Patrick Cruz, a multimedia reporter for Rappler covering transportation, among other beats. Every day, millions of Filipinos navigate a chaotic, congested, and often perilous transport system. But the true cost of our daily commute isn’t just measured in lost hours and lost productivity; some lives are also lost on the road.
In Metro Manila alone, the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority records an average of 239 road crash incidents every single day. That is roughly 10 accidents every hour.

The national picture is even more alarming. According to recent data from the Philippine Statistics Authority, 3,133 people already died due to road crashes from January to April 2026 — not even half a year!
This staggering figure makes road accidents the 13th leading cause of death in the country.

The government acknowledges that this is a crisis. The Philippine Road Safety Action Plan (PRSAP) 2023–2028, led by the Department of Transportation (DOTr), laid down an ambitious target to reduce road traffic deaths and injuries by at least 35% by 2028. It has a long-term vision of zero road deaths.
But here is the glaring disconnect: ambitious goals require adequate funding, and right now the money simply isn’t there.
The DOTr proposed a modest P111.29 million to fund the PRSAP. However, under the House General Appropriations Bill (HGAB), that allocation was reduced to exactly zero.

Similarly, infrastructure designed to protect our most vulnerable road users has been gutted. The Active Transport Bike Share and Safe Pathways Program — essential for protecting cyclists and pedestrians — received a measly P33.9 million allocation. That is a mere 3% of the proposed P1.13 billion needed to build and maintain safe active transport networks.
Without this funding, millions of Filipinos who rely on active transport are left to fend for themselves on fast-moving, heavily motorized thoroughfares.
Advocates are rightfully sounding the alarm. The Move As One Coalition has pointed out that no funding has been provided for road safety for the past three years.

“There’s no funding for road safety for the past three years, which is why we ask the Senate: Please, if you’re really serious in helping prevent road crashes, in making sure that our most vulnerable are protected, fund road safety,” Move As One Coalition representative Lou Gepuela said during the budget deliberations in the Senate.

The road safety budget now sits in the hands of the Senate. Will our lawmakers finally put their money where their mouth is to protect commuters? Or will we see another year of zero funding for a crisis that claims thousands of Filipino lives?
Let’s keep a close eye on how government officials craft our national budget. Follow our #BudgetWatch page for more stories on where your taxes go (and where they don’t). – Rappler.com

articles.title: UN agency: 29% of Filipinos are aged 10-24, but fertility is below replacement level
articles.summary: The Philippines still has a large young population even as its demographic profile shifts.

blocks.text: November 22, 2026 | 5:40pm
A student uses a paper bag to protect himself from the heat as he leaves school in Manila on March 3, 2025, where classes are suspended due to extreme heat.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — Nearly three in 10 Filipinos are between 10 and 24 years old, equivalent to roughly 34 million people. While that base is considered healthy for a nation, the fertility rate is already below replacement level, according to new United Nations population estimates.
The United Nations Population Fund's State of World Population 2026 report estimates the Philippine population at 117.7 million this year, with people aged 10 to 24 accounting for 29%.

The report notes country's total fertility rate at 1.9 children per woman, below the 2.1 births commonly considered the level needed for a population to replace itself from one generation to the next.
The Philippines then has both a large cohort of young people remains a major part of the population and lower fertility that gradually changing the age profile of generations that follow.
The Philippine share of people aged 10 to 24 is higher than both the global average of 24% and the Asia-Pacific average of 23%, according to the report.
Fertility, meanwhile, is lower than the global rate of 2.2 children per woman but slightly higher than the Asia-Pacific rate of 1.8.
The report estimates that 26% of Filipinos are under 15 years old, while 68% are between 15 and 64 and 6% are 65 or older.
"Both situations, high fertility and low fertility, will require sound, rights-based and forward-looking policies," the report said.

UNFPA's 2026 report suggest that demographic shifts affect youner people's employment, housing, education and economic security as well as their decisions about relationships, independence and whether and when to have children.
It said demographic outcomes ultimately reflect individual choices and whether people have the resources and opportunities to make those choices freely.

Governments would therefore have to adapt policies covering human capital, employment, migration, care systems, healthy ageing and social protection rather than focus narrowly on raising or lowering fertility, the UN agency said.
Fertility decline already visible
The UN estimate is consistent with the Philippines' most recent national demographic survey.

While the UNFPA's 2026 demographic table estimates Philippine fertility at 1.9 children per woman, newer national survey data show the decline has gone further. The Philippine Statistics Authority's 2025 survey puts the rate at 1.7, from 1.9 in 2022 and 2.7 in 2017.
The transition is also visible in the country's changing age structure.

The 2024 census showed that children under 15 made up 26.7% of the household population, down from 30.7% in 2020. People aged 65 and older, meanwhile, accounted for 6.6%, up from 5.4% four years earlier.
The working-age population, those between 15 and 64, increased to 66.7% of the household population from 63.9% in 2020.

articles.title: Burnham should ‘move on’ from Brexit, says Theresa May, as critics hit out over closer EU ties – UK politics live
articles.summary: Issue dominates Sunday broadcast round following Friday’s deals on trade and youth mobility

blocks.text: Welcome: Burnham should 'move on' over Brexit, says May
Good morning and welcome to our UK politics blog.

Brexit – or reversing it, 10 years after the event – is the topic dominating the Sunday politics shows this morning after major deals were struck with the EU on Friday on trade, travel, emissions and visas for young people.
Andy Burnham says these are the first steps towards rebuilding “the bridges broken all of those years ago” with “our nearest neighbours and our largest market”.

While he’s voiced support for re-joining the bloc, he’s also stressed that all options are on the table and there’s a long road ahead in convincing the British public and securing the unanimous assent needed from the 27-nation bloc.

Critics have piled in this morning, warning how tricky of an endeavour this could be. Ex-PM Theresa May, whose government was brought down by Brexit in 2019, has told the BBC that the divorce “is done” and he should “move on”.

That interview’s coming up on Laura Kuenssberg’s show later this morning. Meanwhile over on Sky, Brexiteer Michael Gove is hosting Reform and Tory naysayers as well as the European relations minister. I’ll recap their comments.
Key events

items: 17m agoThe new EU-UK deals
20m agoWelcome: Burnham should 'move on' over Brexit, says May

blocks.text: Theresa May spent three years as prime minister (2016-2019) trying to negotiate the Brexit deal, before resigning.
She has told the BBC this morning she is “aghast” at the idea of Burnham resurrecting the issue, warning him of the enormous effort ahead:

double quotation markWhat I saw was that the extent of those negotiations, the hours that have to be put in - it’s across the whole of government. It’s not just prime ministerial time, cabinet ministers’ time, officials’ time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations. Because you have to negotiate hard in order to make sure that you’re getting out what you want.

double quotation markAnd that’s one of the reasons why I look slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham is talking about, further negotiations of going into the EU. And also we, as a country, we voted for Brexit. When I was prime minister I was very clear, we should deliver on that vote. So I’m afraid my message to him really is, you know, people voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on.
The new EU-UK deals
A summit in Brussels this week produced agreements which will:

items: Allow 100,000 young adults from each side to live and work in the other’s countries for up to three years
Scrap border checks on plant and animal products, which Burnham says will lower the cost of food
Link emissions trading schemes, lowering carbon taxes on some exports

blocks.text: The PM says these first package of deals will create opportunities for young people and keep supermarket prices down. Marks & Spencer, Morrisons, Co-op, has been among the supermarket giants welcoming the move for customers.
At Brussels, there were also commitments to keep negotiating other areas. One key subject to be sorted out in the next six months is university fees for European students in the UK and vice versa.
An EU official briefing media said negotiations hadn’t been easy but there had been good will to find solutions.

articles.title: South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal
articles.summary: Choi Kyo-jin admits last-minute measures to stop AI-assisted cheating during the college entrance exam caused chaos.

blocks.text: "As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.
"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.
The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.
Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.
These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.
His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.
This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.
This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.

Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.
The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.
It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.
Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.
All this made even honest test takers paranoid.
Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.
Another told Yonhap he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

articles.title: Indian opposition party’s youth wing warns of more Meta protests after police clashes
articles.summary:
Members of Congress party clashed with police outside tech company’s offices on Friday

The youth wing of India’s main opposition Congress party warned of more protests against Meta’s removal…

blocks.text: The youth wing of India’s main opposition Congress party warned of more protests against Meta’s removal of some of its members’ ⁠accounts, ⁠a day after clashing with ​police outside the tech firm’s locals offices.

In Hyderabad on Friday, protesters ‌carrying placards and chanted slogans as they stormed into ‌the building that houses Meta’s offices, smashing plants to the ground and clashing with police, according to footage released by the Indian Youth Congress’s X account.
The Indian Youth Congress on Saturday posted warnings on X that it would “storm your offices across the country and stage protests” unless the Instagram accounts of its leaders were restored.

Two such accounts were restored after Friday’s protests, but thousands of accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government remain restricted, Manu Jain, who is in charge of social media for ⁠the youth group, told Reuters on Saturday. Meta must explain how its algorithms restrict posts and must restore accounts taken down ​on government orders, he added.
India is Meta’s biggest market by users and the company declined to comment on Friday’s demonstrations.

blocks.caption: Congress members burn signs during a protest in Mumbai. Photograph: Indian Youth Congress/IYC/Reuters

blocks.text: Debate is growing in India about potential ⁠risks to free speech from the increasingly strict efforts of Narendra Modi’s government to remove social media content it objects to. India’s IT ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Meta has said it restricts ​content in India to comply with local laws.

Modi’s government says it orders content to be taken down only if it breaches local laws, can harm public safety ⁠or national security. Congress has long accused Meta and other social media platforms of curbing dissent online by removing accounts.

A video ‌from Friday’s demonstration showed protesters spray-painting anti-Meta slogans on walls outside the building that houses its Mumbai office and clashing with security guards who tried to stop them.
In Gurugram near New Delhi, Congress workers chanted slogans and held banners reading “restore youth Congress accounts”, online posts showed.

An opposition politician from Telangana state criticised Congress workers over what he called vandalism at Meta’s Hyderabad office, saying it ​had undermined the city’s reputation as a safe destination for businesses.

blocks.caption: Police clash with Youth Congress members at a protest in Hyderabad. Photograph: Indian Youth Congress/IYC/Reuters

blocks.text: Pradeep Bhandari, a national spokesperson for Modi’s ruling party, also criticised Congress’ actions on Saturday, saying they had “not only vandalised and destroyed Meta’s office in Hyderabad” but were also “flaunting it on social media”.
“This is Congress Model: Vandalise offices of Private companies,” he wrote.

Reporters Without Borders has ​said the removal of journalistic content from social media ​has been on the rise in India this year, and free speech activists say a new government rule gives social media ​companies hardly any time to review ‌and decide on takedown requests.
In ​February, Modi’s government ordered social media companies ​to take down unlawful content within three hours of being notified about it, tightening an earlier 36-hour timeline.
Meta disclosures show that it restricted more than 5.4m posts or accounts in India under local laws in the first half of 2026, second only to Indonesia and up from about 70,000 in the whole of 2025.
“The large majority of these items included instances where we were obligated to proactively restrict content … based on local law requirements,” Meta said.

Montreal-based telecom has submitted $31-billion proposal for Telus to review

· Posted: Nov 22, 2026 4:00 AM EST | Last Updated: 31 minutes ago

Quebecor Inc. CEO Pierre Karl Péladeau is defending his company's $31-billion bid to buy Telus Corp. amid concerns over competition in Canada's telecom sector, arguing the cost of wireless plans is dropping and non-Canadian companies are trying to expand.

"Telecom assets are strategic for our country — we all know this. And then therefore, we need to make sure that we're going to be on the same footing," Péladeau said in an interview on Rosemary Barton Live airing Sunday morning.

The Montreal-based telecom, media and entertainment company said on Monday that it submitted a non-binding proposal to Telus in June to serve as a basis for negotiations and that the Vancouver-based corporation is currently reviewing an enhanced proposal submitted by Quebecor earlier this month.

Quebecor's move comes three years after the federal government approved Rogers Communications' acquisition of Shaw Communications on the condition that Freedom Mobile be sold to Quebecor to preserve a four-player market.

Péladeau told CBC chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton that his company has been servicing Freedom Mobile and the Canadian market "pretty efficiently, and our results talk by themselves. We look forward to being able to continue to do the same with the Telus assets."
Quebecor's $31B bid to buy Telus: What it means for your phone bill
Asked how a merger of this size would help with Canadians' wireless costs, Péladeau said prices continue to fall after his company acquired Freedom Mobile.
"Our earnings are growing, our free cash flow is growing," he said. "Why would you change a successful strategy?"

According to Canada's annual telecom report, consumer prices for cellular services declined in recent years but ticked back up in 2025. Canada still had some of the highest wireless prices compared with other developed countries.

items: If Quebecor buys Telus, less competition could mean higher cellphone bills, experts say

blocks.text: Quebecor is currently Canada's fourth-largest telecom company. With its $14.77-billion market capitalization and Telus's $21.72-billion market cap, the potential deal would make Quebecor larger than Rogers or Bell by that metric.

Péladeau also framed the proposed bid as a way of protecting Canada's sovereignty, noting Elon Musk's satellite internet provider Starlink services parts of the Canadian market and is likely hungry to expand its operations.

"[Starlink's] business model is the world, like Netflix's business model was the world," Péladeau said, adding that Netflix "destroyed a Canadian industry" despite not having a licence with the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC).
Quebecor is currently Canada's fourth-largest telecom company, with a $14.77-billion market capitalization. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

Telus says it has formed a special committee to review the offer and determine the value of the potential deal. So far, the committee has discovered a number of "significant risks," John Manley, the chair of Telus's board of directors, said in a statement on Monday issued by the company.
Telus also takes issue with how the Quebecor proposal values the company.
Manley said Telus would continue to engage with Quebecor, the government and regulatory authorities about those concerns while exploring alternatives.
The federal perspective so far

In its news release on Monday, Quebecor acknowledged that Canada's Competition Bureau — along with other authorities, such as the CRTC and Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada — will need to approve the deal.
Earlier this week, Prime Minister Mark Carney said more competition, lower prices and better service would be key to any decision regarding the telecom sector.
'This is the last thing we need': NDP asks feds to block Quebecor's Telus bid

Carney declined to comment directly on Quebecor's proposal but said that under certain circumstances and depending on the market structure, an oligopoly situation can lead to more competition with fewer players. He didn't elaborate further.
Péladeau said he doesn't think anyone would disagree with Carney's comments, noting that even if there are three Canadian companies, there will still be other competition, like Starlink.
On Friday, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said his party has not yet seen the proposal but would study it and base its judgment on the principle of lowering prices for consumers.

items: Why Quebecor wants to buy Telus and what it could mean for British Columbians

blocks.text: Poilievre also criticized Carney's comments, saying he has never seen "any economist anywhere in the world say that oligarchies ultimately bring prices down.... Once again, Mr. Carney favours the corporate power brokers over the consumers."
NDP Leader Avi Lewis has called on the Competition Bureau to cancel the sale, saying it will increase costs for consumers and trigger layoffs.

"We already pay some of the highest cellphone prices in the world," he said. "I just think it's so obvious to the vast majority of people who are suffering under this cost-of-living crisis that this is just yet another thing where the big boys just ... swallow up another company."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Benjamin Lopez Steven is an associate producer for CBC's The House and a digital writer with CBC Politics. He was also a 2024 Joan Donaldson Scholar and a graduate of Carleton University. You can reach him at benjamin.steven@cbc.ca or find him on X at @bensteven_s.
