articles.title: Why the U.S. midterms might have ended JD Vance's presidential hopes
articles.summary: Vice-President JD Vance's presidential ambitions for 2028 could be among the more significant political casualties of the Democratic blue wave in this month's midterm elections.

image.caption: JD Vance's chances of becoming the Republican presidential candidate in 2028 may have suffered a significant blow, with reports suggesting that U.S. President Donald Trump has begun to sour on his vice-president. (Tom Brenner/Pool Getty Images No)

blocks.text: JD Vance's presidential ambitions for 2028 could be among the most significant political casualties of the Democratic blue wave in this month's U.S. midterm elections.
His chances of becoming the Republican candidate in two years may have suffered a more recent blow, as reports suggest U.S. President Donald Trump has begun to sour on his vice-president.

"Despite years of work to keep his feet glued to Trump’s MAGA coattails, [Vance] is probably losing any semblance of hope that he’ll get to be a GOP frontrunner in 2028," New York Intelligencer staff editor Chas Danner wrote in an article under the headline "JD Vance’s presidential dream is being snuffed out."

items: JD Vance blames Iran war for midterm thumping. Is he really blaming Trump?

blocks.text: "At the beginning of the year, Vance was widely seen as the GOP’s presumptive 2028 nominee. He may end the year as the presumptive also-ran, if that."

Over at the conservative magazine National Review, senior writer Noah Rothman also weighed in on what he views as Vance's diminishing political fortunes, saying, "Those who invested in JD Vance’s political stock ... may be looking to offload their holdings."
Vance hasn’t publicly said if he will run for president in 2028, but before the midterms, he was considered a front-runner, with perhaps the highest name recognition of any potential candidate.

However, since the midterms, Vance's aspirations "have suffered, because he's Donald Trump's vice-president," said Michael Traugott, a research professor emeritus at the University of Michigan's Center for Political Studies, in an interview with CBC News.
Exit polls suggested Republicans lost the election over issues relating to inflation and the cost of living, government corruption and the war in Iran.
"The problem is that the vice-president can't separate himself very easily from the administration's policies," Traugott said.
Donors express concern about Vance

According to the Wall Street Journal, after the Democrats' success in taking the House of Representatives and Senate in the midterms, some Republican donors began making calls to senior party members and expressing concerns that they couldn't back Vance, because he's too tied to an unpopular administration.
There are reports that Trump has grown frustrated with Vance's position on Iran. (Mark Schiefelbein/The Associated Press)

This illustrates the challenge Vance faces: Do Republican primary voters want a candidate who has broader support among the general public but isn't directly connected to the president, or will they only support someone who has Trump's endorsement?

"There’s a real challenge of how you position yourself to be viable in a general election while winning a primary that still requires you to bow down and kiss the ring,” Igor Volsky, a Democratic strategist, told Reuters.

Trump hasn’t endorsed Vance or anyone else. Reports have also emerged recently that Vance himself is not so sure about a run, particularly in the wake of the Republicans' disastrous showing in the midterms.
In Republican primaries, Trump still commands a lot of votes and a lot of respect, Martin Cohen, a political science professor with James Madison University, told CBC News.
"I would definitely think that the front-runner would be the candidate with Trump's endorsement, if he does give one," he said.
Vance blamed Iran war for midterm losses
That means Vance will have to get his boss's approval, as well as the support of the MAGA base, while "trying to distance himself a little bit, at least," Cohen said.
Vance's attempt to distance himself from the administration may have already begun, with possible consequences.
Following the midterms, Vance, in a lengthy post on X, levelled much of the blame for Republican losses on the war in Iran.

"If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so," Vance wrote. "Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest."
JD Vance blames Iran war for midterms. Is he really blaming Trump?
Vance, who according to reports has for a while privately expressed reservations about the war, has simultaneously argued that there's "no daylight" between him and the president on Iran.
In response to the X post, Trump agreed Iran may have been a factor in the midterm losses. But he also insisted that invading Iran was the right policy decision.
Trump told reporters that Vance's post should have added, "'If you had it to do again, would you do it again?' The answer is yes."
Soon after the X post, the vice-president, who had been leading negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, was taken off the file.

Posting on Truth Social, Trump said his administration no longer needed a deal with Iran and that he wanted Vance to focus "his complete and total attention" on alleged crime and corruption in Democratic-run cities and states.
Abe Greenwald, the executive editor of Commentary magazine, called Trump's sidelining of Vance a "remarkably skillful work of public humiliation."

Karen Beckwith, a political science professor with Ohio-based Case Western Reserve University, said in an email to CBC News that Trump's removal of Vance from any responsibility for negotiating or interacting with Iranian counterparts "undermines Vance as a potential presidential nominee in 2028."

Meanwhile, Fox News host Brian Kilmeade lashed out at Vance after his interview with Kilmeade's colleague Laura Ingraham, in which Vance said there were some who want the Iran war to go on indefinitely.
Kilmeade rejected that assertion, calling it "another straw man" argument from Vance, while adding that "he never should have been vice-president."
Trump reportedly frustrated with Vance

Beckwith said this could leave Vance without any substantive achievements on which to campaign for the 2028 nomination — unlike potential opponents like Secretary of State Marco Rubio or Republican governors and senators.
While Trump may have soured on Vance, he reportedly has been praising U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. (Mark Schiefelbein/The Associated Press)

Asked about his social media post about Iran at a news conference on Friday, Vance, flanked by both Trump and Rubio, said the president makes the decision, that the president has said he would attack Iran again and that it's his job to support the president.

Vance's comments followed a New York Times report earlier this week that Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with how Vance has framed his assessment of what went wrong in Iran, complaining to aides and allies that Vance should have made a point of saying the president made the right decision in going to war with Iran.
According to the Times, Trump has instead been praising Rubio, a strong supporter of the U.S. war against Iran, as a potential presidential candidate.
While past polls have shown Vance as the leading Republican candidate for 2028, a recent poll from Emerson College had Rubio as the top choice.

Presidents in recent history, dating back to Ronald Reagan, have all publicly endorsed their vice-presidents who sought to be their party's candidate for the presidency. That includes Joe Biden's endorsement of Kamala Harris in 2024, despite Biden having been pressured by members of his own party to not run for second term.

"I don't think that Donald Trump is going to be shy about endorsing somebody," Traugott said. "Ordinarily, we would think the vice-president would have an advantage ... so the fact that he may be souring on this relationship is very important. Even if they were to say that [Trump] was remaining neutral, that would be a slap in the face of that."

Yet some political observers are cautious about writing Vance's political obituary just yet. Republican strategist Mark Bednar told CBC News that Vance has developed good connections to a large donor base within the Republican party over the past couple years.
Meanwhile, Republican strategist Barrett Marson told CBC News that Trump may have actually done Vance a favour by taking him off the Iran file.
"That is an absolute blessing. The less one has to do with this immensely unpopular war, the better you are off politically."

Marson added that there's still a lot of time before 2028, meaning things could improve to Vance's benefit. For example, gas prices could come down significantly, interest rates for homes could drop and voters could start to view the economy in positive terms.
"Two years is just an eternity," Marson said. "Especially in Donald Trump's America."

articles.title: Will Canadian workers refuse to handle Israeli goods? Why unions increasingly say they should
articles.summary: A movement to cut off Israeli goods is spreading across Canada's unions. The Canadian Labour Congress, which represents more than 3 million workers, passed a resolution last month declaring trade,…

image.caption: Palestinians inspect damage to a building and tents a day after they were hit by an Israeli airstrike in Gaza City last week. The Canadian Labour Congress passed a resolution last month calling on workers to refuse to handle weapons and military equipment destined for Israel. (Jehad Alshrafi/The Ass

blocks.text: Canada·New

A movement to cut off Israeli goods is spreading across Canada's unions. The Canadian Labour Congress, which represents more than 3 million workers, passed a resolution last month declaring trade, services and relationships with Israel to be “hot cargo," emphasizing a call for workers to refuse to handle weapons and military equipment destined for Israel.
Canadian Labour Congress calls on workers to refuse handling weapons and other goods destined for Israel
A movement to cut off Israeli goods is spreading across Canada's unions and workers are preparing for potential battles with their employers.

The Canadian Labour Congress (CLC), which represents more than three million workers, passed a resolution last month declaring trade, services and relationships with Israel to be "hot cargo" and calling for workers to refuse to handle weapons and military equipment destined for Israel. The CLC also resolved to cut ties with the Histadrut, Israel's largest trade union organization.

The moved followed similar resolutions passed by numerous local and provincial labour groups over the past year, including the Ontario, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and Labrador labour federations.

Next week, the B.C. Federation of Labour will vote on a resolution that would "support affiliate locals and unions in refusing to engage with" Israeli goods and specifically ask the B.C. government to stop importing and selling Israeli wines.
A BCFL spokesperson said in an email that the union does not comment on resolutions before delegates have had a chance to debate them.

The movement to isolate Israel with economic pressure is growing as its deadly strikes on Gaza continue after a ceasefire deal was signed more than a year ago. Gaza health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire went into effect in October 2025, while Israeli officials say five Israeli soldiers have been killed.

items: UN commission says Israel has continued to commit genocide in Gaza since truce
Tracking Palestinian, Israeli deaths since the Gaza ceasefire went into effect

blocks.text: "I think the vast majority of union activists have come to see that this is a situation where people of conscience, and workers of conscience, need to do what they can to oppose Israeli crimes and our complicity in them," said Kevin Levangie, a member of the Labour for Palestine steering committee that pushed for the resolutions across Canada.

A report by the UN's Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian ‌Territory including East Jerusalem and Israel stated last month that Israel has continued to commit genocide since the ceasefire. Israel dismissed the charge as part of a "misinformation campaign."

Israel is facing accusations of genocide before the International Court of Justice, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is wanted on an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Gaza.
Union says Palestinian workers made request

Levangie, a member of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers Atlantic in Halifax, says the Canadian government is not doing enough to stop the flow of weapons to Israel, or the import of products manufactured in illegal settlements in Palestinian territories, so it "falls on Canadian workers" to ensure they are complying with their obligations under international law.

Levangie visited the West Bank as part of a union delegation in September and October, where he met with Palestinian groups, including trade unions, who have asked unions in the West to take on this work.
"We're honouring a request that was made by Palestinian workers," he said.

"In that way, it's very similar to the South African context of the 80s and 90s, where South African trade unions, South African civil society organizations, were asking for us to isolate apartheid South Africa until the freedom struggle was won."
Kevin Levangie, a member of the Labour for Palestine steering committee, says workers want to comply with international law. (Submitted by Kevin Levangie)

Canadian dockworkers, postal workers and retail workers joined international campaigns declaring South African goods as hot cargo in the 1980s to pressure the country's government into ending apartheid.

Canadian workers also took hot cargo actions to protest Argentina's human rights abuses and suppression of trade unions in 1979 and joined a trade union boycott of Indonesia in 1999 to protest the country's military occupation of East Timor.

items: Jet fighter maintenance parts, bombs shipped to Israel via U.S., groups say in new report
Report suggests arms still flow from Canada to Israel despite denials

blocks.text: Canadian unions have not acted on the CLC resolution, though workers in other countries have taken action.

Italian workers staged a day-long general strike last month, blocking roads, causing rail delays and cancellations and disrupting airports to protest Israel intercepting an aid flotilla that was carrying food to Gaza.

Canada's unions did not participate in a global day of strike on Oct. 30, which saw efforts to disrupt weapons transfers to Israel as part of a broader anti-war protest at 113 ports across 22 countries.
Critic says Israel singled out
The CLC's resolution has created tension within the labour movement, according to Kim Kazur, labour consultant and adviser with the Canadian Jewish Labour Committee advocacy group.

A retired Ontario Public Service Employees Union member, Kazur says she feels unions are unfairly singling out Israel on the world stage and the resolutions are a way to "hide behind" what she views as "Jew hate."
Kazur says unions should "stay in our lanes" and not contribute to "divisive political ideology," adding workers could end up putting themselves at risk of being fired.

items: 12 Jewish teachers file human rights complaints against group of Ontario school boards, unions
Winnipeggers hit the streets to support Israel, stand together, 3 years after Oct. 7 attacks

blocks.text: "The idea of a union encouraging its members to do some type of disobedience is not OK," she said.
Levangie denied accusations of hate and noted Labour for Palestine regularly collaborates with advocacy group Independent Jewish Voices in its organizing work.
"We in Labour for Palestine are strongly opposed to antisemitism and all other forms of hate," he said.
Advocates say they want to end Canada's involvement in manufacturing F-35 parts that could end up on Israeli jets. (Amir Cohen/Reuters)
Workers could face discipline

Levangie acknowledges a concern about discipline or retaliation by employers if workers refuse to handle certain goods — from components of F-35 fighter jets that are manufactured in Canada, to oranges shipped from Israel to Canadian grocery stores — but says the declaration of hot cargo is the labour movement's "greatest power."
The tactic is often used in the context of labour disputes, says Andrew Stevens, an associate professor at the University of Regina's school of business.

The BCFL issued a hot cargo edict on Nov. 2 — in solidarity with striking Trigon employees with the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 523 — ordering workers not to handle Trigon coal and petroleum products.

items: How are 3 labour disputes affecting the Port of Prince Rupert?

blocks.text: Moving to concrete action can be complicated, however, especially on a heated political issue.

"If an individual worker engages in this, I think people are going to see it as insubordination, which means that they could be subject to discipline up to and including termination of employment," Stevens said.
If two or more workers deliberately refuse orders to unload goods or procure services, he says that would be deemed an illegal strike.
Is Israel erasing evidence of alleged war crimes in Gaza?
Stevens says workers will need strong support from their unions and labour organizations if they plan to carry out the CLC's resolution on the ground.
"Its strength is really going to be premised on the support from the unions themselves," he said.
CBC News has reached out to the CLC for comment but has not heard back.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kevin Maimann is a senior writer for CBC News based in Edmonton. He has covered a wide range of topics for publications including VICE, the Toronto Star, Xtra Magazine and the Edmonton Journal. You can reach Kevin by email at kevin.maimann@cbc.ca.
With files from Reuters

articles.title: How the Alberta government could fill a new pipeline with royalties paid in oil
articles.summary: To overcome one of the biggest challenges facing Premier Danielle Smith’s ambitions to build a large oil export pipeline to the West Coast, the Alberta government could decide to fill the pipeline…

image.caption: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith attends the Oil Sands Expo in Fort McMurray, Alta., on Sept. 16. The Alberta government is looking for oil producers to sign long-term contracts to ship on the proposed Pacific Link pipeline to the West Coast. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary·Analysis

To overcome one of the biggest challenges facing Premier Danielle Smith’s ambitions to build a large oil export pipeline to the West Coast, the Alberta government could decide to fill the pipeline with oil collected as royalties from industry.
Royalties-in-kind mean province can collect oil instead of cash — then use it to ensure pipeline goes ahead

One of the biggest challenges facing Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s ambitions to develop and build a large oil export pipeline to the West Coast is having oil companies sign long-term contracts to actually use the proposed project.

If that hurdle becomes too big to overcome, the Alberta government could turn to a relatively unknown policy that allows the energy royalties it receives to be paid in oil — and then use that oil to service the pipeline.

Companies have to pay a royalty to the provincial government for any oil and natural gas produced in Alberta. These monthly royalties add billions of dollars in revenue to provincial coffers each year.

But some industry experts say the provincial government could instead use the "royalty-in-kind" policy to collect enough oil to fill the proposed Pacific Link pipeline, which would transport oil from the Edmonton area to a port near Vancouver.

items: Alberta announces royalty program as part of plan to double oilsands production

blocks.text: "If there needs to be more barrels that are diverted and are sent on the Pacific Link when constructed, for sure the Crown could elect to take more and more of its royalty in bitumen and physically allocate it to the Pacific Link," said Grant Sprague, a former deputy energy minister in Alberta.

For now, Smith is focused on encouraging the largest oil companies in the province to ramp up oil production, which is why the premier unveiled a new incentive program last week focused on promoting the construction of new oilsands facilities.
A view of Suncor's Base Plant oilsands mine. Suncor is one of the companies considering whether to proceed with expanding production in the oilsands. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)
More production is the ideal way of filling the Pacific Link pipeline, said Sprague, since the royalty-in-kind program would not help Alberta’s overall goal of increasing oil exports.
"It's a diversion. It's never additive. And I think the real goal has got to be to have sufficient production to fill — maybe not fill, but to service all of the existing pipelines," said Sprague.
"… Short answer: it's not a panacea."
Financial repercussions
Requiring companies to pay royalties in oil could also come at a financial cost for producers.

Oil companies have long-term contracts on other export pipelines to ship a certain amount of oil. If a producer would not have as much oil to fill their space on the pipelines, they would still have to pay for the amount of pipeline capacity they are signed up for.
That would result in oil producers paying for shipping on "air barrels."

Former Suncor chief executive Mark Little said he's "very certain" the Alberta government is considering the option to take payment in barrels of oil — and companies would feel the squeeze if it went ahead.
"It's a hit on the company's financial performance unless they expand," Little said.
"I think we're going to see some capital get invested just because they're either going to go willingly or get somewhat forced."

Alberta could access enough oil to fill the million-barrels-per-day Pacific Link pipeline by using the royalties-in-kind program, said a government official, speaking on background. However, the official said, it is not the government’s intent to do so, since it is confident the oilpatch will increase production.

items: Why Danielle Smith wants to give a subsidy to the oilpatch despite near-record profits

blocks.text: The Pacific Link project faces other challenges, including legal challenges filed by three First Nations in Alberta in an attempt to overturn the federal government’s designation of the pipeline as a project in the national interest.
The designation allows the federal government to fast-track and consolidate the approval process for the pipeline under the Building Canada Act.
'If they want to acquire some barrels, just go buy them'

Foregoing royalty payments in cash could also blow a hole in Alberta's budget. Other ramifications include souring the investment climate at a time when Alberta is trying to attract tens of billions of dollars to grow its energy sector and double oil production.

"If you're trying to attract new investment to increase growth, threatening people ain't the way to do it," said Richard Masson, former chief executive of the Alberta Petroleum Marketing Commission, the province’s commercial oil and gas agency that runs the royalty-in-kind program.
"Royalties-in-kind is just a mechanism that complicates life, creates uncertainty and doesn't create an extra barrel to ship," he said.
Richard Masson, former chief executive of the Alberta Petroleum Marketing Commission, does not think using the royalty-in-kind program is a good idea for the province. (Justin Pennell/CBC)
If the provincial government needs oil to fill its pipeline, it’s much easier to purchase barrels on the open market, he said.
"Alberta gets its royalties in cash every month at the market price. If they want to acquire some barrels, just go buy them," said Masson. "Easy-peasy."

The Alberta government has said one of the reasons for having the royalties-in-kind program is to have "more control over the province’s resources, allowing for the expansion of egress and market access."
Alberta announces royalty program as part of plan to double oilsands production

Some large oilpatch companies have been reluctant to build new oil production facilities because of a lack of support from shareholders. Despite lucrative oil prices, many investors would rather oil companies continue to produce hefty profits, as opposed to spending billions of dollars to invest in new projects.

items: Alberta bill would force oil and gas companies to save money for cleanup of each new well drilled
Northern Alberta residents question safety of proposed carbon capture and pipeline project

blocks.text: The chances of the provincial government using the policy are relatively small, considering the financial harm it could cause some oil companies — but it does provide a pathway for the proposed pipeline to proceed even if oil companies don’t sign contracts committing to use it.

At the same time, the policy gives the provincial government an important tool to motivate the oilpatch to invest in pumping out more crude, even though it would complicate its relationship with Alberta's largest industry.
"There's this really interesting tension that I've never seen before," said Little, the former Suncor CEO.

articles.title: WhatsApp is a 'lifeline' for refugees. Advocates fear it could be severed in fight over federal bill
articles.summary: Meta said this week that Bill C-22 could force it to "consider" withdrawing encrypted services like WhatsApp from Canada. Rights advocates say that would cut refugees and other newcomers off from a…

image.caption: A Meta representative says the tech giant would 'need to consider' withdrawing services from Canada such as WhatsApp that would be affected by the federal government's lawful access legislation, Bill C-22. (Ramil Sitdikov/Reuters)

blocks.text: When Raymond Gukiina came to Canada in 2022 as a refugee, he used WhatsApp to stay in touch with his family back home in Uganda.
But Gukiina also turned to the popular messaging app to help other refugees and asylum seekers who were struggling to find safe places to live amid a housing crisis in Toronto.

"We opened up a WhatsApp group that had mostly refugees that were sent out of the shelters or living on the streets ... to share information" about shelter beds and other services, the 26-year-old said.

Gukiina, now executive director of the National Network for Immigrants and Refugees-Canada, a non-profit that grew out of the WhatsApp group, said the platform remains key for newcomers to get support in their new communities and maintain ties to loved ones abroad.

But a recent Senate committee hearing has fuelled concerns that a lawful access bill being advanced by the federal government could affect messaging services such as WhatsApp and cut vulnerable people off from the platform they rely on.
Raymond Gukiina says WhatsApp is a key tool for refugees and other newcomers to Canada. (Submitted by Raymond Gukiina)

That's because major tech companies have said they may be forced to suspend services that offer end-to-end encryption if the controversial legislation, known as Bill C-22, which would give law enforcement more access to private communications and data, comes into force.
"Shutting it down [would be] really a tragedy," Gukiina said of WhatsApp.

Alina Murad, director of federal government relations at The Refugee Centre, a non-profit group in Montreal, also described WhatsApp as "a very, very crucial tool" in the refugee resettlement and integration processes.
"It's a lifeline in many ways," she said.
"So if you take away this tool that, for the most part, everyone in the world is familiar with and knows how to use with ease, it leaves people vulnerable — extremely vulnerable."
Meta would consider pulling apps from Canada over 'lawful access' bill
The legislation

Bill C-22, which is being studied in the Senate, would require technology companies to adapt their systems to be able to provide private communications to Canadian law enforcement and the CSIS spy agency during investigations.
Companies would also be forced to retain users' metadata for six months.

The government has said the measures will help create "a modernized legal framework that helps ensure that CSIS can investigate threats to the security of Canada and law enforcement agencies can effectively detect, deter and respond to crime."

But at a Senate committee hearing on Monday, representatives for Meta, which owns WhatsApp, and Signal, another encrypted messaging service, said Bill C-22 would hamper their ability to offer end-to-end encryption in Canada.

items: Meta would 'consider' pulling services from Canada if lawful access bill passes as is

blocks.text: Rachel Curran, Meta's head of public policy for Canada, said the company "would need to consider" withdrawing affected services — effectively, WhatsApp — if the legislation passes.

"In a similar situation, when Apple was served with a technical assistance order that it could not comply with without weakening or breaking encryption in the U.K., it chose to withdraw those affected services from the market," she said. "And I think we would need to consider the same option."

Udbhav Tiwari, vice-president of strategy and global affairs at Signal, also told the Senate committee on Monday that the firm would be forced to either "engineer a vulnerability" into its platform or refuse to comply with the law.
"And at that point in time, we will have no choice but not to serve Canadian users."

David Taylor, a spokesperson for Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree, told CBC News in an email Friday that the legislation does "not permit or require companies to introduce systemic vulnerabilities or so-called 'back doors.'"

Amendments adopted in the House of Commons also clarify that "service providers cannot be required to break encryption or introduce systemic vulnerabilities, that ministerial authorities cannot be used in place of judicial warrants and that any data-related requirements are strictly limited to metadata, with reduced retention periods and clear legal thresholds," Taylor said.
"The proposals on encryption in C-22 are similar to those in Australia, where WhatsApp continues to operate. They are stronger than those in the United Kingdom, where WhatsApp is available."
Group chats key
Nevertheless, the legislation has fuelled fears that WhatsApp service could be affected.

WhatsApp says more than three billion people around the world use its platform. While usage varies by country, a 2023 survey by the U.S.-based Pew Research Center found that it had "broad reach" in middle-income countries in particular.

Ashika Niraula, a senior research associate at Toronto Metropolitan University's Global Migration Institute, studies how highly skilled migrants and international students use digital platforms before and after they get to Canada.
WhatsApp says more than three billion people around the world use the messaging platform. (Dado Ruvic/Reuters)
She said WhatsApp groups — where more than 1,000 people can exchange messages in a single digital space — have emerged as a key place for newcomers to get information about life in Canada.
That ranges from how to rent an apartment, open a bank account or find affordable groceries to navigating the Canadian immigration process.

The group chats help newcomers feel less isolated while creating a place to speak openly with people who share their cultural backgrounds or languages and have gone through similar experiences, Niraula said.
"It can help [make] settling into a new country feel less overwhelming."
Encryption offers 'level of safety'

At the same time, WhatsApp remains an easy and cost-effective way for newcomers to stay in touch with relatives in their home countries, said Lauren Lallemand, co-executive director of the Canadian Council for Refugees.
"Not being able to get back in touch with your family members who you've been separated from" can have very real effects, including on peoples' mental health, she said.

items: Privacy watchdog urges Senate to further amend Liberals' controversial lawful access bill

blocks.text: "If it's no longer possible to use WhatsApp in Canada but it continues to be available across most other countries ... there's a sense of people in Canada being left behind."
Lallemand also said the fact that WhatsApp is encrypted "provides some level of safety" for people who fled persecution in their home countries — and losing that encryption could put them at risk.

"People who are journalists, human rights defenders, refugees in Canada — they often already face repression transnationally, like surveillance threats and intimidation by foreign governments," she said.
"So it is doubly dangerous to be introducing laws that could further target communities that are already very vulnerable."

articles.title: How a rainy afternoon in Montreal inspired an iconic Canadian board game
articles.summary: The bestselling Canadian board game of all time has sold more than 100 million copies worldwide, in 17 different languages. On the game's 45th anniversary, co-creator John Haney offers a personal…

image.caption: Scott Abbott, left, Chris Haney and John Haney in 1982 on a boat docked beside the Old Boat Works, also known as Sheppard Boatworks, in Niagara-on-the-Lake, where the initial assembly and packaging of the first Trivial Pursuit games took place. (Submitted by John Haney)

blocks.text: The Sunday Magazine

The bestselling Canadian board game of all time has sold more than 100 million copies worldwide, in 17 different languages. On the game's 45th anniversary, co-creator John Haney offers a personal account of the game's creation in his new book, My Trivial Pursuits: The Inside Story of the Board Game That Conquered the World.
45 years later, what’s the secret behind Trivial Pursuit’s enduring appeal?
LISTEN | How Trivial Pursuit inspired generations to stay curious :
The Sunday Magazine18:54How this Canadian's questioning colour wheel inspired generations to stay curious
Scott Abbott says he remembers it like it was yesterday.
It was a rainy Saturday in Montreal, December 15, 1979. His roommate, Chris Haney, had just returned from grocery shopping with a Scrabble game in hand.
The two had been gearing up for a Scrabble showdown, but the game's $11 price tag sparked a conversation that would send them down a life-altering path.
“There must be a lot of money in games,” Abbott recalls Haney saying. “Why don’t we invent a game?”
Abbott threw out one word: trivia.

The idea wasn't entirely out of left field. Abbott, then a sports journalist with The Canadian Press, and Haney, a photo editor with the Montreal Gazette, often spent late nights at the Press Club firing trivia questions back and forth.
So Abbott grabbed a pencil and a scrap of paper, settled down at the kitchen table and started sketching.
And that was the birth of Trivial Pursuit a general-knowledge board game that became a global cultural phenomenon.
An archival image of 270 Landsdowne Ave. in Montreal where the idea for Trivial Pursuit was birthed on Dec. 15, 1979. (Submitted by John Haney)

The bestselling Canadian board game of all time has sold more than 100 million copies worldwide, in 17 different languages. The game also spawned television adaptations and made a fortune for its four creators — Abbott, Haney and his brother, John Haney, and their lawyer friend, Ed Werner. Early investors who put up just $1,000 saw their stakes grow to more than $1 million, Abbott says.

John Haney, now 80, offers a personal account of the game's creation in his new book, My Trivial Pursuits: The Inside Story of the Board Game That Conquered the World, released for the game's 45th anniversary.
“It’s legacy for me and for my children and grandchildren to actually know what happened,” Haney told Piya Chattopadhyay on The Sunday Magazine.
A game that spans generations
Abbot says he and the other founders were "flabbergasted" by the game's success.
“We were stunned at the beginning. We thought the game would appeal to our generation, baby boomers, and then we found out quickly that it appealed to everybody from eight-year-olds to 88-year-olds.”

Earl Holland Jr. of Salisbury, Maryland, remembers growing up playing Trivial Pursuit with his older sisters as a five-year-old child in a household that was obsessed with Wheel of Fortune and Jeopardy.

A self-described trivia enthusiast who “read encyclopedias” for fun, Holland Jr. remembers being drawn to the game’s “frantic pace” and “knowledge-building”. Decades later, that early fascination came full circle when he appeared as a contestant on the American television adaptation of the board game, hosted by LeVar Burton. His episode aired in late October.

Earl Holland Jr., far right, standing beside other contestants and host LeVar Burton, second from left, for the taping of an episode on the second season of The CW's Trivial Pursuit game show, on October 10, 2025. The episode aired on October 22, 2026. (submitted by Earl Holland Jr.)
For Holland, the secret ingredients behind Trivial Pursuit's enduring appeal are a combination of its ability to evolve with the times and bring people together — plus its impeccable timing.

“Its birth … it coincided pretty much around the era of the rebirth of quiz shows and Jeopardy and things like that,” said Holland. “It's a social activity. I think its ability to span decades and be flexible and versatile is something that is huge with different audiences, no matter how old you are.”
And if you ask the games’ creators, that was the whole point.
“A professor can play with a street sweeper. They compete together on the same level,” Haney said.
And that appeal may have been baked into the game from the very beginning.
From kitchen table to worldwide sensation

Michael Wurstlin was a 26-year-old freelance graphic designer when Haney and Abbott approached him in 1979 with a piece of cardboard covered in glued-on scraps of paper and a request to design their board game.
Wurstlin went on to create the iconic board artwork and scroll logo for the original Trivial Pursuit Genus edition, in exchange for five shares in the company.
But he wasn’t immediately convinced the project was destined for greatness.
“They were very scruffy guys, chain-smoking, I’m pretty sure they were drunk half the time,” Wurstlin said.
Still, he says he believes their irreverent, anti-establishment spirit was precisely what set the game apart.
One of the co-creators, John Haney, pictured with the original mockup for Trivial Pursuit, presented to graphic artist Michael Wurstlin in 1979. (submitted by John Haney)
Behind that laid-back attitude, however, was an almost obsessive commitment to getting the questions right.

“It became an all-consuming obsession,” said Abbott, recalling how they scoured everything from newspapers and magazines to television, movies and books for materials. “We couldn’t sit down for lunch without reading a ketchup bottle from top to bottom to see what questions might be on it.”
In a pre-Google world, verifying the answers to all 6,000 questions required onerous double-sourcing. Even then, Abbott says the first printing wasn’t without mistakes.
The first eight of thousands of questions John Haney wrote for the first edition of Trivial Pursuit. (submitted by John Haney)
A copy of a letter the Trivial Pursuit creators wrote to their shareholders asking for help selecting their "five favourite questions and answers." (Submitted by John Haney)
Getting the game into stores proved just as difficult.
After plenty of rejection, in 1981 a couple of stores in Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont., finally agreed to take a chance on the fledgling game.
There was nothing like seeing that game on a shelf. It was like a dream come true.John Haney, Co-creator of Trivial Pursuit
Demand quickly outpaced expectations. Before long, people were lining up around the block at Toronto's then-famous toy store, Mr. Gameways' Ark, to get their hands on a copy.
“We sold [close to] 1,200 games in basically less than two months before Christmas of ’81,” Abbott said. “By September 1982, we sold… 20,000.”

They got a Canadian distribution deal with Chieftain Products Inc., which held the Canadian rights to Scrabble at the time, and then an American distribution agreement with game manufacturer Selchow & Righter.
That deal helped propel Trivial Pursuit from a hometown hit into a global sensation.
By 1984, nearly 20 million games had been sold in the United States alone.
Former U.S. president Ronald Reagan and others play Trivial Pursuit aboard Air Force One in 1985. (Submitted by John Haney)
A 1988 TV Guide cover featuring all four of Trivial Pursuit's creators, promoting a TV movie based on their story, which was featured on CBC. (Submitted by John Haney)
Abbott recalls realizing just how famous they'd become during a 1985 press tour in Australia.

“We’re at the zoo in Melbourne, and we’re walking down a pathway, [some] 10 year old kids in front of us–they turn around and they say, ‘look, it’s the Trivial Pursuit guys!’ and they’re all clamoring and jumping all over us,” he said.

According to the Canadian Museum of History, Trivial Pursuit helped fuel a board-game boom throughout the 1980s and ’90s, inspiring Canadian inventors to chase similar success. Few came close, however.
Haney said the decision to sell to Hasbro in 2008 was simple.

"It had gotten too big and our baby had left the nest and taken on a life of its own." Haney says Hasbro kept the game going, bringing out new editions that he and his co-founders wouldn't have had the energy to do themselves.
"So we were very happy to sell it. We had a few beers that day.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kayla McLean is a web journalist with CBC News in Toronto. She grew up in Brampton, Ont., and received her bachelor of arts in media production at Toronto Metropolitan University. Before joining CBC in 2024, she worked as a breaking news reporter at Global News Toronto — covering everything from crime, sports, festivals and politics. She also reported for Global News's current affairs show, The New Reality, covering stories with a focus on racial equality and climate justice. She also previously held positions as a chase producer and writer for CTV News Channel.
Audio produced by James Chaarani

articles.title: Agnes Callamard: US sanctions vs ICC could jeopardize Rodrigo Duterte case
articles.summary: 'There is only one response to the USA threats and sanctions: it must be protecting the ICC. Not appeasing the predator,' Callamard says

blocks.text: LAUNCH. Amnesty International Secretary General Agnès Callamard calls for justice for drug war victims during the November 20 launch of 'Walang Pahimakas' in Quezon City, on November 20, 2026.
Mia Magdalena-Fokno
'There is only one response to the USA threats and sanctions: it must be protecting the ICC. Not appeasing the predator,' Callamard says

items: Agnes Callamard, Amnesty International's secretary general, warned that US sanctions against the ICC could put at risk its operations and the trial of former president Rodrigo Duterte.
Callamard emphasized that if the ICC cannot function due to these sanctions, it risks losing its credibility and independence.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Amnesty International secretary general and human rights activist Agnes Callamard warned that the United States’ sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC) could imperil the court’s operations, including the case of former president Rodrigo Duterte.

At the sidelines of the event, the Amnesty secretary general told Palawan News that these sanctions could cause the collapse of the court. “If the ICC is unable to function, the ICC will collapse. Or the trial will deliver the verdict that will have lost its credibility. At all levels, whether it’s operational or political, it’s bad news.”

Callamard was in the Philippines for Rappler’s Social Good Summit on Saturday, November 20, where she and other advocates talked about the need to build a community amid threats of Artificial Intelligence. As United Nations Special Rapporteur on Extrajudicial Killings, she was barred by the Duterte administration from entering the country. The Marcos government lifted this ban only last September.

Callamard told Rappler, “The trial of ex-president Duterte is due to start on 30 November. It could take one year or probably more until judgment. If no action is taken to protect the ICC against the US sanctions, the trial may never proceed.”

In an interview with Rappler, Callamard said: “I was told that just this week, in a meeting of the state parties to the ICC, the diplomats of the most powerful countries, including Canada and the UK, and other G7 states, have insisted the only way forward is to negotiate with the US and agree to their demands. They continue to refuse to protect the ICC.”
According to Callamard, the US is giving the ICC until April to comply with the following:

items: No ICC jurisdiction over non-state parties or “an impunity carve-out for the USA”
Dropping of ICC investigations and arrest warrants in the Palestine situation
Immunities for heads of state

blocks.text: The Amnesty secretary general said that if the powerful countries that are part of the ICC “are prepared to negotiate with the US, the ICC will lose its independence and credibility.”

“The failure to protect the ICC is a betrayal of the mothers and fathers, sons and daughters of the Philippines that have spoken up against Duterte’s senseless war, against threats and intimidation,” she added.

Duterte has been detained in The Hague, Netherlands since March 2025 after he was arrested due to three counts of crimes against humanity case. His case stemmed from the alleged killings of the Davao Death Squad and his bloody war on drugs that killed nearly 30,000 people, according to several human rights organizations.
In April, the ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I confirmed all three charges against the former president. His trial will start on November 30 at the ICC Trial Chamber III.

blocks.caption: ICC wraps up pre-trial hearings as Duterte’s November 30 case nears

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump, in the last years, has been pushing to sanction the ICC which has jurisdiction over genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and crimes of aggression.

In February 2025, Trump authorized economic and travel sanctions against those involved in the ICC probe into US citizens or allies like Israel. He imposed sanctions, in the same year, against four ICC judges over the issuance of an arrest warrant for Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu and a past decision to open a case into alleged war crimes by US troops in Afghanistan.

Just last August, the US government imposed sanctions against ICC President Tomoko Akane and Abdoulaye Seye, a senior ICC trial lawyer. But the most concerning development is the ICC-wide sanctions that the Trump administration is planning to announce soon.

Entity-wide sanctions would bar US citizens and companies from giving the ICC funds, goods, or services without permission from the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control. This would be tricky because banks often comply with these sanctions since they are dependent on access to the American financial system, according to Reuters.
Apart from this, ICC-wide sanctions could affect the court’s IT services and insurance, investigations, and payments to employees.

blocks.caption: Trump administration prepares sanctions vs ICC, sources say

blocks.text: Callamard urged European governments to “use their ‘blocking’ law, which bars European companies from complying with foreign sanctions. She also called on central banks in Europe to give the court bank accounts,” Palawan News reported.

She told Rappler: “There is only one response to the USA threats and sanctions: it must be protecting the ICC. Not appeasing the predator. They continue to refuse to protect the ICC. They are betraying decades of efforts forged in blood and tears to ensure that no one, absolutely no one should be above the law.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Ombudsman upholds 6-month suspension of ex-Cebu mayor, 5 officials
articles.summary: The Ombudsman rejected the bid to overturn a gross neglect of duty finding against six officials.

blocks.text: November 22, 2026 | 4:50pm
Philstar.com / File

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman has affirmed the six-month suspension without pay of former Dalaguete, Cebu Mayor Ronald Allan Cesante and five municipal officials for gross neglect of duty over the irregular construction of a municipal warehouse on a privately owned lot.
In a November 22 order, the anti-graft body denied the motion for reconsideration filed by Cesante and his co-respondents, upholding its August 29, 2025 decision.
Also ordered suspended were the following Bids and Awards Committee (BAC) members:

items: Edmund Centeno, former municipal assessor and BAC chairperson
Brenda Vergara, former municipal budget officer and BAC vice chairperson
Essandre Amprad, zoning officer II
Donald Abraham Lara, municipal government department head I
Cristina Miranda, administrative assistant V

blocks.text: The administrative case stemmed from complaints filed by Jose Rene Moran and Braulio Moran, who questioned the municipal government's construction of a warehouse on property owned by the heirs of Teodorica Severino and Pedro Moran.

In their defense, the respondents argued that they acted within their authority during pre-procurement proceedings by relying on a "Permit to Enter" signed by Hetzel Moran, who held a special power of attorney (SPA) from the heirs.

The Ombudsman, however, found that the SPA only authorized Hetzel Moran to enter into a deed of exchange with the local government, not to grant the municipality access to build a structure on the land.

"Respondents Mayor and BAC members should not have merely relied on the Permit to Enter but proactively verified from all the legal heirs if indeed Hetzel Moran had the legal authority to allow the Municipality unlimited access over the said lot," the Ombudsman's order read.

The Ombudsman stressed that the officials failed to exercise due diligence to ensure that all property documents were in order before proceeding with the project's procurement, award and construction.

Cesante had argued that as head of the procuring entity, he should not be held liable for procurement lapses committed by the BAC. He invoked the Arias doctrine, a 1989 Supreme Court ruling stating that heads of offices may rely to a reasonable extent on their subordinates when signing documents in good faith.
However, the Ombudsman rejected this defense, noting that jurisprudence dictates the Arias doctrine "is not some magic cloak that can be used to shield public officials from accountability."

In denying the appeal, the anti-graft office noted that the respondents failed to present any newly discovered evidence or demonstrate any grave error of fact or law, adding that their motion merely reiterated arguments already settled in the original ruling.

articles.title: China, ASEAN countries struggle over South China Sea code of conduct
articles.summary: The Philippines wanted a South China Sea code of conduct in place by 2026. But persistent disagreements between China and ASEAN countries are slowing progress toward a deal.

image.caption: Chinese missile frigate Yuncheng launches an anti-ship missile during a military exercise in the waters near south China's Hainan Island and Paracel IslandsImage: Zha Chunming/Xinhua/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: It was supposed to be a breakthrough year. The Philippines had intended to set up a code of conduct with China for the South China Sea during its 2026 ASEAN presidency. However, at the summit in Manila in mid-November they had to abandon their goal. Some 80% of the text had been negotiated, declared Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro, but the key areas of dispute had remained unsolved.

Much more than diplomatic wording is at stake. The South China Sea is one of the world's most important shipping routes, it is rich in fishing grounds and may harbor significant oil and gas reserves. Primarily, however, it's a region of strategic competition: With its so-called Nine-Dash Line (often drawn in red), China claims a large portion of the sea. Its claims overlap with those of the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei.

A code of conduct is to set up rules for parties dealing with one another and prevent incidents at sea from escalating. However, opinions differ, particularly with regard to its binding nature and its geographic scope.

"The basic problem with establishing such a code of conduct is that China is supremely powerful and has no real interest in a legally binding agreement," said political scientist Andreas Ufen, Southeast Asia expert at the German Institute of Global and Area Studies (GIGA). Beijing had little incentive to impose restrictions on itself as long as it was able to pursue its interests in the region even without such an agreement, Ufen told DW.

blocks.caption: The 2026 ASEAN summit in Manila Image: Reuters

blocks.text: Mere recommendations or legally binding set of rules?

The Paracel Islands serve as an example of just how difficult the unresolved issues are. In China, the group of islands is known as Xisha, in Vietnam as Hoang-Sa. Hanoi apparently wants to include them in the code's geographic scope, but China rejects this. An agreement within the ASEAN framework could indirectly affect the territorial claims of the parties involved.

"A fundamental problem is that so far there's no consensus on whether the code of conduct should be legally binding," said Felix Heiduk, head of research division Asia at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP). China and the ASEAN nations have been negotiating an agreement for 12 years without major progress so far.

There were reservations about such a treaty not only in China but also in other ASEAN countries. They would subsequently have to ratify a legally binding agreement under international law in their own countries. A non-binding code of conduct, by contrast, would be little more than a voluntary declaration of intent, Ufen told DW.

The definition of an "incident" is controversial as well. Are coast guard missions with use of water cannons included? Or blockades of supply vessels? Or is the code only applicable when military force is involved? This will determine which actions will be covered by the regulations in the future.

"These are by no means just technical details. Their clarification determines to a great extent whether the code of conduct will in fact be effective or will ultimately remain only a non-binding declaration of intent," Heiduk said. An agreement without valid commitments would bring about little change.
How a small, disputed island wards off China's power claims
Diverging interests

Ufen views China's attitude as a strategic calculation. "I believe that China is interested in keeping the conflict simmering, so to speak, without having to commit itself to a truly binding legal regulation," he said. In this way, Beijing could strengthen its position in the South China Sea without limiting its room for maneuver.

At the same time there are also diverging interests within the ASEAN group. The 11 member states are by no means united. The Philippines and Vietnam are particularly vocal in their opposition to China. Malaysia and Indonesia pursue a more restrained approach. Cambodia and Laos have close economic ties with Beijing and don't have any territorial claims in the South China Sea.

"From the start of the negotiations, the lack of unity within ASEAN has been a problem. In a way, it's a permanent obstacle," Heiduk said. The group makes decisions based on the consensus principle, which basically means that every member state can block a unified position. Recurring confrontations between China and the Philippines exacerbated the problem by undermining trust and making it more difficult to reach compromises.

Ufen also believes that diverging interests are a key impediment. "Reconciling them is extremely difficult," he said. China could take advantage of the discord. Beijing preferred bilateral negotiations with individual countries rather than dealing with an entire, united group of nations.
Fundamental conflicts unresolved

A study published by the Singapore-based Yusof Ishak Institute (ISEAS)reaches similar conclusions. Not only China but internal divisions within ASEAN stalled negotiations. The authors warn against exclusively relying on a comprehensive, legally binding treaty. Initially, partial agreements — for example, on crisis communication, rescue operations at sea or maritime environment protection — could be a first step. Developing the 2002 agreement on a non-binding Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea could also be an intermediate step.

blocks.caption: A Chinese Coast Guard and a Philippine Navy vessel during an encounter in the South China Sea on July 20, 2026Image: Jay Tarriela via X/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Ufen doubts whether Beijing is interested in a binding result. "For this reason, I can't really imagine that China has a real interest in a code of conduct that includes legally binding regulations," he said.

Heiduk warns against overestimating the significance of a potential agreement. "Even if the code of conduct was signed at some point, in whichever shape, that would in no way solve the conflict in the South China Sea," he said. The code could regulate how to handle incidents, but it could not eliminate territorial disputes and competing claims to maritime areas.
Can ASEAN do more to stop the violence in Myanmar?
Hopes for future negotiations

This constitutes the dilemma for ASEAN nations as well, whose foreign policy oscillates between China and US ties: An agreement that's as binding as possible could fail because China and individual member states have reservations. A weak, non-binding code, however, could give the impression everyone agreed but would hardly change conduct at sea.

The American Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) summed up the situationafter the summit in Manila: "Whatever progress was made this year, it is almost certain that the hardest sticking points remain unresolved."

Negotiations will be continued in 2027 under Singapore's chairmanship. Whether this will turn into more than just another diplomatic effort will depend on whether China is prepared to submit itself to regulations which limit its scope of action and whether ASEAN will be able to reach a consensus.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Prosecution ready should VP Sara, Mans Carpio testify in impeachment court - Joel Chua
articles.summary: The prosecution is ready should Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio, testify before the impeachment court, House lead prosecutor and Manila 3rd District Representative Joel…

blocks.text: Published November 22, 2026 4:44pm

The prosecution is ready should Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio, testify before the impeachment court, House lead prosecutor and Manila 3rd District Representative Joel Chua said, as senator-judges aim to secure a verdict before the year ends.

“While we are anticipating that [na haharap si VP Duterte/Atty. Mans Carpio] na possible, dahil kagaya ng sinasabi namin from the very beginning, sila lang ang makakasagot nang lahat ng isyung 'to. Kung sila man ang ipepresenta, naka-ready naman kami,” Chua told Super Radyo dzBB on Sunday.

(While we are anticipating that VP Duterte and Atty. Mans Carpio may appear, as we have been saying from the very beginning, they are the only ones who can answer all these issues. If they are presented as witnesses, we are ready.)

On the 45th day of Duterte’s impeachment trial, defense witness and Trade and Industry Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo testified that Cale88 Foods Corp., a listed business interest of Carpio, is a registered micro, small and medium enterprise (MSME) despite millions in money flows.
The Senate impeachment court has moved the trial dates from November 26 and 27 to December 1, 2, 3, and 4 due to the unavailability of defense witnesses.
Chua expressed satisfaction with the witnesses presented by the defense, saying that their testimonoes and actions are helping the prosecution in winning the case.
“Masaya kami sa mga testigo na ipiniprisinta nila dahil sa tingin namin ay maganda naman ang nagiging performance sa pagtulong sa amin,” Chua said.
(We are pleased with the witnesses the defense has presented because we believe they have been performing well in helping our case.)
“So far, nakakailang testigo na sila, so far wala pa silang naiprepresentang substantial,” he added.
(So far, they have presented several witnesses, but they have yet to offer anything substantial.)

He explained that the prosecution's case focuses on the P817 million in allegedly undeclared wealth in Duterte's Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN), not the issue of whether Cale88 is a registered business or not.
“Hindi namin kinukuwestiyon ang pagiging rehistrado ng Cale88. Ang isyu rito ay yung hindi idineklarang income,” Chua said.
(We are not questioning whether Cale88 is registered. The issue here is the income that was not declared.)
“Dahil ang Article 2 ay about unexplained wealth. Walang kaugnayan kung rehistrado 'yan o hindi. Ang pinag-uusapan dito, ito bang kinita sa Cale 88 ay isinama sa SALN,” he added.
(Article 2 is about unexplained wealth. Whether it is registered or not is irrelevant. The question is whether the income earned from Cale88 was included in the SALN.) —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Inspired by Bernie Sanders: A German agency is using US-Style campaigning to boost the left in 2029
articles.summary: "The Goodforces" wants to see a swing to the left in the 2029 German elections. The agency counts New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Bernie Sanders among its inspirations. Could it transform the…

image.caption: The Goodforces provides digital space for progressive political campaigns on social mediaImage: Neunund20/the Goodforces

blocks.text: Red, red, green — those are the party colors of the left-leaning coalition recently formed in the German state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Now a Berlin-based agency wants to see the same alliance between the center-left Social Democrats, the socialist Left Party, and environmentalist Greens win the 2029 national elections.

The Goodforces wants to help make that a reality with their campaign neunund20 (twenty-nine), taking its cue, in part, from the American left. The agency was set up in response to the rise of the far right across Europe.

Co-founder Patrick Haermeyer told DW that the campaign's aim is "to give people hope and an alternative narrative to: Things are getting worse and worse." He worked as an online organizer for the election team of Bernie Sanders in the US Democratic presidential primaries in 2016 and cites Sanders' "not me, us" campaign as an inspiration.

blocks.caption: Patrick Haermeyer got his inspiration from working with the campaign of US Senator Bernie SandersImage: Karol Roller

blocks.text: Content creation, sharing, networking, campaigning

Neunund20 currently has two strategies: It provides digital space for short-form videos and social media content on political and social topics on Instagram, Tiktok, and Bluesky. At the same time, it tries to connect content creators, activists, NGOs, and political initiatives around shared "progressive" issues.

Users with a particular interest can click to get a link giving them access to archives of relevant social media material that they can then reshare. That feature is modelled on the campaign of New York's left-wing mayor Zohran Mamdani.

And there are other projects. The Goodforces was recently involved in a tactical voting initiative in the September elections in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, intended to keep the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) from winning an absolute majority. Haermeyer says physical campaigns of that kind are necessary to provide essential "interim victories" en route to the next parliamentary elections.

The Greens and the SPD, the two parties recommended by the app created by the organization, made it over the 5% hurdle and into parliament. The help that they received was declared by each party in the form of a €40,000 ($43,900) donation.
Germany's public broadcasters under fire from far-right AfD
Super PAC-style campaigning is new in Germany

The agency sees itself as a kind of Super PAC, modeled on political organizations in the United States that collect money to carry out campaigns without directly supporting a single party or a special candidate.

For Christoph Bieber, political scientist at the University of Duisburg-Essen, the Goodforces is an interesting new type of player on Germany's political scene because it operates outside the country's political parties.

But many of those parties are eyeing the development with disquiet. The far-left, populist, immigration skeptical Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) criticized the Goodforces' intervention in Saxony-Anhalt, telling the newspaper FAZ that it was an "infantilizing, and perhaps even antidemocratic action." The neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP) called the tool "wrong and intentionally misleading." The FDP failed to clear the threshold, while the BSW only just squeaked in. The AfD gained 43% of the vote and its candidate may soon become Germany's first far-right state premier since the Nazi era.
What's behind the rising polarization in German politics?

Haermeyer set up the agency in 2024 along with Peter Jelinek, and both men previously worked for Green Party European Parliament member Michael Bloss. Ahead of that year's European elections, the EU's Green Deal began to come under increasing attack.
That year also ended with the collapse of Germany's first federal coalition between the SPD, Greens, and FDP, after much infighting and attacks from right-wing quarters.

"We noticed that more and more successes and freedoms that we had fought for were being reversed: Things like freedom of movement, border checks, and other things that were coming more and more under fire," Haermeyer told DW. "And we noticed that it was primarily democratic and progressive forces that were being drawn into defensive battles."
Stemming the rise of far-right AfD with digital know-how

The AfD, founded in 2013, already in the age of social media, has successfully targeted younger voters with in its online campaigns. But the older parties, in particular, have struggled. The Goodforces saw a need for support in the online environment and is now seeking to plug this gap.

The social media accounts of the campaign neunund20 contain posts on domestic German topics, such as the current negotiations to form a red-red-green coalition government in Berlin, and the country's new military service law. They also highlight "wins" in Spain in the protests for affordable housing and for US Democrats in the midterms.

Haermeyer stresses that the issues the agency highlights are determined together with a wide range of grassroots organizations and activists. "The campaign is not agreed in conjunction with the SPD, the Left Party, and the Greens," he said.
Agency funding comes from commissions and small donations. Haermeyer says that contributions generally range from $20 to $50.
Why Germany's political center is losing ground
Big-tent parties in Germany in decline for decades
Bieber sees the emergence of non-party campaigning, long an accepted practice in the US, as a bid to compensate for the shortcomings of traditional parties.

"It is an omission of the parties," he said. "For years they have been saying we have to modernize, we have to become more open and get away from rigid membership structures. There are legal regulations governing the organization of political parties in Germany, but perhaps it could be more flexible and open."

The center-left and center-right big-tent parties have been in decline for decades. Membership of the SPD dropped from 943,000 in 1990 to some 348,000 at the end of 2025. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) has seen a fall from 750,000 to under 357,000.

Party membership is particularly low in former communist eastern Germany. Centrist parties have also struggled to attract younger voters. A report by the Deutsche Kinder und Jugendstiftung (German Children and Youth Foundation) showed that only 20% of young people felt their concerns were taken seriously in the 2025 German elections and that trust in parties was low.

In the United States, campaign financing comes predominantly from donations, and lobby groups can buy influence by contributing unlimited amounts to super PACs. In Germany, party funding comes, in part, from taxpayers and membership fees, and donations are capped. However, Bieber warns that whereas there are strict rules regarding the disclosure of donors to US Super PACs, these do not exist in Germany.

The political scientist does not believe that US-style campaigning is going to take hold in Germany, but he does see potential dangers: "This could be a door opener to make others consider whether they want to go in this direction in the field of campaigning. And he added: "If it becomes rife, it could lead to a further devaluation of parties and their structures."

articles.title: Highly lucrative: Bank of England directors illegally profited from post-abolition enslavement in Cuba
articles.summary:
New research finds that the British-led Cobre Mining Company helped industrialise Manchester via copper deposits and enslaved African people

•

blocks.text: British businesses run by long-serving directors of the Bank of England profited from “brutal” enslavement in Cuba for decades after slavery’s abolition in the British empire, according to research.

Men and boys were enslaved in prison conditions at the El Cobre copper ore mine near Santiago de Cuba, which supplied British firms during the Industrial Revolution, the historian Chris Evans has found.
In the 1840s, Cuba was the most important foreign source of copper ore for the UK. Copper was critical to Manchester’s cotton industry, railways and telegraphy.
Previous research has revealed that dozens of financiers involved in the founding in 1694 of the Bank of England invested in enslavement.
Now, Evans’s research reveals that ties between key figures in the UK’s financial system and enslavement of African peoples continued even after the government outlawed it.
Britain abolished its trade in enslaved people in 1807 and passed legislation abolishing slavery in most of its empire in 1833.

However, as Britain’s Slavery Abolition Act was coming into force, “City of London figures” were developing mining of El Cobre’s copper ore deposits, an operation which depended on enslavement in Spanish-controlled Cuba.
Key players in the highly lucrative operation included the Bank of England directors Charles Pascoe Grenfell (1790-1867) and William Thompson (1792-1854), acting in a private capacity.

Enslaved copper miners at El Cobre were likely to have been trafficked to Cuba by illegal voyages from the Bight of Biafra, in modern-day Nigeria, as Evans details in his book, Slavery’s Long Goodbye – Capitalism, Nationalism and Christianity in the Age of British Emancipation.

The death rate at El Cobre means it is likely that thousands of Africans were exploited there. Their life stories remain largely undocumented. At the time, slavery was legal in Cuba but the importation of enslaved people was not.
As a partner in the Cobre mining and export company, Grenfell was a driving force in enslaved miners’ exploitation.

Cobre was “likely to be the largest slave enterprise in the western hemisphere” by the 1840s, Evans said. Investors who held Cobre shares from the outset received £102 in dividends for every £40 share between 1836 and 1865.

blocks.caption: Enslavement at El Cobre ended after Cuban revolutionaries captured the town from Spanish forces in November 1868. Illustration: Amgueddfa Cymru/National Museum of Wales

blocks.text: Grenfell was also a partner in a Swansea-based smelter Pascoe, Grenfell & Sons, which bought imports from the mine, in an era when the Welsh port was the centre of the global copper trade.
Meanwhile, Thompson, a former lord mayor of London, exploited enslaved miners through the ore export firm he directed, the Royal Santiago Company.

The UK is facing increased pressure to make a formal apology to Caribbean and African nations for Britain’s centuries-long perpetuation of transatlantic chattel slavery. Commonwealth leaders say “structured dialogue” with the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, will begin in the next year.

While the Tory leader Kemi Badenoch has claimed Britain has nothing to apologise for, scholarship – dating back to the Trinidadian statesman Eric Williams’s 1944 book, Capitalism and Slavery – reveals the global impact of the colonialism and chattel enslavement that was integral to British capitalism’s success.

Evans, a former professor at the University of South Wales, said: “As Britain ostentatiously winds down its own slave system in the 1830s, British capital is boosting slavery elsewhere in the western hemisphere.

“The illegal trade, involving French and Spanish merchants, was flourishing and substantial. There were British (anti-slavery) patrols off the coast of Cuba, but they’re relatively few in number and intercept only a very small proportion of slave ships.”
Conditions at El Cobre were “extremely brutal”, with daily violence and torture. “Slave catchers” were employed to snatch miners who tried to escape to the mountains.
after newsletter promotion

In 1817, under British pressure, Spanish authorities signed a treaty that banned trafficking enslaved Africans to Cuba. But as Cuba’s sugar and coffee plantations relied on enslaved African workers, local colonial authorities ignored it, with 25,000 captives arriving in 1859 alone.

blocks.caption: Charles Grenfell was a partner in a Swansea-based smelter Pascoe, Grenfell & Sons, which bought imports from Cuba. Illustration: Digitised by Bethan Jones/Amgueddfa Cymru/National Museum of Wales

blocks.text: In 1843, pressure from the British and Foreign Anti-Slavery Society prompted legislation intended to prohibit British subjects from owning enslaved people in other jurisdictions, after undercover investigations exposed British mining companies’ activities in Brazil and Cuba, including at El Cobre.

But after lobbying by mining interests, parliament diluted the legislation, allowing companies to retain enslaved workers as their “property” and hire others. The concessions prompted abolitionists to withdraw their support for the law, which failed to end the exploitation.

Neither Grenfell nor Thompson appears to have faced legal penalties for their involvement. Grenfell became the Liberal MP for Preston in the late 1840s, later boasting that his father had been an abolitionist. Grenfell remained a B of E director until 1864.

Enslavement at El Cobre finally ended after Cuban revolutionaries captured the town from Spanish forces in November 1868. The rebel commander proclaimed the miners’ emancipation on New Year’s Eve, and formerly enslaved workers later joined Cuba’s liberation army.
Evans’s book explores Britain’s overlapping histories of slavery, capitalism and missionary Christianity through the lives of Grenfell and two of his cousins.
Evans added: “The British in the early 19th century had started to understand slavery as a national sin.
“In the classical age of abolition, you could do things like abstain from eating sugar from the West Indies.

“But with copper, you can’t do that because it’s embodied in the industrial world, and, in the age of joint-stock capitalism, you have many British people who invest in mining companies who genuinely didn’t know these companies were using enslaved workers.

“Slavery was rendered invisible by the complexity of industrial society. But British engagement with slavery continued long after Emancipation. It involved the mercantile-financial elite of London as well as hundreds, possibly thousands, of rank-and-file investors from the Victorian middle class.”
A Bank of England spokesperson said: “We have previously acknowledged the role of former governors and directors in the slave trade.”

articles.title: Recto lauds PH's 'successful' ASEAN Summit hosting, urges action on deals
articles.summary: Executive Secretary Ralph Recto on Sunday commended the Philippines" “successful hosting” of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits, stressing the need to follow through on agreements reached…

blocks.text: Published November 22, 2026 3:52pm

Executive Secretary Ralph Recto on Sunday commended the Philippines’ “successful hosting” of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits, stressing the need to follow through on agreements reached during the meetings.
In a statement, Recto, who chairs the ASEAN National Organizing Council, thanked government agencies and other partners that helped organize the summit.

“Led and guided by President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., the Philippines successfully hosted the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits, which were international in productive participation and global in positive impact,” Recto said.

“As Chair of the ASEAN National Organizing Council, I salute the hard work and long hours put in by government agencies and partners to carry out the President’s directive of a summit and meetings that showcase our country’s best and the ASEAN spirit of solidarity,” he added.
The Philippines, which holds the rotating chairmanship of ASEAN this year, hosted the 48th and 49th ASEAN Summits in May and November, respectively.
Recto said the summit's success should also be measured by how the agreements reached would benefit the country and its people.
He cited the Philippines' hosting of two new ASEAN centers for creative industries and maritime cooperation as among the key outcomes of the meetings.
“The one for creative industries will incubate great startups. The maritime cooperation center, on the other hand, will help advance negotiations on the South China Sea Code of Conduct,” Recto said.
He noted that despite the hundreds of meetings held during the summit, several key agreements still needed to be finalized and implemented.
“The summit may be over, and the fanfare may have died down. But the work that follows is no less important than the work that brought us here—and deserves no less dedication,” Recto said.
“Maraming salamat sa inyong lahat. Karangalan ng Pilipinas ang tagumpay na ito. At dapat bawat Pilipino ang makinabang sa bunga ng ating pagsisikap,” he added.
(Thank you very much to all of you. This success is an honor for the Philippines. And every Filipino should benefit from the fruits of our hard work.)— MCG, GMA News
