articles.title: US: ICE arrests 2 at Seattle airport in 'chilling' scenes — governor
articles.summary: Washington's governor has denounced the arrests made by ICE officers at Seattle's airport, calling the incident "horrific."

image.caption: ANti-ICE protesters confronted police at the airport after the arrestsImage: David Ryder/REUTERS

blocks.text: Masked US immigration officers have detained two people on an airport jet bridge in Seattle as passengers boarded a flight to Los Angeles, prompting criticism from Washington state Governor Bob Ferguson and concerns from Alaska Airlines.

The arrests took place at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport around 8 a.m. local time (1600 UTC) on Saturday. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) said the operation targeted Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, a Mexican national who had overstayed his visa.

Agents also arrested Sofia Hernandez Mejia, who they alleged threw hot coffee at the ICE officers during the confrontation. ICE said she had also overstayed her visa and would face a charge of assaulting a federal officer.
When ICE comes knocking: the fight against Trump's deportations

Videos of the incident circulated on social media, showing officers struggling with a person on the ground as passengers look on. One woman could be heard shouting that her daughter was being taken away and that she had a work permit.
Washington governor slams 'out of control' ICE
Governor Ferguson, a Democrat, described the footage as "horrific" and "chilling", accusing ICE of being "completely and totally out of control."
He urged Alaska Airlines to ask federal immigration authorities to leave the state's airports and said he would make the same appeal to other airlines operating at Seattle-Tacoma.
Alaska Airlines said it had received no advance notice of the enforcement operation and was working to understand the circumstances.
The airline also expressed concern over the incident, which it said had been distressing for passengers and employees.

The operation drew criticism from April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, who said it had caused fear and disruption during one of the busiest travel periods of the year.
The flight was delayed, with Alaska Airlines saying many passengers were transferred to other flights. The original service eventually departed at 11 a.m. local time.

articles.title: Nartatez vows impartiality after VP Sara slams PNP
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Sunday assured impartiality among its personnel after Vice President Sara Duterte earlier claimed that the organization has become "the enforcement arm of…

blocks.text: Published November 22, 2026 3:26pm

The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Sunday assured impartiality among its personnel after Vice President Sara Duterte earlier claimed that the organization has become "the enforcement arm of politicians."

“As an institution, we remain guided by the Constitution, the rule of law, and our commitment to serve all Filipinos fairly and impartially, with every action grounded in facts, evidence, and due process,” said PNP chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. in a statement.

“Impartiality is a principle that we strive to uphold in every police operation and public service. Our commitment is to treat everyone with fairness, respect, and compassion, while providing equal protection under the law regardless of one's position or political affiliation,” he added.

The PNP responded to Duterte after the latter told Nartatez "to refrain from paying lip service to the claim that the organization is apolitical—a claim that virtually every Filipino knows to be untrue."
The police earlier said there was "no rescue or release" of a former household staff member of the Vice President and four other individuals.
The PNP pointed out that the concerned former staff members of Duterte were not being held captive when police accompanied their lawyers to a hotel in Taguig City on November 17.
In its latest statement, the PNP said that two legal counsels sought assistance from Fort Bonifacio Police Sub-Station 1 and requested police personnel to accompany them to the hotel.

It added that the five persons voluntarily went with police personnel to the police station. But they declined to execute affidavits regarding their alleged captivity and did not identify any person responsible for the supposed threats or coercion.

“The PNP remains ready to listen, receive complaints, and provide appropriate police assistance to anyone who feels threatened or unsafe. We will act on every report in accordance with established procedures," said Nartatez. —Vince Angelo Ferreras/RF, GMA News

articles.summary: Nepal's rapper-turned-prime minister Balendra Shah is in New Delhi for his first foreign bilateral trip since taking office. He is expected to discuss flood recovery, trade and energy in his talks…

image.caption: Former rappy Shah is Nepal's youngest ever prime minister Image: Niranjan Shrestha/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: November 22, 2026
Nepal PM Balendra Shah set to arrive in Delhi
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah is set to arrive in New Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit, his first bilateral trip since taking office in March.
The 36-year-old former rapper will meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday. He will also meet Foreign Minister S Jaishankar and briefly visit President Droupadi Murmu.

Reconstruction after August's devastating floods is expected to dominate the talks. The disaster left some 1,500 dead and more than 5,200 missing, with roads, bridges, power plants, farms and homes destroyed.
Nepal estimates rebuilding will cost $4.78 billion.
Nepal flood victims come to terms with massive loss
Nepal is also pressing for an extra route for commercial flights to Bhairahawa and Pokhara.

"India is a major and important partner for Nepal," Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai told reporters, saying the leaders would discuss trade, transit, investment, energy, connectivity and infrastructure.
New Delhi said the visit "reflects the importance India attaches to its relations with Nepal," AFP reported. Local media reported that talks may also touch upon unresolved border disputes.

India is Nepal's largest trading partner, accounting for more than 60% of its imports, worth $8.6 billion, versus China's 13%, according to World Bank figures. India and China regularly compete for influence in Nepal.
Shah will be accompanied by Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle and Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal.

articles.title: Lacson flags P241B in 'fragmented ayuda' in 2027 budget
articles.summary: Senator Panfilo Lacson on Sunday criticized P241 billion worth of fragmented assistance programs in the Senate version of the proposed 2027 national budget, saying these would not generate the…

blocks.text: Published November 22, 2026 3:12pm

Senator Panfilo Lacson on Sunday criticized P241 billion worth of fragmented assistance programs in the Senate version of the proposed 2027 national budget, saying these would not generate the productive investments needed to revive the economy.
In a social media post, Lacson said the amount was already lower than the P263 billion allocated for similar items in the House version of the General Appropriations Bill (GAB).

"True. Government construction plunged by -29% as shown by the January-September 2026 national accounts. Agriculture, forestry and fishing: -4.8%; industry: flat; investment: public construction down 15.1% as you mentioned," the senator said.

Lacson said the Senate should reconsider the allocations, arguing that the P241 billion in "fragmented" aid programs and funding for thousands of multipurpose buildings would not address the country's economic concerns.

"In relation to the 2027 budget measure which the Senate will tackle next week, I will insist that these concerns cannot be addressed by the P241B in fragmented ‘ayudas’ in the Senate version - already reduced from the House GAB’s P263B; and 3,950 multi-purpose buildings, on top of another 1,584 MPB’s under the LGSF-Financial Assistance to LGU sub program," he said.
These are not expenditure investments, but patronage aka ‘papogi’ spending," Lacson added.
He also questioned funding for 3,950 multipurpose buildings (MPBs), on top of 1,584 MPBs covered by the Local Government Support Fund (LGSF) from 2022 to 2026.
Lacson said these allocations were examples of patronage-driven spending rather than productive investments, which the government should prioritize amid slowing economic growth and rising inflation.
He cited the 2.1% gross domestic product (GDP) growth in the third quarter of 2026, down from 2.4% in the second quarter, as well as inflation rising to 7.8% in October from 7.2% in September.

The senator also questioned allocations for the Medical Assistance for Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients (MAIFIP), Tulong Panghanapbuhay sa Ating Disadvantaged/Displaced Workers (TUPAD) and Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations (AICS).
He said funding for MAIFIP should instead be coursed through the Universal Health Care program, which is already mandated by law.
Lacson argued that these assistance programs were not needs-based, claiming that beneficiaries were often determined by their connections to political sponsors rather than their eligibility.

“Again, this is patronage-driven. Those who benefit are the ones with connections. It is not needs-based. It is like having a sponsor or a political backer who gets you assistance, even if you are not qualified or deserving,” he said.

Initial findings on the proposed 2027 budget also showed that several multipurpose buildings had received appropriations in 2024, 2025 and 2026, but no structures had been built at their designated sites as of 2026.
Lacson said the Senate should prioritize spending that would stimulate economic activity when it takes up the 2027 budget measure next week.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89
articles.summary: In a statement to Italian media, his family remember him as "the greatest jeweller of our time".

blocks.text: Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.
His family announced the news, remembering him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", according to Italian media.
Paolo Bulgari was Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984 and its jewellery pieces have adorned Hollywood stars and royalty including Diana, Princess of Wales.
The company Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come".
The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.

Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewellery, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome.
Paolo Bulgari joined the company shortly after leaving school, becoming an expert in gemstones - eventually leading the business and overseeing international growth.

articles.title: Fire at confectionary factory in Indonesia leaves at least three dead and dozens missing
articles.summary:
Relatives of the missing victims flocked to the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones

A fire at a confectionery factory west of Jakarta has killed three people with 36…

blocks.text: A fire at a confectionery factory west of Jakarta has killed three people with 36 remaining missing, an Indonesian rescue official says.

Drone footage showed large parts of the factory destroyed, with the roof collapsed in places and smoke still rising from the complex. Photos and videos shared by rescuers show officers entering the charred building in search of the missing victims on Sunday, with small fires still burning in some spots.
Relatives of the missing victims flocked near the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones, footage aired by local broadcasters showed.

blocks.caption: A drone view of emergency crews gathered outside the factory in Indonesia’s Banten province. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: The Fonusa Agung Mulia factory, located in Cikande in Indonesia’s Banten province about 50km from the capital, caught fire on Saturday afternoon, search and rescue official Rizky Dwianto said on Sunday.
“All elements of the joint SAR [search-and-rescue] team are making maximum effort to locate the victims while prioritising the safety of personnel in the field,” he added.
Rizky said four people were injured and taken to a nearby hospital and health clinic.
Firefighters were alerted about 4.30pm on Saturday and found the building already engulfed in flames when they arrived, fire official Tubagus Machfudz told local broadcaster Kompas TV.

blocks.caption: Smoke rises from the factory on Sunday. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: “When we arrived … a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company’s protection system was functioning properly or not,” he said.
The Banten province governor Andra Soni told reporters overnight that an estimated 60 people were inside the factory when it caught fire.
The cause of the incident is still under investigation, the local disaster agency said in an Instagram post on Sunday.

blocks.caption: Crews from Indonesia’s Basarnas search and rescue agency inspect the site. Photograph: BASARNAS/AP

blocks.text: Deadly fires are not uncommon in Indonesia.
In December last year, a blaze that was likely caused by a drone battery explosion tore through a seven-storey building in Jakarta and killed at least 22 people, police said.
In 2023, at least 13 people were killed in the country’s east after an explosion at a nickel-processing plant.

Vice President Sara Duterte’s spokesperson Paolo Panelo has until Monday, November 23, to respond to the show-cause order issued against him by the Senate impeachment court over his remarks questioning the impartiality of several senator-judges.
Senate impeachment court clerk Renato Bantug said the order was sent to Panelo via email on Friday, November 20.
“By email sent last [Friday] ang show cause order vs Paolo Panelo, given until tomorrow to respond,” Bantug said.
The show-cause order stemmed from Panelo’s remarks alleging that some senator-judges were acting as prosecutors in Duterte’s impeachment trial.
Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo raised the matter on Day 45 of the proceedings, asking Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero if the court could take action on Panelo’s statements.
Panelo, however, maintained that his remarks were protected by his constitutional right to free speech.

“I welcome the opportunity to demonstrate that my comments were fair, made in good faith, and did not impede, obstruct, or degrade the administration of justice, and are thus constitutionally protected,” he said in an earlier statement.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Gilas Hiraya out to chase Philippine women’s basketball dreams
articles.summary: Armed with a new name and fresh off an Asian Games silver-medal breakthrough, Gilas Hiraya sets its sights on historic women’s basketball milestones in 2027

blocks.text: STALWARTS. Gilas Hiraya stars Amyah Español (left) and Kacey dela Rosa hope to carve out a new era for Philippine women’s basketball.
UAAP
Armed with a new name and fresh off an Asian Games silver-medal breakthrough, Gilas Hiraya sets its sights on historic women’s basketball milestones in 2027

items: The Philippine women's basketball team has been rebranded as Gilas Hiraya to establish its own identity and aspirations ahead of significant competitions, including the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
The name 'Hiraya,' meaning dreams, hopes, and aspirations in Tagalog, was chosen to reflect the team's unique identity and to inspire women in the Philippines beyond basketball.

The team has seen recent success, including a silver medal at the Asian Games, and players express gratitude for the support and recognition of their hard work and dedication to growing women's basketball in the country.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Shifting to a refreshed identity, the newly christened Gilas Hiraya looks to bear the fruit of the hoop-crazy nation’s hopes, dreams, and aspirations in a huge 2027.
Gilas Hiraya, the new name of the Philippine women’s basketball team, was unveiled this month to establish its own identity as an emerging force in Asian hoops.

The rebrand comes ahead of a pivotal year in which both the 3×3 and 5-on-5 squads will chase a spot in the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, alongside the country’s hosting of the FIBA Women’s Asia Cup at the SM Seaside Arena in Cebu next year.
“It’s really a deliberate decision to give them an identity of their own in order to shape a pathway that is unique for them,” Samahang Basketbol ng Pilipinas (SBP) executive director Erika Dy said.
“We don’t want them to just follow the footsteps of the men’s team or the men’s program,” she added. “We want them to be able to create their own dreams and aspirations for Philippine basketball.”
According to Dy, the idea of giving the women’s team its own name was suggested by FIBA secretary general Andreas Zagklis during a meeting in Shenzhen, China, in July 2025.
Zagklis pushed for the rebrand upon learning that the women’s team used to be known as “Perlas Pilipinas” before aligning its identity with the broader Gilas Pilipinas program in 2019.

Following lengthy discussions with numerous stakeholders, including the UAAP and the players themselves, Hiraya stood out among the other shortlisted names and was officially picked by the SBP on October 27.
“Part of why we chose the word Hiraya, which represents dreams, hopes, and aspirations — it’s a deep Tagalog word,” explained Dy, herself a former basketball player and coach for Ateneo.
“It’s because we really believe that our women’s program can represent that for all the women in the Philippines. It actually goes beyond basketball.”
With a fresh identity, Gilas Hiraya is riding a wave of sustained success, buoyed by a 3×3 silver-medal finish at the Asian Games and a deep tournament run by the 5-on-5 squad in the same meet.
Helping lead the way are Asiad silver medalists Kacey dela Rosa of Ateneo and Amyah Español of Far Eastern University.

“I’m just grateful that we have our own identity now as a women’s basketball team. And I just think every player on the women’s team is very dedicated to growing the sport of women’s basketball in the Philippines,” said Español.
“I’m just thankful that we have such a great support system who believes in us to have our own identity as the women’s team.”
For Dela Rosa, a two-time UAAP MVP, the identity shift reflects the program’s continued development under program director Bacon Austria and head coach BT Toews.

“As Filipinos, we put in a lot of work, like hard work, and we want them to know how much hard work we put in and sacrifices outside the court,” Dela Rosa said. “We also want them to recognize us — we are a team that dreams big.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: COP31 climate talks close to final deal, says summit president
articles.summary: The draft omits mention of the fossil fuels that scientists say are driving climate change, an issue that has been at the center of the fractious talks

blocks.text: JUSTICE. A member of Fridays for Future holds a placard at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, on November 16, 2026.
Umit Bektas/Reuters
The draft omits mention of the fossil fuels that scientists say are driving climate change, an issue that has been at the center of the fractious talks

ANTALYA, Turkey – UN climate talks in Turkey approached a final deal on Sunday, November 22, with the announcement of a new package that COP31 presidents Australia and Turkey hope will achieve consensus on how to advance the fight against global warming.
The new draft deal was released two days after the conference in Antalya was scheduled to end.

If approved, it would acknowledge for the first time that global warming is on course to exceed the 1.5-degree Celsius (2.7-degree Fahrenheit) threshold that countries had sought to preserve, while calling for faster development of carbon-removal technologies to eventually reverse the overshoot.

The draft omits mention of the fossil fuels that scientists say are driving climate change, an issue that has been at the center of the fractious talks. Instead, it includes language referring to a previous COP at which governments had agreed to transition away from oil, gas, and coal.
“We believe that we have put forward a text which all the parties can agree upon,” COP31 President Murat Kurum told a plenary session early on Sunday.
He said the conference would reconvene in the morning to approve the deal.
Environmental group 350.org said it was disappointed by the draft’s failure to mention fossil fuels explicitly, as well as its encouragement of carbon-removal technologies.

“Carbon capture is one of the biggest scams of the overshoot era, and our leaders are on the verge of falling for it,” said Sara Shaw, the group’s campaigns and networks director, referring to the practice of trapping carbon dioxide before it reaches the atmosphere.
Shaw said the draft deal opens the door to more fossil fuel development.
Observers to the closed-door talks said Saudi Arabia and other big oil-producer nations had pushed hard in negotiations for keeping fossil fuels out of the text, and carbon removal in.
A representative for the Saudi delegation declined to comment.

The new text followed intensive consultations between Australia, which is leading the talks, Turkey, which is hosting the meeting, and nearly 200 delegations from many of the world’s richest, poorest, largest and smallest nations.
The presidency gave delegations several hours to raise any objections to the deal, with a session scheduled at 0700 GMT to begin approving it.

Australia’s task, supported by Turkey, has been to find a deal that balances the needs of nations most vulnerable to climate change with those whose economies depend on either the production or consumption of fossil fuels.

This year’s COP is the first since the UN’s environmental body confirmed that the rise in global temperature was set to blow past 1.5 degrees, a threshold all countries agreed over a decade ago to try not to exceed, and beyond which extreme weather impacts intensify. – Rappler.com

articles.title: DENR encourages cycling for cleaner air
articles.summary: The Department of Environment and Natural Resources on Sunday encouraged the public to consider using a bicycle as an alternative mode of transportation to address air pollution in the country.

blocks.text: NATIONAL BICYCLE DAY
Published November 22, 2026 2:28pm

The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) on Sunday encouraged the public to consider using a bicycle as an alternative mode of transportation to address air pollution in the country.
The department also highly suggested to the public to consider walking or riding a bicycle for short trips.

“As I have always said, everyone can help fight climate change. When we rethink our ways of travelling, when we walk or ride a bike instead of driving, we become part of the solution to the climate crisis,” said DENR Secretary Juan Miguel Cuna in a statement.
The National Bicycle Day, which is observed every fourth Sunday of November under Proclamation No. 1052, falls on November 22 this year.
The DENR also launched the Bike-to-Work Campaign for its personnel, which encourages department employees to get into cycling.

"The Department's campaign seeks to encourage sustained cycling among its workforce beyond the annual celebration. The initiative, undertaken in partnership with the Environmental Management Bureau (EMB) and the DoTr Active Transport Project Office (ATPO), aims to promote active mobility, reduce dependence on motorized transportation, and contribute to cleaner air and lower greenhouse gas emissions," the DENR said.
"It will also feature a GHG (Greenhouse Gases) Calculator that will help employees estimate benefits of their work-related bicycle commutes," it added.
There are concentrations of particulate matter (PM) 2.5 in the air, according to the Manila Observatory.

The common sources of PM 2.5 pollution in Metro Manila are motor vehicle exhaust, construction site dust, road dust, practices related to waste management, and the burning of organic matter, known as biomass burning. Contributions also come from natural sources, such as sea salt. —Vince Angelo Ferreras/KG, GMA News

articles.title: No bias among senator-judges, part of our job is to test credibility of witnesses-- Win Gatchalian
articles.summary: Senator Sherwin Gatchalian on Sunday dismissed claims that some senator-judges were biased in the impeachment proceedings against Vice President Sara Duterte, saying their role is to assess the…

blocks.text: Published November 22, 2026 2:18pm

Senator Sherwin Gatchalian on Sunday dismissed claims that some senator-judges were biased in the impeachment proceedings against Vice President Sara Duterte, saying their role is to assess the credibility of witnesses.

“Kasama 'yan sa trabaho ng senator-judges to test the credibility nung testigo, lalo na may mga testigo na nakakalimot, hindi alam. Wala kang choice to test the credibility at to test kung sino itong taong ito. Ginagawa rin naman 'yun ng Prosekusyon, ginagawa rin naman ng Defense 'yun– pwede ring gawin ng senator-judges 'yun,” Gatchalian told Super Radyo dzBB.

(Part of the senator-judges' job is to test the credibility of witnesses, especially if some forget things or don't know the answers. They have no choice but to test the credibility of the witness and determine who this person is. The Prosecution does it, the Defense does it, and the senator-judges can also do it.)

“Pagdating sa bias, dalawang panig 'yan: pwede kang maging bias for the respondent or against the respondent. Pero nakikita naman natin na as much as possible, 'yung mga senato-judge natin ay objective ang pagtatanong natin,” he added.
(When it comes to bias, you can be biased for or against the respondent. But we can see that, as much as possible, our senator-judges are asking questions objectively.)

Gatchalian made the statement after the Senate impeachment court issued a show-cause order against Duterte’s spokesperson, lawyer Paolo Panelo, over his comments regarding the alleged partiality of several senator-judges.
Panelo had asserted that some senator-judges were acting as prosecutors.
Following the issuance of a show-cause order, Panelo invoked his right to free speech in making critical statements about senator-judges.

"I welcome the opportunity to demonstrate that my comments were fair, made in good faith, and did not impede, obstruct, or degrade the administration of justice, and are thus constitutionally protected," hee said.
Panelo assured that he would formally respond to the show cause order within the prescribed period upon receiving it. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Dozens missing as deadly fire hits Indonesian candy factory
articles.summary: A fire at a confectionery factory in Indonesia's Banten province has killled at least three people. Dozens are also unaccounted for after the blaze, which destroyed large parts of the facility.

image.caption: The fire broke out on Saturday afternoonImage: Mohammad Hashemi Rafsanjani/AFP

blocks.text: Indonesian rescue teams are searching for 36 workers who remained unaccounted for after a fire at a candy-making factory killed at least three people, officials said on Sunday.
The fire occurred at the Fonusa Agung Mulia factory, around 50 kilometers (31 miles) west of the capital, Jakarta, in the Serang district of Banten province.
What do we know about the Indonesian confectionery factory fire?
The factory caught fire on Saturday afternoon, local search and rescue agency official Rizky Dwianto said.
"All elements of the joint SAR (search-and-rescue) team are making maximum effort to locate the victims while prioritizing the safety of personnel in the field," he added.
Rizky said four people injured in the blaze had been taken to a nearby hospital and health clinic. Eleven more were said to have been rescued alive.

blocks.caption: Rescue teams have been scouring the factory for survivorsImage: BASARNAS/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The governor of Banten province, Andra Soni, told reporters overnight that 60 people were believed to have been inside the factory when the fire broke out.
Drone footage shows the fire destroyed large sections of the three-story building, bringing down the roof in some places.
Survivors said the fire started in a cooling unit on the third floor.
The factory produces Milkita, an Indonesian brand of milk-based candies and snack products.
Deadly industrial fires in Indonesia
Indonesia has seen a series of deadly industrial fires in recent years, raising questions about the country's workplace safety standards into question.
Among other disasters, at least 22 people were killed in a fire last December that broke out in a seven-story building in Jakarta after a suspected drone battery explosion, police said.
An explosion in a nickel-processing plant in the east of the country killed at least 13 people in 2023.

articles.title: Dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory
articles.summary: At least three people were killed and four injured in a fire at a confectionary factory over the weekend.

blocks.text: At least three people have been killed and 36 were still missing after a fire at a confectionary factory in western Java on Saturday.
Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for the missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.
Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.
The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause.
Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire.

Photos and footage of the scene showed the large factory taken over by flames during the night, firefighters battling the flames, and first responders retrieving at least one body from the wreckage on Sunday morning.
"All members of the joint SAR team are making every effort to locate the missing victims while prioritising the safety of personnel on the ground," the rescue agency said.
Relatives of the missing workers had gathered outside the factory waiting for updates, according to local broadcasts cited by AFP.
Firefighters had been called to the building at 1630 local time (0930 GMT) but it was already engulfed in flames, broadcaster Kompas TV reported, citing fire official Tubugas Machfudz.
"When we arrived (on location)... a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company's protection system was functioning properly or not," he said.
The factory is owned by PT Fonusa Agung Mulia, according to search and rescue authorities.
On LinkedIn the company describes itself as a subsidiary of UNIFAM, one of Indonesia's largest food and beverage companies.

articles.title: ‘Serious error of judgment’: outrage over military AI event at Berlin arts complex
articles.summary:
Kraftwerk Berlin, part of same development as techno club Tresor, transformed into ‘war room’ for arms firm event

With their cavernous post-industrial venues, teeth-grinding four-by-four…

blocks.text: With their cavernous post-industrial venues, teeth-grinding four-by-four beats and bouncers that look like Blade Runner extras, Berlin’s nightclubs trade on a reputation for bleakness. A recent event at one of the city’s most legendary clubland institutions, however, has proven too dystopian even for seasoned techno-heads.

On 11 November, the Kraftwerk Berlin arts complex had its central hall transformed into what visitors described as something resembling a war room, with maps and aerial footage projected on to concrete walls, drones hanging from the ceiling, and guards in flak jackets patrolling the premises with sniffer dogs.

Those who flocked to the venue – which hosts the experimental music festival Atonal and is part of the same complex as the techno club Tresor – had come for the launch of Clarity, an AI targeting system developed by the German arms startup Helsing.

Kraftwerk Berlin this week apologised for a “serious error of judgment” and vowed to revise its commercial rental department’s booking policy, after outrage over the event rippled through Berlin’s music scene. The row has raised uncomfortable questions about the commercialisation of the German capital’s famed nightlife, and the culture sector’s traditional pacifism at a time of growing security threats.

blocks.caption: Club Tresor in Berlin. Photograph: Ullstein Bild/Getty

blocks.text: The Munich-based Helsing was founded in 2021 and counts the Swedish tech entrepreneur and Spotify co-founder Daniel Ek among its investors and board co-chairs. On its website, it describes Clarity as an agentic intelligence platform designed to use drone, satellite and sensor data to lock on to targets.
It claims that human operators ​remain responsible for approving any strikes.

Helsing says Clarity is “developed and built in Europe under European control”. The market leader for battlefield software is Palantir’s Maven, the system that has powered US military strikes on Iran this year. European governments have been scrambling for alternatives to US-developed systems. France’s domestic intelligence service has already announced it is dropping Palantir for a homegrown rival.

But European governments’ boosting of their arms industries is also clashing with an anti-militaristic cultural consensus – nowhere more so than in the former cold war pressure cooker of Berlin, where nightclubs became spaces to dance away the anxieties of the arms race.

blocks.caption: People trying out Palantir’s Maven system at the Defence Security Equipment International event in Tokyo last year. Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/Reuters

blocks.text: “The fact there is a war in Europe and that Ukraine needs German support should not mean that we switch off all our critical faculties,” said Michail Stangl, a Berlin-based music curator and DJ. “We are already seeing how AI-driven targeting systems are being used in Gaza, and it’s hard to imagine that once a company like Helsing develops a successful arms system, it would not sell it on to authoritarian regimes, domestic police, or organisations like Frontex to be used against migrants.”

Speaking to the German broadcaster RBB at its launch event, a Helsing spokesperson said none of its military systems were designed to identify persons, and that Clarity was built to seek out objects such as radar systems, launch pads and ships.
It also said Clarity’s agents specialised in “looking for patterns of behaviour”, which could be interpreted as relating to human activity. Helsing did not respond to a request for comment.
after newsletter promotion

The Clarity launch event was condemned in the strongest terms by Tresor, a nightclub and record label that acted as a bridge between post-Wall Berlin and Detroit’s electronic music scene in the 1990s. “It has no place in the spaces our community has built⁠,” it said in a statement.

Tresor’s founder, the Berlin nightlife entrepreneur Dietmar-Maria “Dimitri” Hegemann, is also the managing director of Kraftwerk Berlin. Hegemann has called the booking “unacceptable”, saying it was done by “a staff member at the company responsible for Kraftwerk’s commercial rental business”, without him being consulted. Given his central role at the arts complex, and the level of planning usually required for such a high-security event, this has surprised some Berlin clubland insiders.

That Berlin’s former underground music venues are rented out for commercial purposes is no longer a deviation from the norm. As recently as 19 October, Kraftwerk Berlin hosted an investment summit organised by the German government and featuring a podium discussion between the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, and the chip manufacturer Nvidia’s then chief executive, Jensen Huang.
In a Q&A released after the Clarity row, Kraftwerk Berlin said it had declined a proposed Palantir-sponsored event in 2022 after consulting its cultural teams.

Defenders of such commercial usages point out that many of Berlin’s nightclubs are struggling with rising rents and plummeting bar revenues. Kraftwerk Berlin may not be one of them, however. The total assets of its operating company, Schaltraum Berlin, were reported in June as having a value of €4.3m (£3.6m).

articles.title: Europe is entering a ‘supercycle’ of national elections. Their outcomes could shake the EU’s foundations
articles.summary:
The effects of the continent’s coming polls will be felt far and wide – and could well turn into ‘key tests’ of the bloc’s resilience

In late 1998, Tony Blair was prime minister of Britain,…

blocks.text: In late 1998, Tony Blair was prime minister of Britain, Lionel Jospin was prime minister of France, and Gerhard Schröder had just been elected chancellor of Germany. The EU had 15 member states and pro-European, centre-left parties were in power – either alone or in coalitions – in all but two of them.

Brisk economic growth was lifting living standards. Eastward enlargement was under way. In Washington, Bill Clinton was pursuing the same brand of “third way” centrism as a middle path between free-market capitalism and traditional socialism. The EU felt like it had the tide of history behind it.

blocks.caption: Celebrations at the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin on 31 December 1999 to welcome the new millennium. Photograph: Peer Grimm/EPA

blocks.text: Not quite three decades later, the continent’s politics once again seem to be tilting in a single direction – except this time, the momentum appears to belong to the nationalist far right, and could bring a significant unpicking of the postwar European consensus that built the EU.

Between the end of this month and the end of next year, an extraordinary electoral sequence will sweep the bloc. Voters in four of the EU’s five biggest member states, by population and economy, head to the polls, with parliamentary elections also due in Estonia, Finland, Greece and Slovakia, and regional ballots in Germany.

Spain kicks off the cycle with a snap general election on 29 November, with prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s socialist coalition facing probable defeat to rightwing parties in the shape of the conservative People’s party (PP) and far-right Vox, which already govern together in some Spanish regions.

Next come presidential and parliamentary elections in France in the spring. The clear frontrunner in the presidential race is Marine Le Pen of far-right the National Rally (RN), well ahead of the far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon and a hopelessly divided mainstream opposition.

When Poland votes later next year, nationalist parties that between them command nearly half the national vote could well unseat the liberal coalition of prime minister, Donald Tusk, despite recent splits. And in Italy, Giorgia Meloni, whose Brothers of Italy party has far-right roots, hopes to secure a second term in elections due before the end of 2027 – while facing pressure on her right flank from the upstart National Future party.

Paradoxically, this nationalist surge arrives amid strong public support for the EU. Shocked by the chaos of Brexit and seeking reassurance in an increasingly alarming world, a record 74% of Europeans say their country benefits from membership, and very few Eurosceptic parties now advocate leaving outright.

The Eurosceptics and nationalists do, however, still view the bloc as a top-down project that undermines national sovereignty, and aim to transform it into an altogether looser association of sovereign nation-states. In the words of the Italian political scientist Natalie Tocci, that means this coming electoral supercycle could “dramatically change the face of Europe” – triggering not simply “a slow erosion of the European project but a hollowing out, if not an outright implosion”.

All elections differ and national specifics loom large. But analysts agree the underlying forces at work here are connected: sluggish growth, ageing populations, strained public finances and a spiralling cost of living have chipped away at support for Europe’s traditional catch-all centre-left and centre-right parties. The wave of youth-led protests sweeping Europe is only the most visible sign of deep voter discontent.

Meanwhile, nationalist parties have become increasingly adept at conjuring and exploiting an ever-evolving list of supposed threats and crises, from migration and vaccines to the green transition, support for Ukraine, globalisation, international elites and supranational institutions – narratives bolstered by Russian disinformation and overt backing for “patriotic” parties from Donald Trump’s White House. As a result, politics has fragmented, and polarised: nearly one in four voters now backs far-right parties – a share that has grown almost fivefold since the mid-1990s.
after newsletter promotion

The rise has not been linear: over the past year or so, while the far-right Alternative für Deutschland scored a historic regional election victory in eastern Germany, in the Netherlands Geert Wilders’s Freedom party lost nearly a third of its seats, Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz was soundly beaten in Hungary and the far-right Sweden Democrats shed support for the first time in 16 years.

But the underlying upward trend appears clear – fuelled above all, political scientists argue, by media normalisation and mainstreaming of far-right ideas, most notably on immigration. Centre-right parties are gradually dismantling “firewalls” that once barred cooperation with the radical right. At the European level, the centre-right European People’s party has increasingly turned to farther-right groups to roll back parts of the European green deal and tighten migration rules.

For the EU, the biggest impact of this election supercycle could be in the European Council of national leaders, which now features just three centre-left heads of government out of 27. If Eurosceptic leaders in France, Spain and Poland join those of Czechia, Italy, Romania, Slovakia and Slovenia by the end of 2027, they would not have the numbers to rewrite EU law – but they would constitute a formidable blocking minority.
EU budget negotiations, future enlargement, aid to Ukraine and deeper integration in essential fields such as defence, energy, finance and technology could all face paralysis, analysts warn.

Safety in numbers, notes Tocci, could change current leaders’ behaviour in the council. Meloni’s relative restraint has been dictated, in part, by her relative isolation among mainstream peers such as Tusk, Sánchez and France’s Emmanuel Macron (alongside Rome’s reliance on €200bn in EU recovery funds).

blocks.caption: Giorgia Meloni and Emmanuel Macron in Antibes, southern France. Photograph: Manon Cruz/Pool Reuters/AP

blocks.text: If she were instead sitting down with the likes of Le Pen, Poland’s far-right Law and Justice (PiS) leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, and a Vox-backed Spanish government, with National Future’s hardline Roberto Vannacci breathing down her neck at home and those EU funds winding down, she might have less incentive to play pro-EU ball.

Analysts agree, though, that the decisive battleground is France. Le Pen’s election platform sets her on a collision course with Brussels: she aims to cut €11bn from France’s EU budget contribution, hold a constitutional referendum to proclaim the supremacy of French over European law, and breach various single-market rules.

And France “carries very significant influence over the EU”, said Mujtaba Rahman of the Eurasia Group consultancy. Compared with Orbán, he notes, a president Le Pen would have “far more leverage to carry out the far-right playbook of subverting the EU’s law-based, supranational architecture”.

Until now, Brussels has contained disruptors such as Orbán largely because there were rarely more than two or three round the table. A cohesive Eurosceptic bloc would leave the EU unable to enforce rule-of-law standards, further integrate economic and security policies or, indeed, agree on anything much at all. The first victim would very probably be Ukraine, with Le Pen leading a blocking caucus against further aid.

Three decades on from 1998, Europe’s coming elections, concluded Stefan Lehne of the Carnegie Europe thinktank, could well turn into “key tests of the EU’s resilience”. The threat to the bloc might not be immediate or existential, he said, but the medium-term risks were significant.

“A stronger role for the radical right may be unlikely to dismantle the EU as it exists today,” Lehne said, but could “prevent it from becoming what it needs to be to deal with the challenges of the future”. And gradually but inevitably, prolonged failure to act collectively as and where needed would lead a “loss of relevance”.

articles.title: [Tech Thoughts] Considering AI to help you think through problems? Same here.
articles.summary: Would inviting a little AI into my life help with brain fog at work? It might be able to help, but it'll take time to know how useful it'll be in the long run.

blocks.text: Would inviting a little AI into my life help with brain fog at work? It might be able to help, but it'll take time to know how useful it'll be in the long run.

items: The author reflects on their ongoing struggles with brain fog and cognitive difficulties following a COVID-19 illness, impacting their ability to write and plan effectively.
Despite initial resistance, the author considers integrating AI tools into their workflow as a potential solution to help manage their cognitive challenges and improve productivity.
Encouraged by his wife, the author plans to explore how AI can assist in organizing thoughts and tasks, recognizing it as a tool that could alleviate some of his struggles.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
It’s been a strange few years since COVID-19 came about.

I fell ill from it a few years back, and without noticing it, it slowly dawned on me that I’d been struggling with my thoughts. In the years following getting sick with COVID-19 and recovering from it, it felt as if I had never completely recovered.
I felt like I was suffering from brain fog and had trouble imagining what my days would look like or how to plan and organize my writing.

For a while, reading would help. I’d read up on topics I wanted to discuss for this column, for example, and I’d be able to react to the information. There was, however, a decided difficulty in being proactive.

It’s as if I wanted to go for a walk in a field and was suddenly stopped by vision-obscuring trees everywhere I looked. I had information and things I wanted to do (and deadlines, to boot), but I had trouble planning properly because I couldn’t connect my thoughts into plans, and put plans into action.

There’s no definitive way to test for what caused my brain fog — the American Brain Foundation says it could be a symptom of being sick from COVID-19, chronic fatigue syndrome, insomnia, or even lyme disease. Adding to that, there’s no official diagnosis for this feeling or sensation of being slower than I used to be, but it has threatened one of the things I hold dear to me: my ability to write stuff the way I want to.
My wife, whom I recently shared these feelings of anxiety with, told me something that felt both logical and like a betrayal of the things I write about here when it comes to artificial intelligence.

She advised me to get used to the idea of adding even just a little AI to my life. I tried to imagine it in much the way I would use eyeglasses, or to put it back to the analogy of my suddenly-appearing mental forest, perhaps I could use it like a chainsaw that wouldn’t cut down everything in my path, but would help with some of the trees in front of me.
Maybe using AI could help me see the outlines in my mind a little better.
It started with little things, like audio transcription for work quotes, which worked well enough.
Like any other tool, it felt like I was being forced to adjust to or relearn something I could do myself. But I kept trying anyway.

Quietly, I’d rely on AI search results to help me sift through information just a little faster, or use the work-based AI-powered summarizer on our content on Rappler for a three-sentence overview. I’d check the outputs for accuracy or truthfulness, fix any issues and, in the case of AI searches, make sure to cite the appropriate sources.
These were helpful, but it left me scared too. Could it help me be more proactive? Can it plot out points of action so I could have more information as to what story leads might be pursuable?
Honestly, I wasn’t sure and I didn’t know, and that’s one other point of fear.

I’d been focused on the potential problems AI can bring — from the environmental to the economic and moral implications of AI use — that it didn’t dawn on me that with some work, it could be just a simple tool for helpful solutions for people having trouble with cognition or planning.
My wife, who put this idea in my head, knows well-enough about using AI to help with her unfathomable workload.
Tonight seems like a good time to ask about what tools she uses to get her job done, and maybe learn how to better use AI to shore up my now-glaring weaknesses. – Rappler.com

articles.summary: Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said US Secretary of State Marco Rubio wants the Philippines to address concerns surrounding the Pax Silica initiative before moving forward with the agreement.

blocks.text: Published November 22, 2026 1:40pm
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said US Secretary of State Marco Rubio wants the Philippines to address concerns surrounding the Pax Silica initiative before moving forward with the agreement.
Gatchalian said Rubio told him during US President Donald Trump's state visit to the Philippines that the government should be given enough time to resolve issues surrounding the initiative.

“He said he knows there are many issues and problems. We should not rush things and should give the Philippine government time to address these concerns,” Gatchalian said in an interview with Super Radyo dzBB on Sunday.
Gatchalian said the United States was monitoring the situation and recognized the need to resolve concerns involving both Pax Silica and the Luzon Economic Corridor before proceeding.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. recently hosted Trump for a bilateral meeting and a state luncheon at Malacañang. Rubio accompanied Trump during the visit and also met with Gatchalian.

Pax Silica is a US-led economic security initiative aimed at building a global supply chain for artificial intelligence and the semiconductor industry. The Philippines is among the 24 countries that have signed on to the initiative.

As part of the initiative, a 1,600-hectare AI-focused industrial hub is being eyed in New Clark City, Tarlac. The proposed development is expected to process critical minerals and manufacture high-tech components for AI and semiconductor industries.
The project is expected to generate jobs and boost government revenues and tax collections through AI processing, chip manufacturing and mining.
However, environmental groups and other stakeholders have raised concerns about the initiative's potential environmental impact and the displacement of local communities.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Police say man whose body lay undiscovered in Sydney bushland for 12 days was killed in suspected hit-and-run
articles.summary:
Joshua Howard, 31, is believed to have been struck by a car and thrown over the guardrail as he was walking home from a party in Rouse Hill

  • Get our

blocks.text: The twin brother of a man whose body lay undiscovered for 12 days after he was killed in a suspected hit and run in Sydney says it has left him feeling like half a person.
Joshua Howard was last seen at a bus interchange in Parramatta, in western Sydney, about 10pm on 7 November.

The 31-year-old was reported missing the following day and detectives later established he had been walking along Garfield Street East in Rouse Hill, in the city’s north-west, about 12.45 that morning.
An extensive search for began in the Rouse Hill area on Thursday with help from Blue Mountains Rescue, the New South Wales State Emergency Service and the Rural Fire Service.
His body was found by police in a bushland gully near Windsor Road in Rouse Hill about 2.45pm on Friday.
Superintendent Jason Joyce said police believe Howard was hit by a car as he was making his way home from a friend’s Diwali party.
“We believe he’s been walking along the side of the road and then been struck, and that’s propelled him over the guardrail into the bushland,” Joyce told reporters on Sunday.
“Based on his injuries … we believe there was some level of force of him being struck by the vehicle.”
It took police 11 days to start the land search because they were initially trying to track Howard’s movements through CCTV footage and doorknocking houses in the area, Joyce said.
Howard’s parents, Peter and Sue, described him as a loving son and sibling to his twin David and older brother Matthew.
He was a talented artist who graduated from the National Art School and always carried a sketchbook and pen with him, they said.
“When he was missing, David went through his room to see whether all those books were gone,” Sue Howard told reporters.
“But they were all there, indicating he was coming home that night.”
after newsletter promotion
She said her family was heartbroken to learn they had likely driven past him the day after he was killed, without knowing his body was there.
“Our poor boy was there for 12 days,” she said.
She said David was particularly devastated, telling her: “I feel as if I’m half a person now.”
Peter Howard pleaded for anyone with information about the suspected hit and run to contact police.
“We don’t want Joshua’s passing to be wasted,” he said.
“We want drivers to know the impact of speeding or whatever happened.
“Think of others. Stop. Ring triple zero and take responsibility for [your] own actions.”

articles.title: South Korea education minister resigns after AI cheating scandal engulfs university exams
articles.summary:
Choi Kyo-jin said he ‘failed to prepare adequately’ for entrance exams, which this year had phones banned and checks for cameras hidden in clothing

South Korea’s education minister resigned…

blocks.text: South Korea’s education minister resigned on Sunday after an AI-assisted cheating scandal that erupted in the lead-up to the country’s key university entrance exams.

The country has been gripped by fears of AI-assisted exam cheating since last Sunday, when the top scorer in a national tax accountant exam confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to achieve a near-perfect score, just four days before the crucial university entrance exam known as the suneung.
The confession sent officials scrambling to roll out a slew of preventive measures for the entrance exams last week, including blocking public wifi in testing areas.
But the education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, struggled to reassure the public, and teachers’ unions criticised the government response as belated.
The annual eight-hour suneung determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects.

“The exam concluded without any major incidents … However, as the minister in charge, I do not believe I am immune from public criticism that we failed to prepare adequately in advance,” Choi wrote on X.
“Now that the exam is over, I take full responsibility and hereby offer my resignation,” he added.
President Lee Jae Myung accepted his resignation, the presidential office said.

blocks.caption: A student turns in her tablet and smartphone at a high school in Seoul ahead of the suneung exams. Photograph: Jintak Han/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Asked during a parliamentary hearing on Monday whether he was confident that authorities could catch would-be cheaters on exam day, the 72-year-old Choi replied: “Due to my age, I am not confident I could.” His response quickly drew public backlash.
Choi did not appear at press conferences in the days leading up to Thursday’s exam, where a vice minister instead announced the preventive measures.

South Korea goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft take-offs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended. The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre.

In the aftermath of the cheating scandal earlier this month, the government announced that smart devices would have to be turned off and handed in for the suneung, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials would also inspect all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars, sleeves and buttons for concealed cameras.
The government also sent emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sounded at full volume and could not be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who has not handed in their device.
Officials said 111 cases of misconduct involving electronic devices were identified during Thursday’s exam, nearly half of which were detected through the emergency alerts.
With Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Keep the faith: Nisperos rediscovers confidence after yearlong PVL injury layoff
articles.summary: Once one of the Philippines’ biggest names in high school and college volleyball, Akari star Faith Nisperos now fights to stay healthy and finally unlock her true potential in the PVL

blocks.text: BACK IN FORM. Akari star Faith Nisperos celebrates a play in PVL action.
MIX GATPANDAN/RAPPLER
Once one of the Philippines’ biggest names in high school and college volleyball, Akari star Faith Nisperos now fights to stay healthy and finally unlock her true potential in the PVL
MANILA, Philippines – For years, Faith Nisperos was a name thrown around in numerous conversations as one of Philippine volleyball’s brightest future stars.

From her time in high school with the dynastic Nazareth-NU Lady Bullpups, to her stint with the Ateneo Blue Eagles in college, and finally, to her jump to the pros with the PVL’s Akari Chargers, Nisperos always had hype surrounding her, and lived up to it for the most part.

In recent times, however, Ateneo’s former “Queen Eagle” had quietly faded into the volleyball landscape’s backdrop, grounded and clipped by a major knee injury that kept her sidelined from April 2024 until July this year.

Save from a brief and scoreless one-game appearance last January 31, Nisperos sat out more or less 15 months’ worth of a budding volleyball career, before finally shaking off her injury tag for good at the start of the 2026 PVL On Tour, and played every game since then.

The 26-year-old spiker then marked the end of a breakthrough 2026 with a 15-point winning effort — her highest scoring mark since November 2024 — in what was otherwise a no-bearing game against ZUS Coffee last November 17.

Though Akari failed to make the playoffs for the 2026 All-Filipino Conference Siklab Series, Nisperos nonetheless felt like a champion after ending the year on a winning and, more importantly, healthy note.

“I’m really happy because I’m finally here. This is me, and this is my territory,” she said in Filipino. “I have to also give credit to my coaches and my teammates who are beside me throughout my process of going back into the game.”

Despite only playing one to two sets at a time due to the Siklab Series’ “all-to-play” requirement, Nisperos still averaged a respectable 6.5 points per game, and played in all of Akari’s eight elimination round matches that netted a 3-5 record.

Though restrictions were in place, Nisperos did not downplay the difficulty of both finding her confidence back, and striving for consistency amid the ever-present dangers of reaggravating her injury.

“It has been months of mental preparation, because I knew that I would return to form one day, I just didn’t know when,” she continued. “Part of the mental preparation was us getting back under pressure again, going through so much scrutiny, and so much responsibilities.”

“I also had people who helped me throughout that mental process. Again, I go back to my coaches and teammates, who also reminded me that I got this. ‘You’re Faith, remember that. You’re strong,’ they said. They always reminded me who I really am.”

Heading into 2027 for the next two All-Filipino Conferences, Sigla and Sinag, Nisperos is raring to further rediscover her true, peak form — the Faith Nisperos that once won V-League MVP in college and led Ateneo to the Final Four as the main star.

“It’s a common denominator for us athletes that we want to get better as time proceeds,” she continued. “I feel like I just want to be more consistent, and improve my non-scoring skills like receiving and defense.”
“Improvement is always one of my biggest goals as a player. I’ve wanted that for such a long time, to improve myself further.”
Stars who faded into obscurity due to injuries are a dime a dozen in all sports. Nisperos could have gone that route, and could very well still go that route, if her fortunes don’t hold.

After all, she’s never had the best of luck. Prior to her yearlong injury spell, Nisperos also lost two more years of her career after her college rookie season was cut short due to the onset of the 2020 pandemic.
But she’s not holding herself to what-ifs stemming from a rocky past.
True to her name, Nisperos always kept the faith — faith in the process, in her potential, and in the light of a future that she fought hard to keep bright. – Rappler.com

articles.title: UN chief warns landslides, drought threaten Banaue rice terraces
articles.summary: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned that the Philippine Cordilleras' centuries-old rice terraces and surrounding communities face growing climate threats.

blocks.text: November 22, 2026 | 12:21pm

In a video on Instagram on Saturday, Nov. 21, 2026, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned that the Philippine Cordilleras' centuries-old rice terraces and surrounding communities face growing climate threats.
Guterres via IG; Philstar.com composite
MANILA, Philippines — For centuries, Ifugao communities have sustained the rice terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras through an intricate system for managing mountain land and water.
Climate change is now testing that resilience with both destructive rainfall and the threat of prolonged drought.

United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres used a visit to Banaue to warn that increasingly severe weather is endangering the terraces and the communities whose water, food and livelihoods depend on them.

"The dramatic impacts of the climate crisis can be felt everywhere around the world. I have just witnessed them again here in Banaue, in the Philippines," Guterres said in a social media post Saturday, November 21.
The Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras are a UNESCO World Heritage site shaped and maintained through generations of indigenous knowledge.

"When these rice fields were built, my country did not exist yet," Guterres said in a video recorded at the site. "It demonstrates the enormous value of the cultures and civilizations of this region."
But the landscape is already showing the effects of more extreme weather.

"Last year we had landslides in this fantastic site. This year we are afraid of drought," Guterres said. "Climate change is having a dramatic impact everywhere, but also here in the rice fields of the Philippines."

In his accompanying post, Guterres said typhoons and landslides had severely damaged the terraces in recent years. A stronger El Niño, he warned, could bring prolonged drought and threaten water supplies, food security and livelihoods.
He called for a faster shift away from fossil fuels, greater use of renewable energy and wider access to early-warning systems.

"The only effective response is urgent climate action: ending the addiction to fossil fuels, accelerating the shift to renewables, delivering early warning systems for all, and protecting the most vulnerable," Guterres said.
He described the terraces as an "extraordinary testament" to the Ifugao communities' understanding and management of their environment. — with John Marwin Elao

articles.title: People should shape AI’s future, says UN panel member Leslie Teo
articles.summary: 'AI is a powerful tool we should build, we should share, but we should always make sure that humans — all stakeholders — have a say in this future that we create,' Leslie Teo says at the 2026 Social…

blocks.text: 'AI is a powerful tool we should build, we should share, but we should always make sure that humans — all stakeholders — have a say in this future that we create,' Leslie Teo says at the 2026 Social Good Summit
MANILA, Philippines – “What can you do to make sure our future, our children’s future, is one that we would wish, not one that is imposed on us?”

Leslie Teo, a Singaporean economist and artificial intelligence executive who serves on the UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, posed that question during his speech at the 2026 Social Good Summit on Saturday, November 21. He outlined ways to develop AI as a positive force for society.
Teo challenged the notion that AI is beyond people’s ability to shape and control.
“Today AI gives us powerful possibilities, but, just like the ideas of economists, the future is for us to determine,” Teo said.
Teo compared the potential benefits of AI development to a pie that economists envision growing larger.

“The fact that the pie grows doesn’t mean that you as an individual benefit. The fact that a consumer benefits doesn’t mean that a society grows. And even if the pie is larger, who gets the slice? Who chooses? Who has a say?” Teo explained.
He said responsible AI development could help address gaps in expertise and efficiency, along with other problems countries face.
Teo advocated for open access to AI tools, saying this would allow communities to shape how the technology is developed and build tools that address their own needs.
“We all don’t need to build frontier models; in fact, that would be very foolish. But many AI tools — many things that matter when it comes to real impact — are open and free,” said Teo.
He added, “If we don’t understand the technology, we can never trust it, we can never use it.”

blocks.caption: Maria Ressa: Understand AI to defend ourselves from ‘predatory’ tech

blocks.text: Teo said learning about AI and building tools to solve specific problems may be easier than people imagine. Developers can also set their own criteria for measuring the tools’ success.
Defining their own benchmarks for success, Teo said, allows developers to retain control over the tools they build.
“If you give someone else the ability to define what is success, you are giving away your sovereignty,” Teo said.
As an example, Teo said there were 8,000 languages in the world, with 1,300 languages in Southeast Asia, but that most models can do 10 at best.”
He asked, “What happened to the rest? Who defines what is good?”

Teo said communities can maintain their sovereignty and address local problems by developing specialized tools that reflect their own needs, rather than relying on Western standards of what is “good.”

blocks.caption: At Rappler summit, human rights figures call for solidarity amid AI threats

blocks.text: Teo also envisioned a future in which AI development becomes more like Linux: frontier models would continue to exist, but open-source and free models would become more widespread as developers share and build on existing technology.

Teo also emphasized that humans should remain in control of AI and other emerging technologies, rather than allowing these systems to dictate how people can act. To illustrate his point, he compared two call centers with different approaches to using AI.

In the first call center, technology helps human agents find accurate information about customers’ problems, acknowledge mistakes, and resolve issues. In the second, AI monitors agents’ productivity and time spent on calls. They must follow a script and cannot or do not deviate from it.
“AI is a powerful tool we should build, we should share, but we should always make sure that humans — all stakeholders — have a say in this future that we create,” Teo said.
This human-centric approach to AI, he explained, is meant to keep AI development sustainable and pointed toward future growth,
Teo ended his speech by returning to the pie analogy, saying his vision of a better world was not about who got the biggest slice.

“It’s about relationships. It’s about society. For me, this is what we want to build with AI. We want to build a better place for our children, where relationships matter, creativity — notwithstanding all the things AI can do — is still very much a human thing, and so is understanding meaning,” Teo said.
“It’s not about a bigger pie. It’s about a meaningful world — much, much more important than just the pie.”

The 2026 Social Good Summit, themed “We, The Humans,” focuses on promoting and defending human rights, community, and shared values as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly widespread. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ICC prosecutors: Duterte defense request violates evidence rules
articles.summary: They said the defense challenged material before it became evidence.

blocks.text: November 22, 2026 | 11:52am
Photos courtesy of the International Criminal Court show former president Rodrigo Duterte during his first in-person appearance before the tribunal since his arrest in March 2025.
Photos / ICC | via The STA / Janvic Mateo

MANILA, Philippines — International Criminal Court prosecutors have asked judges to reject an attempt by former President Rodrigo Duterte's lawyers to challenge undisclosed material before it is formally submitted as evidence, arguing that the request is premature and procedurally improper.
The dispute was outlined in a four-page public filing dated November 20 that was heavily redacted, leaving the underlying issue and contested material undisclosed.

The prosecution originally submitted the response confidentially on November 13 after Duterte's defense and the Common Legal Representatives of Victims filed observations requested by Trial Chamber III.

Prosecutors took no position on the broader issue before the chamber. They argued, however, that the defense went beyond the requested observations by seeking an undisclosed ruling in limine, or before the material was introduced during trial.
"The Defence's request to [REDACTED] goes well beyond the scope of the requested observations from the Chamber, namely, [REDACTED]," the prosecution said.
Prosecutors said the request also violated the ICC's Rules of Procedure and Evidence and a protocol set by the chamber for challenging the admissibility of evidence.
Under Rule 64(1), parties must "raise issues as to admissibility of evidence, including on any of the standard evidentiary criteria, at the time when the evidence is submitted to the Chamber."
The defense could raise its concerns once prosecutors formally submit the contested material, rather than "improperly couching the request" in procedural observations, the filing said.
Prosecutors also sought to correct what they called a "mistaken submission" by the defense. The public filing redacted the disputed statements and the prosecution's explanation.
"For the above reasons, the Prosecution requests that the Chamber reject the Defence's request to [REDACTED] in limine," the filing said.
Trial set for November 30
Duterte's trial on charges of crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder is scheduled to open at the end of the month.
Proceedings will begin at 10 a.m. in The Hague, or 5 p.m. in the Philippines. Judges will first verify that Duterte understands the charges and ask whether he admits guilt or pleads not guilty.
The trial follows Trial Chamber III's ruling that Duterte is fit to stand trial and capable of effectively exercising his fair-trial rights during the proceedings.

articles.title: Analog TV stays on until Jan. 15 as NTC extends shutdown
articles.summary: The Mega Manila analog TV shutdown has been delayed nearly two months.

blocks.text: November 22, 2026 | 10:55am
This photo shows an undated picture of the National Telecommunications Commission's building in Quezon City.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — Analog television broadcasts in Mega Manila will remain on air until Jan. 15, 2027 after regulators postponed Sunday's scheduled shutdown to give households more time to prepare for the transition to digital TV.
The National Telecommunications Commission moved the analog switch-off from Nov. 22 under Memorandum Order No. 011-11-2026, extending the transition by nearly two months.
"There remains a need to sustain and intensify its dissemination to the public to ensure that affected households are adequately informed of the analog TV switch-off schedule," the NTC said.
Existing analog television stations in Mega Manila were directed to continue operating and simulcasting their programs until the new deadline.

Broadcasters must also continue airing public service announcements about the switch-off on both analog and digital television and expand their information campaigns through radio, social media and print.
The extension was backed by the Kapisanan ng mga Brodkaster ng Pilipinas following consultations involving broadcasters and government agencies.
Who is covered
The first phase of the country's analog switch-off covers the National Capital Region and nearby areas including Bulacan, Rizal, Cavite, Laguna, Pampanga and Bataan.

The original deadline was set under NTC Memorandum Circular No. 005-11-2025, which gave television broadcasters in the covered areas 12 months to migrate to the Integrated Services Digital Broadcasting-Terrestrial standard.
Digital TV viewers are not affected by the extension.

Households that still receive television through analog signals will eventually need a television with a compatible digital tuner or a digital set-top box to continue watching free-to-air broadcasts once analog transmission ends.

A Department of Information and Communications Technology-commissioned survey showed that around 80% of television households in Mega Manila were already receiving digital broadcasts as of December 2024.
About 1.1 million households, however, were still dependent on analog television, according to the DICT.
Assistance concerns

GMA Network, the country's largest private broadcaster, had asked the NTC to delay the November 22 shutdown, citing unresolved implementation details for a government program intended to help vulnerable households make the transition.

The proposed assistance program involves the DICT, NTC, Presidential Communications Office and other agencies and is intended to prevent households from losing access to free-to-air television because they cannot afford or obtain the equipment needed for digital reception.
At the time of GMA's request, NTC Deputy Commissioner Alvin Blanco said implementation guidelines for the assistance program had yet to be finalized.
The NTC's latest order cited the need for further public information rather than the assistance program as the reason for extending the deadline.
The Philippines is implementing the analog shutdown in phases rather than nationwide at once.

After the Mega Manila transition, the government plans to assess implementation before expanding the switch-off to other regions in succeeding years, with a nationwide digital broadcasting ecosystem targeted by 2030.
